heading: Documentation
text: Run coding agents in a container on your computer. Choose what they can read and reach, then review the work they produce.

heading: The idea
text: An agent needs to edit files and run commands to finish a coding task. On your computer, those same permissions can let it read private keys, upload code or delete the wrong folder. co:op limits the files and network destinations it can reach. co:op runs the agent in a box: a disposable container with your project mounted inside. Your home folder, SSH keys, cloud credentials and other projects are not mounted into the box. Known secret files in the project, such as .env files and private keys, appear empty to the agent. The agent can edit the visible project files and run commands in the container. Interactive sessions, forks, loops and preset roles use the same container protections. One exception: an editor connected over ACP can act on your computer for the agent, with the editor's own permissions. See Editors.

heading: Install
text: co:op runs on macOS and Linux, on amd64 or arm64 machines. You need Git and Docker. The installer downloads a single executable; you do not need Go or a copy of the source: curl -fsSL https://coop.dryga.com/install.sh | sh The script puts coop in ~/.local/bin. If it finds Docker, it also builds the sandbox image and runs coop doctor to check it. If you install Docker later, run those two steps yourself: coop build --egress open && coop doctor Container runtimes, building from source and verifying a download

heading: Quickstart
text: For your first run, follow the general sandbox walkthrough, or choose the guide for your coding agent: Run Claude Code in a sandboxClaude sign-in, connectors and the container boundary. Run Codex CLI in a sandboxChatGPT device sign-in, API accounts and Codex settings. Run Gemini CLI in a sandboxAI Studio keys, Google routes and supported authentication. Run Grok CLI in a sandboxGrok device sign-in, account access and network rules. Sign in once, then run the setup and launch commands from your project directory: coop login claude# sign in, once per account coop init# set up the project coop claude# start the agent in the box For a new project, coop init creates settings and a task queue with filtered networking. It preserves existing project settings. coop claude starts Claude Code in the box. Arguments after the agent’s name go to the agent, so coop claude --continue resumes your last session. co:op handles a few options itself, including --peer and --egress. Put an option after -- to send it to the agent instead. For a bigger or riskier change, you don't have to work in your checkout at all. Write the work down as a task, and let a fork do it in its own copy while you keep working: coop tasks add "Add JSON output"# queue the work coop fork feature claude --loop# a fork works on it coop fork review feature# review it like a PR coop fork merge feature# then merge it Before you start the fork, fill in the generated task.md with the problem, what done means, the approach and the subtasks. More in Forks and The loop.

heading: Run an agent
text: coop claude is one way into the box. The other agents start the same way, and so do a plain shell and a single command when you want to work in the box yourself: coop claude# Claude Code coop codex# Codex, in the same box coop gemini# Gemini coop grok# Grok coop shell# a shell in the box coop run -- npm test# one command in the box Every agent starts with its permission prompts turned off, so it works through a task without stopping to ask at each step. Why permission prompts are off The container limits which files and network destinations the agent can access. Within those limits, it can work without asking you to approve each command. Review the files it changes before running them on your computer. Before the agent starts, co:op shows you what it set up: which secrets it hid, which account it signed in with and what the box can reach on the network. Accounts, models and presets

heading: The sandbox
text: The box is a disposable container with your repo mounted inside. Its mounts determine which host files the agent can access. co:op mounts your repo at the same path it has on your computer. The agent edits your real files, so changes appear in your editor as it works. The standard setup also mounts that repository’s agent settings and history, plus a shared dependency cache. It does not mount your other projects. Each repository keeps its own agent settings and conversations. The box cannot read other projects’ conversations. A helper outside the box authenticates provider requests, keeping reusable credentials away from the agent. The agent can change its local settings and history; review changes you do not trust before using them again. Your Git identity, not the box's The agent commits as you. co:op gives the box a trimmed Git config with your name and email, your global gitignore and commit.gpgsign=false, but never your signing key, so the box's commits are authored by you and left unsigned. If your global Git config has commit.gpgsign=true, co:op signs agent commits on your computer, where your key stays. It does this when an interactive run exits, after each coop loop cycle, and during coop fork merge. Editor sessions do not sign commits automatically. Run coop sign to sign the current branch’s unpushed commits. This lets agent work meet a protected main branch’s signature requirement. Files, images and services

heading: Hiding secrets
text: Your repo is in the box, and repos hold secrets of their own: .env files, private keys, live API tokens. co:op hides those by name before the agent starts, and coop check-secrets finds the ones hiding inside ordinary files. co:op covers known secret files with empty read-only files, and secret directories with empty read-only directories. These include .env, *.pem, *.tfvars, secrets/, .ssh and other common names. The agent can see the names but cannot read or change their contents. Templates ending in *.example, *.sample or *.template stay visible so the agent can understand your configuration. The built-in list can't know where your repo keeps its own secrets, like live keys in config/stripe.live.json. List those in a .coopignore file at the repo root, one pattern per line, and they're hidden the same way. Comments go on their own lines: .coopignore # a file name, hidden at any depth prod.yml # a path from the repo root config/stripe.live.json # a folder, hidden whole vault/ Use .coopignore to hide project files from the agent. .gitignore controls Git, not the box. An ignored file such as serviceAccount.json is still readable if no hiding rule covers it. Add private files to .coopignore. A token inside an ordinary source file remains readable. coop check-secrets scans files you would commit for known provider tokens and long random values assigned to secret-like names. It reports each match as file:line so you can inspect and remove it. Add --include-ignored to check files Git ignores too. The command fails if it finds a possible secret or cannot finish scanning, so you can use it before a run or in CI. If you have confirmed a finding is a false positive, record the exception in .coopsecretsignore. Everything about hiding secrets

heading: Networking
text: Filtered networking allows the box to reach its AI provider and the destinations you approve. Other connections are blocked. Visible files and prompts can still be sent to an allowed destination. coop init turns filtering on for a new project, with egress: filtered in .agent/project.yaml. The box can then reach its provider's own endpoints, like api.anthropic.com for Claude, and nothing more until you approve it. The block works on the network itself, not through a proxy setting, so curl, an SDK and any subprocess are blocked the same way. When the agent needs more, such as a documentation site, add a rule to the same file: .agent/project.yaml box: egress: filtered egress_rules: - to: {domain: "docs.example.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] A rule takes effect only after you approve it with coop approve in your terminal, so an agent can't widen its own access by editing the file. The coop net commands show what the box can reach, and what it tried: coop approve# approve the project's rules coop net# what a new run here can reach coop net inspect# a run's connections and blocks coop net blocked <host># how to allow a blocked host Besides filtered, a project can be open (everything) or offline (no network), and open needs your approval too. Filtering also protects API keys: if you sign in with one, the real key stays outside the box and the agent gets a stand-in that works only for that run. Before the first filtered run, co:op checks that Docker can enforce the rules. It repeats those checks when the saved results are no longer valid. Run coop net setup to check ahead of time. The networking guide explains the available rules and each provider’s access. Networking in full

heading: Prove it
text: coop doctor tests these protections. It starts a box, tries to break out of it, and shows the result of each check. The checks use a temporary project and test secrets, not your files or credentials. They test secret hiding, host access, privileges, offline networking, task and credential access, and what a fork contains: Run it after you install, after you update co:op and whenever you change your config. If a check fails, it tells you what to fix. The coop doctor command

heading: Toolchain and services
text: Build the language tools your project needs into its image, and configure databases as services. Later runs can reuse them instead of installing everything again. If your repo has an asdf .tool-versions file, coop init writes an .agent/Dockerfile to install those versions in the image. You can request this setup explicitly with coop init --stack asdf; it also requires that version file. Databases and caches run next to the box as project services, each in its own disposable container that the box reaches by name. They're opt-in: coop init asks, or you pass --services postgres,redis. From then on: coop up# start and wait until healthy coop claude# reach them by Compose name coop down# stop them, keep their data coop down --delete-volumes# also delete their data Services use the same secret-hiding rules as the box, and their published ports listen only on your computer. In filtered mode, the box can reach a service only after you approve a to: {service: "db"} rule. In filtered mode, those services run on a private network with no direct internet access. Their HTTPS requests pass through the filter. If you change a service’s definition, review and approve it again. coop up prints the service names from Compose when they are ready. If it cannot read the service list, it starts nothing and reports the problem. Agents can change data in services they can reach, so use disposable development databases. Deleting their volumes cannot be undone; co:op asks you to confirm first. coop update updates co:op and prepares the box for the project’s network mode. A filtered project, the default, keeps co:op’s pinned client base. Open and offline projects get fresh system packages. To update only the box, use coop update --box-only. Use coop build to rebuild from the pinned base. These commands keep the agent versions fixed to those checked for your co:op release. Toolchains, project images and services

heading: Credentials and failover
text: Each agent runs on an account, and a long run can hit its usage limit. If you sign in to more than one account, co:op switches to the next one instead of stopping. Each account you sign in to becomes a named credential: coop login claude@work# sign in to a work account coop login claude@personal# and a personal one coop credentials# list accounts and sign-ins When a loop hits a limit on one account, it moves to another and keeps going, and waits only when every account is at its limit. Limits are tracked per model and account, so claude:opus@personal stays usable while claude:opus@work waits for its reset. Switching loses no work, because the loop keeps its progress in the task queue and the repo. A loop uses all your signed-in accounts without any setup: a bare provider:model step in its target ladder covers every account, the default first. A pinned provider:model@account runs on just that one, and coop credentials <agent> <name> default chooses the account a plain coop <agent> uses. API keys To use an API key, put ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for Claude, OPENAI_API_KEY for Codex or GEMINI_API_KEY for Gemini in ~/.config/coop/agents/env. On Docker, these work with open or filtered networking. A helper keeps the real key outside the box. Subscription credentials stay outside too. Other Claude and Codex token variables, Vertex’s GOOGLE_API_KEY and Grok’s XAI_API_KEY are refused. See the credential reference for supported sign-in methods. A key in this file becomes the provider’s default credential. A bare KEY line reads the value from your shell and is skipped if unset. Later entries replace earlier ones. When you run a named account you signed in to, co:op leaves the environment key out of that run. This prevents the key from overriding the chosen account, even if you made that account the default. Check limits and usage coop usage shows account limits, reset times and an estimate of what the last 30 days of tokens would cost at API prices. Use coop usage codex@work for one account without changing your default. The estimate includes subscription use. It flags incomplete history, missing prices and editor history it cannot assign to an account. It excludes web and phone use, other machines and charges unrelated to tokens. Checking quota uses the selected account on the host and sends no model prompt. Several accounts and failover

heading: Pick the model
text: You choose the model separately from the account: for one run in the target, like claude:opus, or for good in a preset. coop claude:opus# one run on the big model coop claude:opus/xhigh# at extra-high reasoning effort coop claude:opus@work# on a specific account coop frontier# a preset's lead and roles coop models# the models each agent offers The model in the target overrides every default; see the full order. co:op passes the name to the provider’s CLI without validating it. A model works if that installed CLI supports it. An invalid name produces the provider’s error. Add reasoning effort after a slash in the target, as in claude:opus/xhigh or codex/high. The values are low, medium, high, xhigh and max; the provider decides which it supports. co:op passes the value to Claude’s --effort, Codex’s model_reasoning_effort or Grok’s --reasoning-effort without validating it. For supported Gemini models, it maps low and high to the model’s thinking setting. A thinking setting in your own Gemini config takes precedence. You can use model/effort, such as opus/high, in targets, preset fallback lists, .agent/loop.yaml and COOP_<AGENT>_MODEL. Everything about picking models

heading: Second opinions
text: Different models have different blind spots. For a hard call, the lead agent can ask another model for a second opinion, while it stays the only one changing your code. coop claude --peer codex --peer gemini# two models to ask coop acp claude --peer codex# from an editor Add --peer <agent> to an interactive run, loop, fork loop or ACP session. You can choose a peer’s model and effort, but not its account. co:op enables only the selected peers and keeps their reusable credentials outside the box. coop-consult asks them for read-only advice. The lead decides what to do, edits files, runs checks and commits. Why it stays simple The lead chooses when to ask a peer. Peers cannot edit the repository or ask other peers, so the lead remains responsible for the result. Everything about second opinions

heading: Presets
text: A preset keeps a whole team in one file: the lead, its fallback models and the roles it hands work to. Use one when a lead works with the same helpers every time. In the orchestrator pattern, a lead model plans the work and reviews the results while helpers handle specific roles. Each role is billed at its own model’s price. coop init installs workflow skills but does not create starter subagents. Define roles in .agent/presets/<name>/preset.yaml. Then use the preset name wherever you would choose an agent: coop <name>, coop loop <name>, coop acp <name> or a fork. coop presets init# write the starter "frontier" preset coop presets# list presets, with any errors coop loop frontier# run the loop with it The lead’s agent: setting accepts one target or an ordered list of fallbacks. The loop tries them in that order. A target such as provider:model uses all signed-in accounts; provider:model@account selects just one. Each role has a mode that determines how the lead calls it: Mode What it is native A subagent in the lead's session. co:op creates coop-<role> from the role's model and prompt, using the client's own format. Set subagent: to use one you already have. Every lead in the preset must use the role's provider. Otherwise co:op stops before launch and tells you which role to change. consult A read-only peer, asked with coop-consult <role>. It runs the role's target or ladder, with the role's prompt as its persona, and can't edit files. delegate A worker that can write, run with coop-delegate. It may edit the working tree but never commits; the lead reviews the diff, runs the checks and commits. It falls back to the next model only while the tree is unchanged. Here is a preset with one role in each mode: preset.yaml lead: agent: [claude:claude-opus-5-5, claude:claude-fable-5-1@work] roles: thinker: # thinks in the lead's session mode: native agent: claude:claude-fable-5-1 # a coop-thinker subagent prompt: roles/thinker.md critic: # read-only cross-vendor review mode: consult agent: [codex:gpt-6-astra, grok:grok-4.5] fast: # cheap work that edits files mode: delegate agent: [gemini:gemini-3.8-flash, codex:gpt-6-luna] What co:op generates from it co:op tells the lead which roles are available, when to use them and how to call them. It provides the coop-consult and coop-delegate helpers and creates each native coop-<role> subagent inside the box. These generated files do not change your repo. coop presets init creates editable starter prompts under roles/. A target on the command line, such as claude:opus@work, overrides the preset’s lead. Consult and delegate fallbacks skip providers you have not signed in to. co:op prepares access to each usable target while keeping reusable provider credentials outside the box. A consult replays its saved conversation when it switches targets. A delegate can switch only if the failed attempt left all files and Git history unchanged. Everything about presets

heading: Forks
text: A fork gives the agent its own copy of your repo. You review its work like a pull request and decide what to merge. A fork is a disposable local clone of your repo. Its origin points to the local project, not a hosted repository. The clone starts from committed source, so uncommitted, Git-ignored secrets do not come along. Secrets already in Git history can remain. When to reach for a fork Use a fork to work on a larger change or try several approaches while keeping your original checkout available. Review the result before merging it. Ordinary forks still share some Git storage and trust the agent with Git metadata; the isolated mode described in the fork reference provides stronger separation. Work in the fork, review it, then merge. coop fork review shows the commits and changed files. During merge, co:op rebases the work onto your current branch for a linear history. This happens on your computer, where co:op can sign the commits with your key. If you configure a project check, co:op runs it before merging changes into your branch. Set gate: in .agent/project.yaml, for example gate: make check. The line created by coop init is commented out until you enable it. The check runs in the box on the rebased code. If it fails, nothing is merged and your branch stays unchanged. Use coop fork review --gate to run it before merging. The merge also stops on anything risky coming in: content that looks like a secret, files over 5 MB, and files that run on your computer, like Git hooks, .envrc, editor and agent settings, Compose files, Dockerfiles, CI config and new npm install scripts. Review them, then merge with --force; the checks still run. With --loop, a fork works through tasks on its own: it takes them from your project's .agent/tasks/ queue one at a time, they stay in progress while you review the fork, and merging it completes them. Forks and review

heading: The loop
text: The overnight task queue walkthrough takes you through your first unattended run, including how to stop, resume and review the work. Most agent work is a queue of small, well-defined tasks. coop loop works through the queue on its own, overnight and through usage limits. The loop starts a fresh agent session for each task. The agent reads the task, does the work, runs your checks and commits the result. The loop moves on until no eligible task remains or it reaches --max-tasks. --max-tasks pauses before final review and exits 0 on a successful pause. Run the same command without the limit to finish the review; a pause is not verified completion. Each task is a folder under .agent/tasks/, and the folder it sits in is its state. Fill in each generated task.md before you start, so the agent knows what done means: coop tasks add "Fix the flaky test"# a folder per task coop loop claude# work the queue coop loop claude --peer codex# with a peer to ask In a monorepo, list the members under subprojects: in a committed .agent/project.yaml, and one loop works every member's queue. While the loop works, coop tasks watch shows the live board, including any running forks. For a status line in your shell prompt or tmux, coop prompt prints the repo's state on one line (task counts, and fork or loop activity); it only reads, so it's safe on every redraw. Final review When the queue is empty, a final review compares the completed tasks with their requirements and Git history. It reopens unfinished work, and the loop works those tasks again. By default, review gets three to five rounds, depending on how much the run completed. Tasks still needing work then wait for your decision. Add project-specific review requirements under signoff.prompt in .agent/loop.yaml, such as updating the changelog or regenerating docs. A task that fails one is reopened. Usage limits When the agent hits a usage limit, the loop reads the reset time from the agent's output and waits. If you've signed in to another account, it switches to that account and keeps going. Decisions When the agent needs your decision, it moves the task to 50_blocked/ and writes a decision.md with the question, options and recommendation. The loop continues with other tasks. When nothing else can run, it exits with status 3 to report that a decision is needed. Run coop tasks decisions -i to answer the questions and unblock their tasks, then run coop loop again. Use --preflight to unblock tasks you have already answered. To postpone one, run coop tasks park <id> or press :b in the decision walkthrough. It keeps the question in the backlog; coop backlog promote returns it to the queue. Good fits Small refactors, moving one pattern across dozens of files, a test-coverage or lint list, or the Friday cleanup queue you'd never get to by hand: any work made of many small, checkable steps. The .agent/ folder Everything the loop works from lives in the .agent/ folder that coop init creates. It's the same for every agent, and the agent reads it on every start and after each compaction. The work queue (tasks/ and the backlog) is local working state that Git ignores; the knowledge and settings beside it are committed, so they travel with the project. Path What it's for tasks/ The work queue: a folder per task under 00_todo/, 10_in_progress/, 50_blocked/ and 99_done/. The folder a task sits in is its state; the numbers sort ls in order, and coop tasks shows the plain names. Local working state. the backlog Work for later, as task folders in tasks/xx_backlog/ (coop backlog). Loops never pick it up; coop backlog promote <id> moves an item into 00_todo/ when it's ready. kb/ The knowledge base: maps of each part of the code, and the traps and gotchas the code doesn't show. Agents keep it current as they work. kb/rules/ Your taste, as rules: each correction becomes a "do X, not Y" card. skills/ The workflow skills (spec, work, sweep, investigate, review-board, verify-api); each agent's own folder links to them. presets/ Team recipes: a lead and its roles, like thinker, critic and fast. See Presets. project.yaml Project settings: a monorepo's members, the dev server ports co:op publishes, the box's network setting, and the checks a fork must pass to merge. loop.yaml The stages of coop loop (preflight, work, between, verify and signoff), and the models and prompts they use. Task queues and loops

heading: Parallel forks
text: One loop is one agent working one queue. To get through a queue faster, run several forks at once, each taking the next task from the same queue. Start one fork per agent, with --loop -d so it works in the background. co:op hands each fork one task at a time from the shared .agent/tasks/ queue, so no two forks do the same work: coop fork api frontier --loop -d# the frontier team coop fork web codex@work --loop -d# one on Codex coop fork deps gemini --loop -d# and one on Gemini coop tasks watch# every fork's tasks coop fork merge --all# merge them all Each fork names a target or a preset, whose lead ladder its loop rotates through; give forks that run at once different accounts, so they don't share one limit. coop fork ls shows each fork's state, and coop fork logs <name> -f its output. Why run parallel forks When agents write code quickly, reviewing it takes most of your time. Run the agents in parallel and review their forks in batches. Everything about parallel forks

heading: Evaluations
text: Use evaluations to compare models, presets or loop recipes on repeatable tasks. A separate verifier grades the finished work; the model does not grade itself. Start with a free preview The shipped core suite has three small coding tasks. This command launches no container or provider and spends nothing: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m --dry-run A real run needs a sign-in (coop login codex), a working container runtime and a current co:op box image. If the image is missing, run coop build --egress open from a folder without a project Dockerfile. The build may download dependencies. Then run the suite and read the result: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m# run it for real coop eval inspect# read the result A real run uses your provider account and may spend credits, and a preview checks only the plan, not your credentials or whether the runtime is ready. --timeout is a total time limit, not a money cap; each case also has its own timeout. More configurations or repetitions mean more paid work. Compare before and after To check whether a change helped: Run a suite and inspect the result. Change your model, preset, loop recipe or co:op build, then run the same suite with the same number of repetitions. Use coop eval runs to find the two run IDs, then coop eval compare <before-id> <after-id>. The argument order decides which run is the baseline. Inspect and compare show each configuration's short fingerprint and co:op build. Choose a suite core: three single-agent tasks. Use provider targets, such as codex:gpt-6.1-sol/xhigh, not presets. queue: ten tasks through the real loop, including review and signoff. Use targets or presets, and allow hours, not minutes. For your frontier preset, try coop eval run queue frontier --timeout 2h. Add --loop-config .agent/loop.yaml to test your recipe. Your own: coop eval init ./evals/my-suite creates a working example. Edit suite.yaml, files/greeting/ and the separate verifiers/greeting/verify.sh. The verifier's README explains grading. An example in the source tree: examples/evals/maintenance/ has shell, Python and Node maintenance loops. Its checks confirm that unfinished starting versions fail and completed reference versions pass. It demonstrates a custom comparison, not an official benchmark or a shipped starter. Each target after the suite is a separate configuration, not a fallback. --repeat 3 runs every case three times, and --jobs 2 allows two agent trials at once, though each loop trial works its tasks in order. coop help eval run lists every option. Understand failures before spending again When a run doesn't go as hoped, coop eval inspect shows the trials that didn't pass, their recorded causes, and where to find saved diagnostics and kept workspaces; add a run ID to read an older run. Each trial ends in one of these states: failed: the independent verifier rejected the work. error: running or grading couldn't produce a verdict. A provider's quota refusal is not a model-quality failure. timed_out or pending: the trial ran out of time or didn't start. Grading is incomplete. Incomplete grading means the comparison has no definitive winner. For a sign-in or quota refusal, check coop credentials <agent>. For a timeout, check the case’s suite.yaml limit and the run’s --timeout. A run with no final summary may still be running or may have been interrupted. You can inspect it, but cannot compare or resume it. Trying again starts a new paid run. Review provider output for private data before sharing it. Each trial has a private workspace without the source repository’s Git history. The model cannot read the hidden verifier. That verifier runs afterward in a separate container with no credentials or network access. Trials exclude your MCP servers. co:op turns off native web search and fetch for the candidate and its managed peers and delegates, while leaving terminal and file tools available. This relies on the client following the setting; it is not a firewall that inspects each request. Regular runs keep their normal web tools. Results describe the tested workload, not provider performance in general. Code size can help you review a change, but is not a quality score. Compare two runs Run the same tasks before and after your change, with the same number of repeats. Test one model or preset configuration in each run. compare checks that the saved workloads match. If it cannot match the runs, it shows their results separately. It also reports missing or damaged records. The report shows what changed; you decide whether the result is useful. The evaluation guide explains how the results are compared. Evaluations in full

heading: Editors
text: To steer the agent from your editor instead of a terminal, co:op serves it over ACP, the Agent Client Protocol. Any editor that supports ACP can then drive the agent in the box. coop acp [target|preset] speaks ACP over stdio, so you add co:op as a custom agent in an editor that supports the protocol. Zed supports it today, and others are adding it. The setup is the same everywhere, with one entry for each target or preset you use; in Zed's settings.json, for example: Zed settings.json { "agent_servers": { "coop": { "type": "custom", "command": "coop", // one target; pin it like "claude:opus/xhigh@work" "args": ["acp", "claude"] }, "coop · second opinion": { "type": "custom", "command": "coop", // a named peer; the target pins the lead's model "args": ["acp", "claude:opus/xhigh", "--peer", "codex"] } } } Pin the model, reasoning effort and account in co:op's target inside args (provider[:model][/effort][@account]), not in the editor's own options. The toolbar menus start on that target, and you can still switch them from there. co:op sits between the editor and the agent, so in the editor: A plain session's toolbar has Preset, Provider and Account menus; a session running a preset keeps the Preset menu. Switching accounts, or between models of one provider, keeps the conversation. Switching providers starts a new session and carries over the messages and a one-line note for each tool call, as closely as it can. At a usage limit, co:op moves to your next signed-in account and sends your prompt again, or waits for the nearest reset if every account is at its limit. A box restart (coop build, coop update or running out of memory) replays the handshake, so your editor stays connected. The agent’s permission prompts stay off, just as in a terminal run. ACP also lets it ask your editor to read files, write files or run commands on your computer. A filtered session refuses these requests. An open or offline session forwards them, and the editor controls their permissions. Terminal and loop runs do not have this editor channel. See the ACP security note before connecting an editor. To open a dev server from the box in your browser, list its port under serve: in a committed .agent/project.yaml and bind the server to 0.0.0.0 inside the box. The thread then shows the address the box publishes it on, http://localhost:<port>. Desktop apps don't always get your shell's PATH. If your editor can't find coop, use the full path from command -v coop as the command. Editors and MCP

heading: MCP and remote sessions
text: Agents also use MCP servers, and co:op itself can run as a worker for another system. Define MCP servers once, outside your repo, and co:op makes them available to supported agents, within the project's network setting, while keeping eligible HTTP tokens outside the box. The MCP guide covers local commands, remote HTTP servers, tokens and network settings. As a remote worker, co:op connects out over TLS to a compatible controller, which supplies each job's repository, model targets, network access and limits; co:op fetches the code and runs the model. The worker keeps its private state and model credentials on its own machine, and needs Git, Git LFS and a supported container runtime: coop sessions connect --controller <url> --token-file <path> The worker connector guide has the details. The worker API

heading: Configuration
text: co:op works with its defaults. These are the settings you're most likely to change. Set them as environment variables or in ~/.config/coop/coop.conf; the last three work only as environment variables. Variable What it does COOP_GATE Overrides the project’s gate: setting: the check command run inside the box, such as make check. COOP_EGRESS filtered, the default, lets the box reach only its AI provider and the destinations you approve. open leaves the network open. offline starts a box without network access, including access to the model. Changing this setting does not disconnect an already-running box. COOP_RUNTIME Force docker or container instead of detecting one (detection prefers Docker). COOP_MEMORY, COOP_CPUS Cap the box's memory and CPUs, like 4g and 2. COOP_<AGENT>_MODEL An agent's default model everywhere it runs, like COOP_CLAUDE_MODEL=opus. COOP_CAFFEINATE On by default: while a loop runs, macOS caffeinate keeps the machine from sleeping. Set 0 to turn it off. COOP_HOMES On by default: each selected agent’s repository settings and history are mounted into the box. COOP_HOMES=0 keeps them out, so an agent can't read your agents' settings; presets and peers need them, so those runs stop with an error. COOP_SPINNER On by default: the live spinners animate. Set 0 or false to freeze the spinners and stop the loop's fast redraws while debugging or recording. COOP_CONF Moves the coop.conf file co:op reads its COOP_* defaults from. NO_COLOR Set to any value to turn off color everywhere (no-color.org). On Docker, the box also runs with every Linux capability dropped, no-new-privileges and a process limit. The configuration reference lists every variable. Every setting

heading: Troubleshooting
text: The problems people hit most, and the quickest fix for each. Symptom Fix "no container runtime found" Install Docker for online provider runs, then run coop build --egress open && coop doctor. To pick it explicitly, set COOP_RUNTIME=docker. Apple container supports raw uncredentialed open-network workloads only. "image … not built" Run the coop build command the message names: --egress open, or --egress filtered for a project with filtered networking. Sign-in hangs, or "usage limit reached" Run coop login <agent> again. A subscription limit resets on a schedule, and a loop waits for it on its own. An editor session moves to your next signed-in account and sends your prompt again. Gemini says its Google sign-in client is no longer supported Run host coop login gemini and paste an AI Studio API key from the link it shows. Existing importable plain OAuth accounts also work through the broker; encrypted-only caches cannot be imported. Vertex GOOGLE_API_KEY is refused in every network mode. A background loop won't stop Watch it with coop fork logs <name> -f, and stop it with coop fork stop <name>. A secret is still visible Add its path to .coopignore. coop check-secrets finds secrets hiding inside files. "permission denied" writing ~/.cache or build caches Check who owns the cache volume: coop-cache for the default user, or coop-cache-<uid>-<gid> on Linux (see id -u and id -g). If it has the wrong owner, save anything useful, remove only that idle volume, then run coop build. Never loosen your credential folder's permissions. go or gofmt: "No version is set for command go" The box installs toolchains from .tool-versions with asdf. Add the golang version there. A filtered box installs it only at build time, so run coop build after. COOP_NO_ASDF=1 turns this off. A pinned tool is installed but "not found" in a login shell A login shell (sh -lc, bash -l) reads /etc/profile, which resets PATH and drops asdf's shims. The box adds them back with an /etc/profile.d file; rebuild an older box with coop build to get it. "box image is stale … run 'coop build --egress open'" You changed .agent/Dockerfile or .tool-versions since the image was built. Run coop build --egress open, and the warning goes away. A merge refuses Commit or stash a dirty tree first. If the policy flagged a secret or a large file, review it, then pass --force. Without a terminal, pass --yes. If the gate failed on the rebased tree, your branch is untouched: fix the fork and run the merge again. Zed can't find the agent Zed has to launch coop from a shell where it's on PATH (the installer puts it in ~/.local/bin). Give Zed the full path if needed, and check that coop acp runs in a terminal first. An editor session misbehaves Turn on tracing: set COOP_ACP_TRACE=1 in the agent server's env, or touch ~/.config/coop/acp-debug, which also works on a server that's already running. co:op writes the editor and box traffic to ~/.local/state/coop/acp-trace-<pid>.log, which is size-bounded and pruned. It holds prompts and file contents, so treat it as sensitive. A loop's live view shows provider activity wrong Run the loop with COOP_STREAM_TRACE=1. Each attempt writes the raw JSON lines and co:op's rendered lines under .agent/runs/<run>.streams/. They may hold prompts, tool inputs and model output, so treat them as sensitive. A scaffolded Postgres 18 db exits 1 on coop up Postgres 18 and later refuses a data mount at /var/lib/postgresql/data. In .agent/compose.yml, move the mount up to /var/lib/postgresql. The command reference lists every command's flags, and coop help (or coop <command> --help) is the live reference. Stuck on something that isn't covered? Open an issue. Every command

heading: Install
text: Install co:op, keep it up to date, and verify a download yourself. co:op runs on macOS and Linux, on amd64 or arm64, with Git and Docker: curl -fsSL https://coop.dryga.com/install.sh | sh The script puts coop in ~/.local/bin. It needs curl, tar, and sha256sum or shasum. If Docker is available, it also builds the box image and runs coop doctor. If not, install Docker and run those yourself: coop build --egress open && coop doctor To change what the script does, set these before sh, as in curl -fsSL https://coop.dryga.com/install.sh | COOP_NO_BUILD=1 sh: Variable What it does COOP_VERSION Install this release tag instead of the latest one. COOP_BIN_DIR Install into this folder instead of ~/.local/bin. COOP_NO_BUILD=1 Skip building the box image.

heading: Container runtimes
text: Online providers need Docker, which supports the helper that keeps provider credentials outside the box. Apple container on macOS 26+ can run commands with open networking and no credentials. If both are installed, co:op chooses Docker.

heading: Build from source
text: git clone https://github.com/AndrewDryga/coop && cd coop && make install

heading: Update
text: coop update updates the binary, then prepares the image for this project's network mode. Upgrading lists what to change when a new version needs it.

heading: Verifying a download
text: install.sh comes from the main branch, served by GitHub Pages at coop.dryga.com. You can also fetch it from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AndrewDryga/coop/main/install.sh. The script checks the archive against the release's checksums.txt with sha256sum or shasum, and stops if the file or the tool is missing. If cosign is installed, it also verifies the release signature, which proves checksums.txt came from the release workflow for that tag. To verify by hand before you run anything, download the release files. Set VER to a tag from the releases page, and change darwin_arm64 for another platform: VER=vX.Y.Z ASSET="coop_${VER#v}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz" base="https://github.com/AndrewDryga/coop/releases/download/$VER" curl -fsSLO "$base/$ASSET" curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt" curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt.bundle" # 1. checksums.txt is signed by the release workflow (keyless Sigstore): cosign verify-blob checksums.txt \ --bundle checksums.txt.bundle \ --certificate-identity "https://github.com/AndrewDryga/coop/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$VER" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com # 2. the archive matches the now-trusted checksum (Linux: sha256sum -c -): awk -v f="$ASSET" '$2==f{print $1" "f}' checksums.txt | shasum -a 256 -c -

heading: Uninstall
text: Quit editor sessions, loops and other coop commands first. Then, in each project: Merge or save any fork you still need. coop fork ls lists them, and their folders sit next to the project in <project>-forks/. If the project has services, run coop down. Add --delete-volumes to also delete their data, such as a database. Remove co:op's containers, images and volumes from Docker. The volumes hold caches and any service data coop down kept, in volumes named coop-<project>-<id>_<name>. Each ls shows what the next command removes, so check it first: docker ps -a --filter label=coop docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq --filter label=coop) docker image ls --filter reference='coop-*' docker image rm $(docker image ls --filter reference='coop-*' --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}') docker volume ls --filter name=^coop- docker volume rm $(docker volume ls -q --filter name=^coop-) Removing an image by name keeps it if another tag still uses it. Remove the binary and this machine's records: run history, network approvals and editor sessions. Use your COOP_BIN_DIR if you installed elsewhere, or command -v coop to find the binary. rm -f ~/.local/bin/coop rm -rf ~/.local/state/coop "${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/coop" In each project you approved, delete the hidden approval file. Without the records above, a later install refuses to run there until it is gone: rm -f .coop-network-approval The last step deletes your settings and every account you signed in to with coop login, along with the API keys in agents/env, your presets and MCP servers. If the folder syncs through Dropbox or another service, it disappears from your other machines too. Copy anything you want to keep, then: rm -rf "${COOP_HOME:-${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/coop}" Your projects keep their .agent/ folder and the instruction files coop init added, which are yours to keep or delete. Also remove any coop completion line from your shell startup file and any editor setting that runs coop acp.

heading: Run Claude Code or Codex in a sandbox
text: Set up co:op, run one small task, and review the changes. Before you start macOS or Linux, with Git installed and Docker running A Claude Code or Codex account A project you can build and test, with at least one Git commit

heading: Install co:op and sign in
text: co:op runs your coding agent in a disposable container on your computer. You will use Docker and a terminal for this walkthrough. The agent edits the project you start it from, so choose a checkout where you can review its changes. Host terminal curl -fsSL https://coop.dryga.com/install.sh | sh The installer runs a downloaded script. For checksums and release verification, use the install page. coop version coop login claude Sign in to Claude Code. You keep the same models and subscription limits as in Claude Code. Using Codex instead? Sign in with this command, then use coop codex in step 5. The project, file and network checks are the same. coop login codex Before you continue coop version prints the installed version, Docker is running, and sign-in has completed for your chosen provider.

heading: Initialize the checkout you will use
text: In your terminal, change into the root of your Git project. Check for existing work, then initialize co:op there. Host terminal · project root git status --short coop init Review or commit any changes you already have so you can tell them apart from the agent’s work. To work in a separate copy, follow the fork workflow before starting the agent. coop init may ask which languages and services this project uses. Press Enter to skip a question. A new project uses filtered networking. co:op keeps any existing project settings, so read .agent/project.yaml and the generated instructions to check how your project is configured. Before you continue You know which checkout will change, and you have reviewed its co:op configuration. A disposable container does not undo edits to the mounted project.

heading: Decide what the agent can read
text: co:op hides common secret files, including environment files and private keys, from the container. Check for other private data in your project, including files ignored by Git. Host terminal · project root coop check-secrets --include-ignored Inspect every reported file and line. Remove real credentials from files you intend to commit, fix unreadable files, and rerun the scan. The command returns a nonzero status if it finds a problem or cannot finish the scan. The scanner cannot recognize every secret. Check for sensitive business data yourself and decide what the agent needs to read. Add any other private paths to your existing .coopignore. This example hides a notes directory and a customer export: .coopignore · example additions private-notes/ customer-export.csv .coopignore hides files when the agent starts. Git ignore rules do not. Hiding a file does not remove it from Git or dismiss a scanner finding. Restart the agent after changing which files should be hidden. If you have checked a finding and confirmed it is a false positive, add the exact entry and reason the scanner requests to .coopsecretsignore. The boundary to remember Visible project files and anything you put in a prompt may be sent to the allowed AI provider. Include only the data this task needs.

heading: Check the network and the sandbox
text: Check what a new run can reach before starting the agent. Host terminal · project root coop net For this walkthrough, use filtered access. The agent should reach only its provider and the destinations you approved. If coop net shows open access or an unfamiliar rule, check the networking configuration before starting. If the report says new runs need your approval, run coop approve on the host and review the requested access. Approve only the destinations you need. A new filtered project with no extra rules needs no approval. If your project has an .agent/Dockerfile, review it and the files it copies, then build the image before launching the agent: Host terminal · project root · when using a project image coop build The run’s filtered network rules do not apply during this build. If you change the Dockerfile or its inputs later, rebuild and restart the agent. Now run co:op’s isolation checks: Host terminal · project root coop doctor Read the full report, including checks it could not run. Fix failed checks and follow any setup instructions before continuing. A successful exit alone does not mean every check ran. These checks also do not verify your project’s secrets, dependencies or tests. A dependency or documentation site is blocked On the host, run coop net blocked <host> with the exact hostname that was blocked. Read the proposed rule and add the access you need to .agent/project.yaml. Review it with coop approve, then exit and restart the terminal agent session to use the new access. The networking reference explains rule syntax and approval. Before you continue You have reviewed the network access and the isolation report, and resolved any failures or setup problems.

heading: Start with a task you can inspect
text: Launch the provider you signed in to. On the first filtered run, co:op prepares its own images and checks that Docker can enforce the network rules. It starts the agent only if those checks pass. Host terminal · the same project root coop_review_base=$(git rev-parse HEAD) coop claude The first command saves the starting commit in your host shell. If it fails, stop and fix the problem before starting the agent. Keep this terminal open for the final review. If you use another terminal, find that original commit before comparing changes. Comparing with the latest commit could miss work the agent has already committed. For Codex, run coop codex instead. A useful first prompt asks the agent to understand the project before changing it: Example prompt · inside the agent Read AGENTS.md and find the command for the project’s focused tests. Explain which files and services the check needs. Do not edit files or install dependencies yet. If anything is missing or blocked, report it and wait. Check its answer against the repository. Then ask for one small change, tell it which check to run, and ask it to stop when it can explain what changed and whether the check passed. If a check needs a tool or service missing from the container, follow the project image or services documentation to set it up before expanding the task. Filtered runs do not install your project’s build tools automatically. After setting up the tools and services, have the agent run your project’s actual check in the container. Fix any remaining setup problems before attempting an unattended run. Exit the agent with its normal quit command. Back in the same host terminal, inspect new files, commits, and the complete tracked diff from the starting commit: git status --short git log --oneline "$coop_review_base"..HEAD git diff "$coop_review_base" The diff shows all tracked changes since the starting commit, including work the agent staged or committed. Open any untracked files separately; their contents are not in this diff. Run the relevant project checks yourself and try the behavior you asked the agent to change. Before you continue You have reviewed every changed file and can explain the result. The relevant project checks pass when you run them yourself.

heading: Build on a verified first run
text: Want instructions for your agent? Choose Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI or Grok CLI. Keep the next task small until the project builds and tests reliably inside the container. For a queue that can continue without your supervision, use the overnight walkthrough. Other runtimes and editor sessions Use Docker for the provider sessions in this guide. It supports the helper that keeps your provider credentials outside the container. Apple container can run commands with open networking and no credentials, but cannot replace Docker for this setup. An agent connected through ACP can ask your editor to read files or run commands on your computer. The editor controls that access. Read the editor documentation before using it.

heading: Run Claude Code in a sandbox
text: Run Claude Code on your project with secrets hidden and network access under your control. This walkthrough takes you from setup to a working sandbox, with checks to see how it protects your files and connections.

heading: Before you start
text: You’ll need: A Mac or Linux computer with Git installed and Docker running A Claude account with Claude Code access

heading: Why use a sandbox?
text: Coding agents run commands, install packages, and change files. A mistake can affect more than the project you’re working on. An attacker can also hide instructions in content the agent reads, tricking it into running harmful commands. This is called prompt injection. A sandbox limits what the agent can access and how much damage it can do if something goes wrong. You can give it room to work without giving it access to everything. co:op runs Claude Code in a Docker container on your computer: File access is limited to the project and folders you share. Secret files appear empty or cannot be read. Networking is restricted to the provider and allowed services and websites. Your provider API key or sign-in token is not mounted into the container. Claude Code can still edit the files it can see and send their contents to Anthropic. Its work counts toward your subscription limits.

heading: Install co:op and sign in
text: curl -fsSL https://coop.dryga.com/install.sh | sh If the installer asks you to update your PATH, run the command it prints. Then check the version: coop version The installer runs a downloaded script. Check the install page for release verification. Next, sign in: coop login claude Follow the Claude sign-in instructions shown in your terminal. co:op uses the models and usage limits included in your Claude subscription. Already use Claude Code? co:op keeps separate Claude history and settings for each project. Inside the container, Claude reads ~/.claude/settings.json. See where agent settings live before changing them. Using a custom image? Use co:op’s standard image for this walkthrough. It includes node, curl and Git, which the examples need. A custom image may not include them.

heading: Create a test project
text: To try co:op, run these commands to create a test project. Use the same terminal window throughout the walkthrough: coop_demo_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/coop-sandbox-demo.XXXXXX") && cd "$coop_demo_dir" && git init && printf '%s\n' '# co:op sandbox demo' > README.md && git add README.md && git -c user.name='Sandbox demo' \ -c user.email='sandbox-demo@example.invalid' \ -c commit.gpgsign=false \ commit -m 'Create sandbox demo' && coop init coop init asks which languages and services this project uses. Press Enter at both questions to skip them. It also sets filtered networking for this new project. Create a file with a fake secret: (umask 077; set -C; printf '%s\n' 'COOP_DEMO_VALUE=not-a-real-secret' > .env.coop-demo) && wc -c < .env.coop-demo We’ll use this fake secret to check that co:op hides it from the agent.

heading: Start Claude Code
text: Run this command to check your setup: coop doctor Start Claude Code: coop_review_base=$(git rev-parse HEAD) && coop claude --egress filtered The first command saves the starting commit ID so you can review all changes later. On the first filtered launch, co:op also checks that Docker can enforce its network rules. Claude Code’s header may say Claude API. If you signed in with coop login claude, that is only its label, and your work still counts toward your subscription. Can I use another container runtime? This sign-in setup requires Docker with filtered networking. Host networking and Apple’s container runtime are not supported. Why the agent runs without approval prompts Claude Code has a built-in sandbox for its Bash tool. Here, co:op’s Docker container limits its file and network access. co:op starts Claude with --dangerously-skip-permissions inside the container. Claude can work without asking permission for every command, within the file and network access you allow. The agent can also read or change this project’s saved history and settings.

heading: Verify how co:op hides secrets
text: In Claude Code, run this command. The ! runs it directly in the sandbox: ! wc -c README.md .env.coop-demo macOS Linux The sandbox can read README.md, but co:op blocks access to the secret or shows it as an empty file. If you ask Claude to run the command itself, Claude refuses. coop init adds a rule for .env files to the project’s Claude Code settings, and Claude applies it before the command starts. The ! skips that rule, so this result comes from co:op. Files matching .env.* are protected automatically. To hide other files or folders, add them to .coopignore. To scan project files for credentials, open a second terminal in the demo folder and run: coop check-secrets --include-ignored

heading: Verify that Claude can’t read your login credentials
text: To keep Claude from reading or leaking your login credentials, co:op gives it placeholders and adds the real credentials outside the sandbox when forwarding requests to Anthropic. Ask Claude to run this script to check what it received: node <<'JS' const fs = require('node:fs'); const path = require('node:path'); try { if (process.env.COOP_BOX !== '1') throw new Error(); const marker = 'coop-native-claude-v1'; const auth = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync( path.join(require('node:os').homedir(), '.claude/.credentials.json'), 'utf8')); const oauth = auth.claudeAiOauth || {}; if ((process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN ?? marker) !== marker || oauth.accessToken !== marker || oauth.refreshToken || process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY || process.env.ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN) { throw new Error(); } console.log('PASS: the Claude login file holds a public stand-in, with no refresh token'); } catch { console.error('FAIL: the expected Claude credential setup was not verified'); process.exitCode = 1; } JS If the check fails, investigate without printing credentials or pasting them into a prompt. Commands such as env, printenv and cat can expose them.

heading: See what the agent can connect to
text: Leave the agent running. In another terminal, open the demo project folder and run: coop net coop net check https://example.com coop net check checks the rules without visiting the website. In this new project, example.com should be blocked. If it is allowed, check that you’re in the demo folder. By default, restricted networking lets Claude reach Anthropic’s services to sign in and use your account. You can allow more websites later. MCP servers connected through Claude.ai remain available to Claude Code. To add local MCP servers, follow the MCP setup guide.

heading: Watch a website get blocked
text: Back in the agent session, ask it to visit example.com: curl --noproxy '*' --fail --silent --show-error \ --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 \ --output /dev/null --write-out 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \ https://example.com/ The request should fail, but an error alone does not tell you why. Quit Claude Code, then list its network sessions: coop net runs Find the session you just closed by its start time. Here, its run ID is c4f50b50. Replace that ID with yours in the command below to see why the request was blocked: coop net blocked example.com --run c4f50b50

heading: Allow just one website
text: In the demo’s .agent/project.yaml, add this rule under the existing box entry. Keep the other settings: .agent/project.yaml · example.com rule box: egress: filtered egress_rules: - to: {domain: "example.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] coop approve coop net check https://example.com Approve only the new rule for example.com on TLS port 443. It allows this website, not its subdomains or other ports. The check should now say it is allowed. coop claude --egress filtered The new Claude Code session uses the updated rules. A session already running would keep the old ones. Ask the agent to try the request again: curl --noproxy '*' --fail --silent --show-error \ --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 \ --output /dev/null --write-out 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \ https://example.com/ If it still fails, check the new run’s network receipt for the reason. Leave filtered networking on. Now give the agent a small task: Example prompt Add one sentence to README.md explaining that this is a sandbox demo. Run git diff --check and show its exit status. Do not install dependencies or commit the change. Stop after showing the diff. Check the diff and command output, then quit Claude Code so co:op can finish recording the session’s network activity.

heading: Read the network receipt
text: List the sessions again to find the one where you allowed example.com: coop net runs Here, the session where you allowed example.com is 5ffed706, the newer one. Replace it with your run ID below to inspect its traffic: coop net inspect 5ffed706 The first session showed example.com blocked. This one shows a connection to example.com:443. For the full record, including whether the session and cleanup finished, use JSON: coop net inspect 5ffed706 --json The values shown above mean the run ended, its network record is complete, and cleanup finished. Follow up on any warnings. UNKNOWN means co:op could not measure something. It does not mean zero. To export the receipt: coop net export 5ffed706 What does the export include? coop net inspect … --json puts these fields under receipt. In an export, they are at the top level. Exports hide remote names and addresses by default. Add --include-addresses to include them, and review the file before sharing it. The digest is a checksum, not a signature. See what the network record measures.

heading: Review changes and fix problems
text: Back in the original terminal where you started the agent, review what the agent changed: git status --short && git log --oneline "$coop_review_base"..HEAD && git diff "$coop_review_base" git diff --check "$coop_review_base" && printf 'Diff check passed\n' This compares the project with the commit saved before the agent started, including changes it staged or committed. Open any untracked files separately. Git does not include their contents in the diff. Claude sign-in expired or the account is wrong Exit Claude, run coop login claude and sign in with the right account. Then start a new session. Use co:op’s login command rather than Claude’s login or logout commands inside the container. If you use API billing instead, co:op supports ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Follow the API-key setup. ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN are not supported. A dependency or documentation request is blocked Run coop net blocked <host> in your terminal, replacing <host> with the blocked hostname. Add the access you need to .agent/project.yaml, then run coop approve. Restart the agent to use the new rules. The networking guide explains the rules. If Docker or a sandbox check fails, fix the reported problem before trying again with filtered networking. Ready to use your own project? Follow the general sandbox walkthrough to protect its secrets, set up its tools and approve its network access. Each project needs its own approval. Review and test the agent’s changes before keeping them. For longer jobs, the overnight walkthrough shows how to run a task queue. You can delete the test project at $coop_demo_dir when you’re finished. This does not sign you out. Using another coding agent? Run Codex CLI in a sandboxChatGPT device sign-in, API accounts and Codex settings. Run Gemini CLI in a sandboxAI Studio keys, Google routes and supported authentication. Run Grok CLI in a sandboxGrok device sign-in, account access and network rules.

heading: Run Codex CLI in a sandbox
text: Run Codex CLI in a local Docker sandbox with filtered network access and a clear diff to review.

heading: Before you start
text: You’ll need: A Mac or Linux computer with Git installed and Docker running A ChatGPT account with Codex access

heading: Why use a sandbox?
text: Coding agents run commands, install packages, and change files. A mistake can affect more than the project you’re working on. An attacker can also hide instructions in content the agent reads, tricking it into running harmful commands. This is called prompt injection. A sandbox limits what the agent can access and how much damage it can do if something goes wrong. You can give it room to work without giving it access to everything. co:op runs Codex CLI in a Docker container on your computer: File access is limited to the project and folders you share. Secret files appear empty or cannot be read. Networking is restricted to the provider and allowed services and websites. Your provider API key or sign-in token is not mounted into the container. Codex can still edit the files it can see and send their contents to OpenAI. Its work counts toward your ChatGPT subscription limits.

heading: Install co:op and sign in
text: curl -fsSL https://coop.dryga.com/install.sh | sh If the installer asks you to update your PATH, run the command it prints. Then check the version: coop version The installer runs a downloaded script. Check the install page for release verification. heading: Create a test project
text: To try co:op, run these commands to create a test project. Use the same terminal window throughout the walkthrough: coop_demo_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/coop-sandbox-demo.XXXXXX") && cd "$coop_demo_dir" && git init && printf '%s\n' '# co:op sandbox demo' > README.md && git add README.md && git -c user.name='Sandbox demo' \ -c user.email='sandbox-demo@example.invalid' \ -c commit.gpgsign=false \ commit -m 'Create sandbox demo' && coop init coop init asks which languages and services this project uses. Press Enter at both questions to skip them. It also sets filtered networking for this new project. Create a file with a fake secret: (umask 077; set -C; printf '%s\n' 'COOP_DEMO_VALUE=not-a-real-secret' > .env.coop-demo) && wc -c < .env.coop-demo We’ll use this fake secret to check that co:op hides it from the agent.

heading: Start Codex CLI
text: Run this command to check your setup: coop doctor Start Codex CLI: coop_review_base=$(git rev-parse HEAD) && coop codex --egress filtered The first command saves the starting commit ID so you can review all changes later. Host networking and Apple’s container runtime are not supported. Why the agent runs without approval prompts This guide uses Codex CLI on your computer, not a Codex cloud task. It edits your local project inside co:op’s Docker container. Codex has its own sandbox and approval controls. co:op starts it with --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, so it can work without asking permission for every command. co:op’s container and file and network rules control its access instead. The agent can also read or change this project’s saved history and settings.

heading: Verify how co:op hides secrets
text: Ask Codex to run: wc -c README.md .env.coop-demo macOS Linux The agent can read README.md, but co:op blocks access to the secret or shows it as an empty file. Files matching .env.* are protected automatically. To hide other files or folders, add them to .coopignore. To scan project files for credentials, open a second terminal in the demo folder and run: coop check-secrets --include-ignored

heading: Verify that Codex can’t read your login credentials
text: To keep Codex from reading or leaking your login credentials, co:op gives it placeholders and adds the real credentials outside the sandbox when forwarding requests to OpenAI. Ask Codex to run this script to check what it received: node <<'JS' const fs = require('node:fs'); const path = require('node:path'); try { if (process.env.COOP_BOX !== '1') throw new Error(); const auth = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync( path.join(require('node:os').homedir(), '.codex/auth.json'), 'utf8')); const tokens = auth.tokens || {}; const parts = (tokens.access_token || '').split('.'); const claims = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(parts[1], 'base64url').toString()); if (claims.coop_broker !== true || parts[2] !== 'Y29vcC1icm9rZXI' || tokens.account_id !== 'coop-broker-account' || tokens.refresh_token || auth.OPENAI_API_KEY || process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY || process.env.CODEX_API_KEY || process.env.CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN) { throw new Error(); } console.log('PASS: Codex uses the public broker identity, with no refresh token or API key here'); } catch { console.error('FAIL: the expected Codex credential setup was not verified'); process.exitCode = 1; } JS If the check fails, investigate without printing credentials or pasting them into a prompt. Commands such as env, printenv and cat can expose them.

heading: See what the agent can connect to
text: Leave the agent running. In another terminal, open the demo project folder and run: coop net coop net check https://example.com coop net check checks the rules without visiting the website. In this new project, example.com should be blocked. If it is allowed, check that you’re in the demo folder. What can Codex connect to? Codex can reach the OpenAI services needed for your sign-in method. Some public plugin downloads are also allowed. This does not give Codex general GitHub access or permission to push changes. Codex can also use your connected ChatGPT apps when they’re enabled. To add local MCP servers, follow the MCP setup guide.

heading: Watch a website get blocked
text: Back in the agent session, ask it to visit example.com: curl --noproxy '*' --fail --silent --show-error \ --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 \ --output /dev/null --write-out 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \ https://example.com/ The request should fail, but an error alone does not tell you why. Quit Codex CLI, then list its network sessions: coop net runs Find the session you just closed by its start time. Here, its run ID is a27f2248. Replace that ID with yours in the command below to see why the request was blocked: coop net blocked example.com --run a27f2248

heading: Allow just one website
text: In the demo’s .agent/project.yaml, add this rule under the existing box entry. Keep the other settings: .agent/project.yaml · example.com rule box: egress: filtered egress_rules: - to: {domain: "example.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] coop approve coop net check https://example.com Approve only the new rule for example.com on TLS port 443. It allows this website, not its subdomains or other ports. The check should now say it is allowed. coop codex --egress filtered The new Codex CLI session uses the updated rules. A session already running would keep the old ones. Ask the agent to try the request again: curl --noproxy '*' --fail --silent --show-error \ --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 \ --output /dev/null --write-out 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \ https://example.com/ If it still fails, check the new run’s network receipt for the reason. Leave filtered networking on. Now give the agent a small task: Example prompt Add one sentence to README.md explaining that this is a sandbox demo. Run git diff --check and show its exit status. Do not install dependencies or commit the change. Stop after showing the diff. Check the diff and command output, then quit Codex CLI so co:op can finish recording the session’s network activity.

heading: Read the network receipt
text: List the sessions again to find the one where you allowed example.com: coop net runs Here, the session where you allowed example.com is b5f0aeda, the newer one. Replace it with your run ID below to inspect its traffic: coop net inspect b5f0aeda The first session showed example.com blocked. This one shows a connection to example.com:443. For the full record, including whether the session and cleanup finished, use JSON: coop net inspect b5f0aeda --json The values shown above mean the run ended, its network record is complete, and cleanup finished. Follow up on any warnings. UNKNOWN means co:op could not measure something. It does not mean zero. To export the receipt: coop net export b5f0aeda What does the export include? coop net inspect … --json puts these fields under receipt. In an export, they are at the top level. Exports hide remote names and addresses by default. Add --include-addresses to include them, and review the file before sharing it. The digest is a checksum, not a signature. See what the network record measures.

heading: Review changes and fix problems
text: Back in the original terminal where you started the agent, review what the agent changed: git status --short && git log --oneline "$coop_review_base"..HEAD && git diff "$coop_review_base" git diff --check "$coop_review_base" && printf 'Diff check passed\n' This compares the project with the commit saved before the agent started, including changes it staged or committed. Open any untracked files separately. Git does not include their contents in the diff. Codex cannot sign in or uses the wrong account Exit Codex, run coop login codex and sign in again. Use this command rather than codex login inside the container. This walkthrough uses an OpenAI account. co:op rejects unsupported provider URLs. It keeps separate Codex settings for each project. Inside the container, Codex reads ~/.codex/config.toml. See where agent settings live before changing them. A dependency or documentation request is blocked Run coop net blocked <host> in your terminal, replacing <host> with the blocked hostname. Add the access you need to .agent/project.yaml, then run coop approve. Restart the agent to use the new rules. The networking guide explains the rules. If Docker or a sandbox check fails, fix the reported problem before trying again with filtered networking. Ready to use your own project? Follow the general sandbox walkthrough to protect its secrets, set up its tools and approve its network access. Each project needs its own approval. Review and test the agent’s changes before keeping them. For longer jobs, the overnight walkthrough shows how to run a task queue. You can delete the test project at $coop_demo_dir when you’re finished. This does not sign you out. Using another coding agent? Run Claude Code in a sandboxClaude sign-in, connectors and the container boundary. Run Gemini CLI in a sandboxAI Studio keys, Google routes and supported authentication. Run Grok CLI in a sandboxGrok device sign-in, account access and network rules.

heading: Why use a sandbox?
text: Coding agents run commands, install packages, and change files. A mistake can affect more than the project you’re working on. An attacker can also hide instructions in content the agent reads, tricking it into running harmful commands. This is called prompt injection. A sandbox limits what the agent can access and how much damage it can do if something goes wrong. You can give it room to work without giving it access to everything. co:op runs Gemini CLI in a Docker container on your computer: File access is limited to the project and folders you share. Secret files appear empty or cannot be read. Networking is restricted to the provider and allowed services and websites. Your provider API key or sign-in token is not mounted into the container. Gemini can still edit the files it can see and send their contents to Google. API requests count toward your usage limits and may cost money.
