Run Claude Code in a sandboxClaude sign-in, connectors and the container boundary. Run Codex CLI in a sandboxChatGPT device sign-in, API accounts and Codex settings. Run Gemini CLI in a sandboxAI Studio keys, Google routes and supported authentication.

heading: Run a coding agent overnight
text: Prepare a task, run it in a separate fork, and review the result in the morning. Before you start A completed sandbox setup, with working project checks One small task with a clear finish line A computer that will stay awake

heading: Make the task reviewable
text: Run these commands in the original project on your computer, called the parent project below. The example fixes a flaky login test. Replace its paths, commands and requirements with a real issue you can review in one sitting. In AGENTS.md, record the build and test commands, where changes belong, and when the agent must ask a question. Choose the command that checks your project before you start. co:op calls this the gate. Add it to your existing .agent/project.yaml, keeping the other settings. .agent/project.yaml · example addition # Use your project's real verification command. gate: make check The example uses make check. Use your project’s actual command, confirm that it works in the container, and put it in AGENTS.md so the agent knows to run it. co:op also runs it during fork review and merge. A COOP_GATE setting on the host overrides the project setting. Host terminal · parent project root coop tasks add "Fix the flaky login test" --tasks .agent/tasks Open the generated task.md at the path printed by the command. Keep its metadata and fill in the brief before running the loop. Example task brief · adapt before running Observed tests/login.test.ts fails when another test leaves a signed-in user in shared test state. Expected Each test starts with its own session state. Login succeeds with valid credentials and fails with invalid ones. Verify Reproduce the failure, run the focused login tests repeatedly, then run the project gate. In this example project: make test-login and make check. Reject Deleting or skipping the assertion, weakening the behavior check, or adding a sleep to conceal the race. Leave evidence Record the cause, changed files, commands and actual results in the task log. Stop and ask if the fix requires changing authentication behavior. Before you continue The task names a real failure, a verifiable result and an unacceptable shortcut. The check commands exist in your project and work in the box.

heading: Choose exactly what may run
text: A fork starts from committed source. Review and commit the code, project configuration and instructions the run needs before creating it. Keep co:op’s local task queue uncommitted; the host manages its assignments separately. Host terminal · parent project root git status --short coop tasks ls --tasks .agent/tasks --todo --in-progress coop fork ls The commands in this guide select the root queue, .agent/tasks. Every eligible task in that queue may run, including tasks you added earlier. Check the list before continuing. If you need a separate queue for this run, follow the queue configuration and selection options and use that path in every task, launch and resume command below. Choosing a queue does not limit the number of tasks, runtime or spending. Choose an unused fork name. This guide uses overnight with --isolated, which gives the fork its own Git metadata and object storage. co:op checks the committed changes before bringing them into your original checkout. If the fork already exists, or you use shared services Choose a new name if overnight is already in use, and substitute it in every command below. An existing ordinary fork cannot be upgraded to isolated mode in place. Shared caches, services and host tools still need your trust. Review the committed changes with coop fork review before opening the fork’s raw directory in an editor. Files the agent changed, including Git and editor settings, can run code on your computer. The isolated-fork reference explains these limits. Before you continue The source the fork needs is committed, you have checked which tasks may run, and your fork name is unused. You are still in the parent project.

heading: Launch the fork in the background
text: Start Claude Code in the new isolated fork. If you signed in to Codex, substitute codex for claude in this command and the resume command below. Host terminal · parent project root coop fork overnight claude --isolated --loop --tasks .agent/tasks -d -d runs the loop in the background so you can keep using your terminal. The loop edits and commits in the fork, while the host assigns work from the parent queue. Subscription limits still apply. If you use an API key, the run may add to your API bill. Keep the computer awake and Docker running. coop fork ls coop fork logs overnight Check that the intended fork started and its logs show the expected task. If it stops with a question, answer it and resume the same fork as shown below. Final review can send work back for another pass if it falls short of the task’s requirements. Before you continue The fork name, agent and task in the status and logs match your intended run. Leave it unattended only after this first check.

heading: Stay in control of the run
text: Run these commands from the parent project. The live views occupy their terminal; open another terminal if you want both at once. Host terminal · parent project root coop tasks watch --tasks .agent/tasks coop fork logs overnight --follow Press Ctrl-C to leave a live view. Leaving the log view does not stop the background loop. To stop that loop and its running boxes while preserving the fork’s work: coop fork stop overnight To review pending questions, record your answer in the parent queue. This also unblocks the answered task: coop tasks decisions -i --tasks .agent/tasks After answering a question or stopping the run, use this command to resume the same fork. Repeat the queue path: co:op remembers that the fork is isolated, but it does not remember the previous --tasks filter. coop fork overnight claude --isolated --loop --tasks .agent/tasks -d A command exited successfully. Is the work finished? Read the fork’s status and final-review result. A successful command exit can mean that the fork is waiting for your answer, or that it reached a task limit before final review. Check the result before treating the work as finished. The commands in this walkthrough keep working in the named fork. A direct coop loop instead edits and commits in the current checkout; use the loop reference if that is the workflow you intend. Before you continue Check that the fork is ready and its final review is complete. The task in the parent queue may still be in progress, even when the fork is ready. It becomes complete when you merge the reviewed changes.

heading: Review the result before landing it
text: When the fork is ready, inspect its committed changes. You will then run the project check on a temporary copy that includes the latest changes from your current branch. Host terminal · parent project root coop fork review overnight Read the diff first, especially any changes to build scripts. Then run the configured project check: coop fork review overnight --gate Read the summary to confirm which check ran and what it reported. If no check is configured, --gate can exit successfully without testing the project. The review includes only committed changes. If it warns about uncommitted or untracked fork files, resolve the warning and review again. For the login-test example, look for An explanation of how tests shared session state, backed by a reproduced failure. A focused change that gives each test its own state and keeps the assertions. Tests that cover the original failure and the affected failure path. Commands and results from repeated login tests and the project gate. A completed final review, with all requested fixes addressed. A passing gate verifies only the checks it ran. Check the changed behavior yourself as well. Once the result meets the task’s acceptance criteria, and the parent checkout is clean, merge it from the branch where you want the work to land: coop fork merge overnight Confirm when co:op asks to bring the changes into your branch. It prepares the committed work for that branch, runs the configured check, and merges only if the check passes. It asks separately before removing the fork. If review or merge stops with an error, fix the reported problem and review again. Pushing and deploying are separate actions. Before you continue The reviewed changes are on the branch you intended, you have saved the check result, and the matching tasks in the parent queue are complete. Try a larger run after you have checked this result. How the orchestrator works

heading: The box
text: Control visible files, prepare a project image, and run databases and development servers beside your agent. The box is the container your agent runs in. co:op mounts your project at its real path, but leaves your home folder and SSH keys unmounted. By default its networking is filtered, inside or outside a co:op project, so the box reaches the agent's provider and the destinations you approved. Add --egress open for unrestricted access or --egress offline for none. See restricted networking. For an overview, see the sandbox, hiding secrets and toolchain and services. coop run and coop shell pass piped or redirected input to the command. As with docker run -i or ssh, that input is read as soon as the box starts, even if the command never reads it. In a shell while read loop, give each coop run its own input, as in coop run -- make test < /dev/null, or it takes the lines meant for the loop.

heading: Hiding secrets
text: co:op hides files and directories whose names look like secrets, including .env, *.tfvars, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa*, secrets/, .ssh, dotfiles ending in secrets such as .shell-secrets, and config files such as secrets.env. Source and docs like secrets.go and secrets.md stay readable, and templates (*.example, *.sample, *.template) stay visible. co:op protects these files in one of two ways. On supported Mac Docker runtimes, APFS projects automatically get eBPF protection, enforced in the Linux VM, when the Docker VM supports its BPF hooks and uses cgroup v2 with the cgroupfs driver. Other filesystems, unsupported VM kernels and incompatible container options use mount protection. With eBPF protection, the box can't read or change a secret, including through another letter case, an equivalent Unicode spelling, a symlink or an existing hardlink. Public files stay writable, ordinary public hardlinks work, and .coopignore stays readable and read-only. Each hidden file already in the project, up to 1,000 per launch, also gets an empty read-only file over it. A tool that opens one, such as Terraform with terraform.tfvars, reads it as empty and keeps working, and the secret stays out of reach. The box can't delete or rename a folder that holds a covered file. In a repository, only a file Git ignores gets a cover, because an agent's git add -A would commit a tracked or new file as empty. Add your secrets to .gitignore. eBPF protects everything else: other letter cases, hardlinks, files past the limit and hidden directories. Reading or changing one of those returns Operation not permitted. A file created after the box starts is protected at once when its name is on the built-in list, such as *.pem, *.key or .env: the box can create, overwrite or delete such a file, so installers and key generators keep working, but it can't read one or give it another name. A new file that only .coopignore hides, and a new hidden folder, need a restart. stat still works on a hidden file without a cover, so find and tools that list a folder keep working. It shows the file's real size, times, mode, owner and link count. The box still can't read the contents, and extended attributes read as empty. A hidden symlink shows no target, and readlink on it fails. stat fails on a hidden directory and on everything inside it, and ls -l shows that directory's entry with an error. For tools that scan the repository, co:op sets COOP_BOX=1 inside the box. When it is set, skip paths that return a permission error (EPERM or EACCES) during metadata lookup, directory traversal or file reads. Skip a denied directory's subtree. Report skipped paths so the result makes clear which files were checked, and keep reporting other errors normally. A denied path is unreadable, not an empty file. Don't rely on a successful stat or a list of tracked files to mean that their contents can be read. co:op does not expose a hidden-path list inside the box. Handle the filesystem error rather than trying to reproduce its hiding rules. co:op builds the eBPF helper inside Docker, so you don't need any host packages, filesystem changes or kernel settings. Launches don't test the protection itself, so run coop doctor after you update Docker or OrbStack. It tries to read test secrets in a real box. See filesystem protection for how eBPF protection behaves when you edit files on the host. With mount protection, co:op covers a secret file or directory with a read-only empty one, so stat shows the cover's size and times, not the real ones. On a case-insensitive disk, it also covers the uppercase and lowercase spellings of a hidden filename with up to 11 letters, and every spelling of .coopignore. A longer filename, or a project with too many spellings, can exceed the mount limit. The box or service could then read the file under another letter case, so co:op refuses to launch the agent or service. Either: move the file into a hidden folder, or run coop approve --case-exposure to review the listed files and accept that they stay readable under another letter case with mount protection. co:op remembers your approval. Ordinary coop approve reviews network access and does not accept any file exposure. That approval covers those exact paths, including their future contents, for new agent and service runs. Newly exposed paths need another approval, and running boxes stay unchanged. .coopignore cannot be approved this way. COOP_ALLOW_CASE_EXPOSED_SECRETS=1 exposes the files for a single run. eBPF protects these paths without either kind of approval.

heading: Filesystem protection contract
text: co:op trusts the host and its editors. Each time it starts an agent or service with eBPF protection, it captures the current hiding rules and the protected files and folders, and it keeps checking every file name the box opens against the built-in list. In practice: Ordinary edits to public files work immediately. A path that is already protected stays protected when you edit it or save it atomically on the host, even when a parent folder is replaced. Existing hardlinks keep their protection when the original file is replaced. A new file whose name is on the built-in list, such as late.pem or .env, is unreadable in the box as soon as it exists, in any letter case or Unicode spelling. The box can still create, overwrite, truncate or delete such a file, but it can't read one or give it another name. Restart the affected agent or service after you change .coopignore, create a hidden folder, mark an already-public file or folder as secret, or create an unprotected hardlink to a secret from the host. Protection that is already running does not reload its rules or revoke memory mappings that were already readable. To save a secret atomically, write the temporary file outside the shared tree or inside an already hidden folder. A new temporary file at a public path is protected only when its own name is on the built-in list. Protection follows the file or folder itself, not its path. Removing its hiding rule alone doesn't make a hidden secret public while it still has another hardlink in the project. Remove the other hardlinks and restart before you make the original file public. When you approve a hidden file for a service, the service can read that file, its other hardlinks and your later in-place edits on the host. The approval never allows writes. If the file is replaced, start the service through co:op again so that it can read the new file. A separate helper runs the kernel enforcement, and the agent gets no BPF privileges. If the helper exits, access to the protected share is denied until co:op removes that agent or service. Stopped service containers keep their protection for a later restart. After a VM reboot, co:op's guard runs before an image's start command and its healthchecks, and refuses to run image code under the old protection. Start the service through co:op to get fresh protection.

heading: Your own paths: .coopignore
text: Add a .coopignore at the repo root to hide your own paths: # a file name, matched at any depth prod.yml # an exact path; its final name stays hidden if the parent moves config/stripe.live.json # a directory, hidden whole vault/ Comments go on their own lines, as in .gitignore. prod.yml # note is one pattern, comment and all, and co:op warns about it at launch. An exact-path rule also hides its final file or directory name everywhere that .coopignore applies, so renaming the parent directory can't reveal the secret. If a box moves a hidden file or folder somewhere no rule matches, the next box and co:op's own tools still hide it wherever it appears in the project. This includes a file hidden by config/*.yml and moved by mv config cfg, or a folder moved outside a nested .coopignore's scope. At its original path, the current rules decide whether it's visible. A .coopignore applies below its folder, including to repositories nested inside it, such as submodules or worktrees. co:op also reads the .coopignore files above the project, stopping before your home folder, or just below / when the project is outside your home. Creating sub/.git therefore doesn't let an agent reveal sub/secret.yml to a new box started in sub/. To share hiding rules across projects, put a .coopignore in a parent folder such as ~/Projects/.coopignore. Paths in that file start from its own folder: app/config/*.yml hides config/*.yml in the app project. These rules affect both box visibility and fork merges: coop fork merge refuses changes to a hidden file unless you pass --force, and isolated forks have no override. co:op doesn't apply ~/.coopignore to projects below your home folder, and it ignores a .coopignore in a folder owned by another user, such as /tmp. A .coopignore must be a readable regular file no larger than 1 MiB. If an invalid .coopignore could hide a file that no other rule hides, co:op refuses to start the box and names the invalid file. A normal coop run, coop loop or coop shell mounts your whole working tree, and .gitignore doesn't control what the agent can read. A file Git ignores, such as serviceAccount.json, stays visible unless a hiding rule covers it, so add it to .coopignore. A normal writable run shares your checkout with the agent. The agent can change Git and editor files that later run code when you use tools on the host, including files in a new child repository. co:op adds safeguards to its own host Git commands, but cannot protect other commands you run yourself. co:op's Git commands still follow Git's links to other repository storage: commondir, a .git file pointing to another Git folder, linked objects or refs folders, and objects/info/alternates. An agent can use pointers in .git to make these commands read another repository your user can access. A reset or review can then bring that repository's files into the box. Use coop fork <name> <target> --isolated to get independent Git storage and checks before committed changes enter your checkout.

heading: Secrets inside files: coop check-secrets
text: Use coop check-secrets to look for credentials inside files. It reports each finding as file:line and exits 1 when it finds one. The scan still reports files hidden by built-in rules or .coopignore when Git would commit them. Hiding a file from the box does not prevent committing or pushing it. --include-ignored expands the scan to the whole visible tree. If the scan can't read a file, it fails and names that file, so a permission error can't produce a clean result. It also lists changed files that can affect what runs on your machine, such as commit hooks, editor or agent settings, Compose files and the Makefile. Review them before running anything. This separate report never changes the exit code. To make this check ignore a finding you've reviewed, add the printed entry to .coopsecretsignore at the project root and explain why. The entry identifies that exact finding without storing the credential. Adding a line above the finding doesn't invalidate the entry, but changing the value or moving the file does. The exception applies only to this check. Fork merges, checkpoint uploads and session redaction still check every finding. Check your sandbox setup with coop doctor.

heading: Toolchain: .tool-versions
text: On an open-network run, the base box installs the versions listed in your .tool-versions file using asdf and caches them in a shared volume. It looks for the file from the working directory upwards, then falls back to ~/.tool-versions. A repo with .tool-versions needs no .agent/Dockerfile or other setup for this: cd ~/code/phoenix-app # has a .tool-versions coop claude --egress open # provisions elixir/erlang/node/… from it, then runs the agent The first install of a new toolchain can be slow (Erlang compiles, for example). After that it's reused across runs and repos. Set COOP_NO_ASDF=1 in agents/env to skip installing tools from .tool-versions. co:op still repairs an outdated cached Node shim when needed to keep the agent CLIs running. Installing tools at startup works only with open networking. A filtered run, the default, uses an image that includes asdf but puts no asdf shims on PATH and installs nothing when the box starts. Build your toolchain into an .agent/Dockerfile instead: coop init writes one when it finds a .tool-versions. coop init --stack asdf writes one later. coop build builds it. The default box has no Go, Terraform, Elixir or Rust. When coop init finds one of these languages in a project that has no .agent/Dockerfile, for example Go from a go.mod, it prints the commands that pin it in .tool-versions and build the project's box. Until then the commit check cannot format that language's files, so it skips them and prints a warning.

heading: Your own image: .agent/Dockerfile
text: coop init --stack asdf # writes an asdf .agent/Dockerfile (from .tool-versions) coop build # builds the image for this project's network mode A repository with an .agent/Dockerfile gets its own image tag, and every coop, coop loop, coop fork and coop acp run in that repo uses it. The generated Dockerfile installs the exact versions in .tool-versions, so keep them there and don't repeat them in the Dockerfile. For a different setup, write an .agent/Dockerfile that meets the box contract. When the agent needs a new system package, add it to the RUN line and run coop build again. If you change .agent/Dockerfile or .tool-versions but forget to rebuild, coop notices on the next run and reminds you to run coop build. The selected Dockerfile must be a regular file inside the repo, not a symlink. You can reuse a stage of your app's existing Dockerfile or use your own docker-compose.yml for service containers. Set the paths relative to the repository in .agent/project.yaml: Key Default box.dockerfile .agent/Dockerfile box.compose .agent/compose.yml

heading: Builds and network modes
text: With filtered networking, the default, review the Dockerfile and the files it copies, then run coop build on the host. Plain coop build follows the project's network mode, so it builds the filtered image unless the project or COOP_EGRESS chooses open or offline. coop build --egress filtered asks for it explicitly. A filtered launch uses an image built from files you approved. Running coop build approves the Dockerfile and the files it copies, for this project, Docker daemon and build settings. If only co:op's client base changed or the image is missing, the next launch rebuilds those same files by itself. If the files changed, co:op waits for you, because an agent can edit them and a project build runs them with ordinary networking. Changing a network rule asks only for coop approve, because no build reads .agent/project.yaml and an image never holds it. When changed files need a build, an interactive provider launch in a host terminal can offer Build and continue?, defaulting to No. The prompt shows a saved snapshot of the build files. Review it, because only those saved files are approved for that build. Headless commands and unattended runs never ask: they stop and name the build to run. coop update rebuilds approved files and leaves changed ones for coop build, because an update is not a review. An editor connects anyway, holds your messages and says what to run. See editors. An editor connection with open networking can build a missing project image automatically. Ordinary runs don't rebuild an image after its inputs change: they warn, and you run coop build --egress open yourself. Offline launches never run project build instructions automatically. Project builds use ordinary Docker networking. The restrictions on the running box do not apply during the build, and --egress selects the runtime image without filtering build traffic. See restricted networking for the image checks and the limits of build protection. After a build, new runs use the rebuilt image. Supervised editor sessions that run the replaced image restart and reconnect. Other running boxes keep the old image until their next start. An unchanged image restarts nothing.

heading: Box-only environment: box.env
text: Put non-secret defaults for the box under box.env and commit them with the project. Values are literal strings, so quote values that look like numbers. Your ~/.config/coop/agents/env overrides these defaults. Names beginning with COOP_* are reserved for co:op. box: env: PGHOST: db PGPORT: "5432"

heading: The box contract
text: You can choose your own base image where the network mode allows it, but filtered runs must inherit co:op's fixed client base. An agent box needs the following: It runs as a non-root user. Claude Code refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions as root. That user's home is /home/node. co:op mounts the selected provider folders from agents/ at $HOME/.claude, $HOME/.codex, $HOME/.gemini and $HOME/.grok. On a different base, set COOP_HOME_IN_BOX=/home/<user>. claude, codex, gemini and grok are on PATH (the first three need Node), plus the ACP adapters if you want coop acp. Grok's ACP server is the grok binary itself. It runs git config --system --add safe.directory '*' so Git can use the repository files owned by your host user. They normally appear at the repo's real path. New remote sessions use /workspace inside their private boxes. On native Linux, the user inside the image must have the same UID/GID as your host user so it can read a private checkout and the selected provider's files. co:op builds its managed images with those IDs automatically. If you supply COOP_BASE_IMAGE or another custom image, configure its user to match. Managed images on Docker Desktop for macOS keep UID/GID 1000. co:op sets the working directory itself, so no WORKDIR is required. Here is a skeleton: FROM <your-language-base> RUN <install your toolchain> \ && npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.285 @openai/codex@0.159.2 @google/gemini-cli@0.62.0 \ @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp@0.84.0 @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.0.1 \ && curl -fsSL "https://storage.googleapis.com/grok-build-public-artifacts/cli/grok-1.0.44-linux-$(uname -m).gz" \ | gunzip > /usr/local/bin/grok && chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/grok \ && git config --system --add safe.directory '*' ARG COOP_BOX_UID=1000 ARG COOP_BOX_GID=1000 RUN if id -u node >/dev/null 2>&1; then \ if ! getent group "$COOP_BOX_GID" >/dev/null; then groupmod -g "$COOP_BOX_GID" "$(id -gn node)"; fi \ && usermod -u "$COOP_BOX_UID" -g "$COOP_BOX_GID" node \ && chown -R "$COOP_BOX_UID:$COOP_BOX_GID" /home/node; \ else \ if ! getent group "$COOP_BOX_GID" >/dev/null; then groupadd -g "$COOP_BOX_GID" node; fi \ && useradd -m -u "$COOP_BOX_UID" -g "$COOP_BOX_GID" -s /bin/bash node; \ fi USER node Install Node first if your base doesn't include it. This example also needs the standard useradd, usermod and groupmod tools. coop build passes your host UID/GID as build arguments for project Dockerfiles. When you build COOP_BASE_IMAGE separately, you must supply those arguments yourself. This example pins the client versions checked for this co:op release. If you use another base, update those versions when you update co:op. You can also inherit co:op's base, which supplies the clients for you. Images based on co:op already include Gemini's settings in the root-owned /etc/gemini-cli/ folder. If you build an independent image, add thinking/low.json, thinking/high.json and login.json there too. co:op needs them to set thinking effort for each call and restrict tools during sign-in, and Gemini ignores system settings inside a user-owned home. Before starting a command, co:op's startup scripts check that Claude's selected account settings and trust configuration are ready. Rebuild images that inherit from co:op to get this check. An independent startup script does not provide it.

heading: Inherit co:op's base
text: Start from co:op's image to keep its client setup and add your own toolchain. coop build selects the base image, builds it if needed and passes it to your Dockerfile: ARG COOP_BASE_IMAGE=coop-box # coop build overrides this with the resolved base FROM ${COOP_BASE_IMAGE} # agent CLIs + ACP adapters, asdf, browser libs, non-root node — all inherited USER root RUN <install your toolchain> USER node Each box definition gets its own base-image tag, coop-box:<definition>, which coop build prints. After an upgrade, the next launch builds the new base if needed. A plain docker build of this file needs that tag passed in: --build-arg COOP_BASE_IMAGE=coop-box:<definition>. docker image ls coop-box lists them. Builds also remove old images that co:op owns: its versioned coop-box, coop-clients and coop-network images, plus <project>-filtered images when you explicitly build the project's box. co:op removes an image only when no run has used it for 14 days and no container references it, and it prints the images it removes. co:op leaves older images without its ownership mark alone. Every launch records which image it used, so an older co:op version you still run keeps its base. co:op never removes images you created yourself, regardless of their tags.

heading: Reusing a devcontainer
text: If a repo already has a .devcontainer/, reuse its image as your base and add the agent layer on top: FROM your-devcontainer-image # the team's source of truth for the env RUN npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.285 @openai/codex@0.159.2 @google/gemini-cli@0.62.0 \ @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp@0.84.0 @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.0.1 \ && curl -fsSL "https://storage.googleapis.com/grok-build-public-artifacts/cli/grok-1.0.44-linux-$(uname -m).gz" \ | gunzip > /usr/local/bin/grok && chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/grok \ && git config --system --add safe.directory '*' USER <the devcontainer's non-root user> # If that user's home isn't /home/node, run with COOP_HOME_IN_BOX=/home/<user>. co:op adds secret hiding, its container restrictions, the task queue and the supervisor that runs it. A devcontainer alone mounts the whole workspace, including .env, and a malicious project running under --dangerously-skip-permissions can send the contents of ~/.claude outside your machine. Don't rely on the devcontainer alone to protect those files.

heading: Project services
text: Services such as databases run in separate containers alongside the box. None are added by default. coop init asks which ones you want, or you can pass --services postgres,redis, and it writes their configuration to .agent/compose.yml. In a project with filtered network access, it also asks for a network rule for each service in .agent/project.yaml. Run coop approve once so the box can reach them. coop up # starts the configured Compose services, waits until ready coop claude # the box reaches each service by its Compose name coop down # stop services; stored data is kept coop down --delete-volumes # stop them and permanently delete their volumes (asks first) coop init --services # add another service to a project that already has some An open box joins the services' private network. A filtered box starts the services its approved rules name, so it needs no coop up first, and reaches each one only through its rule. Connect with a URL such as DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:dev-password@db:5432/app_dev, and put it in agents/env.

heading: Development and loop stacks
text: Your development services keep the same Compose project and data between runs. A loop gets its own Compose project, network, volumes and published ports for the entire run. It reuses them across task and provider retries, then removes them when the run ends. If a loop or editor session is killed, the next coop acp, loop or coop down in that checkout removes them instead, and leaves alone the services of a session that is still running. Both stacks can run in one checkout without sharing service data or ports. They still share the source files, so edits are visible through both stacks' mounts.

heading: Starting and stopping
text: When services are ready, coop up prints a message such as ✓ Services ready: db, redis, using the actual service names in Compose order, followed by any URLs it published. If it can't read the service list from Compose, it starts nothing. coop down --delete-volumes lists each of this project's volumes and its contents, then asks before permanently deleting anything. The default answer is No, and -y/--yes confirms without a prompt. Having no terminal never counts as consent. An external: true volume or a project file mounted from the host is never deleted. The next coop up or box launch applies changes to the Compose file, including stopping services you removed, and coop down also stops those services. Each workspace gets a Compose project name derived from its path, so repositories with the same folder name stay separate. Agents can change data in services they can reach, so use disposable development databases. The shared coop-cache volume at ~/.cache keeps downloads between runs. Claude's MCP logs at ~/.cache/claude-cli-nodejs are kept separately: each run starts with an empty log folder, so one project's logs cannot enter another project's box.

heading: Volumes from outside the project
text: An external: true or custom-named volume may contain another project's data. When you run coop up in a terminal, it shows the actual Docker volume name, which services will use it and whether they can write to it, then asks you to approve access for this repository. The review also shows the selected Docker daemon and, for an existing plain local volume, where it stores the data. Only plain local volumes are supported. co:op refuses a volume backed by a bind mount, driver options or a plugin. Mount an explicit repository path instead. co:op creates a missing custom-named volume as plain local storage only after you answer Yes. An approval does not automatically transfer to a different daemon or a replaced volume. Answering No or closing the input stops the command before Compose runs. Automatic box launches, filtered service containers and coop up without a terminal refuse these volumes, even if you approved them before. Named volumes that belong only to this project need no approval prompt.

heading: Secret files in services
text: Services get the same secret hiding as the box, including when they mount the repo or one of its directories. A mount of .env, *.key or a path hidden by .coopignore cannot expose its contents to the service, even when the mount source is itself a hidden file, so an agent-written Compose file can't pass those secrets to a container the agent controls. If a service needs a hidden file, such as a generated development TLS key for Keycloak, mount that individual file read-only with :ro or read_only: true. Run coop up in a terminal to review the eligible files and approve them. Hidden directories stay protected, and so do files that a writable mount can also reach. Use named volumes for data the service needs to change. The approval is tied to: The exact Compose file you reviewed. co:op stores approval outside the repo, so an agent cannot update it by editing the file. After any edit, box launches hide these files until you approve again. co:op explains which files are hidden and why. This checkout's private identity. Copying the Compose file or its marker does not transfer approval to another checkout. An approval saved by an older co:op doesn't count until you renew it with coop up, and automatic starts hide these files until then. The exact files you reviewed. A new secret added under an approved directory mount stays hidden until you approve that file too. When you approve secret files or outside volumes for a service, co:op also records the exact local Docker image ID shown in the review and starts that image with pulling disabled. Changing what a tag points to can't give a different image the same access without review. Run coop up in a terminal to review an updated local tag. If you decline, the old approval stays in place and this startup stops. If the approved image was removed, startup stops before creating a container. Pull the tag, then run coop up to review it again. Before asking for a first approval, co:op may pull an image that is not cached, using Docker's existing registry login. If you decline, the service does not start or receive access. The downloaded image stays in Docker's cache. Services without access to approved secret files or outside volumes keep their normal image update behavior. co:op gives Compose a private Docker client configuration. It keeps the registry login details, including a validated DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG, but leaves out proxy credentials from your host configuration so they cannot reach the services. List the files your services need in the repo, so teammates can review the access request before a service fails to start: # .agent/project.yaml — committed with the repo services: require_real_files: - dev/keycloak/certs/generated/tls.key # a generated dev TLS key Keycloak reads The list helps reviewers recognize expected files, but does not grant access. An agent can edit it, so co:op still asks you to approve the files. In that prompt: Files listed by the repo are marked as expected. Files the repo did not list appear first so you can review the unexpected access. Files added since your last approval are identified. You must approve access separately on each machine. New forks copy these files and their regular siblings that Compose binds from the parent when present. Copying grants no service access. Before starting services, co:op refuses a missing bind source by name; create the file or directory and retry. A requested real file must be a regular file. Compose cannot create an empty directory in place of a missing source, and coop down remains available when a source is missing.

heading: One URL inside and out
text: Some services, such as an OIDC issuer like Keycloak, need the same URL in your host browser and in the app running inside the box. Give the service an expose: port in .agent/compose.yml: services: keycloak: image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak expose: ["8443"] # coop publishes this to a stable, per-workspace localhost port labels: coop.service.scheme: https # scheme for COOP_SERVICE_*_URL (default http) co:op assigns a stable host port for each development workspace or loop run, so concurrent stacks have separate ports. The host port listens only on loopback. Inside the box, https://localhost:<port> reaches the same Keycloak service, so both sides use the same issuer URL without host.docker.internal or broader network access. The box receives COOP_SERVICE_KEYCLOAK_URL=https://localhost:<port>, using the scheme from the label. Host tools can read all workspace service URLs from coop fork ls --json. The same URL needs open egress. A filtered box reaches a service only through its approved rule, at the service's name, so it receives COOP_SERVICE_KEYCLOAK_URL=https://keycloak:8443 for each expose port its rule allows. The services it starts run on a private network with no host port, so use open egress for a service your host browser must reach too.

heading: What a Compose file may do
text: co:op sends .agent/compose.yml to your host's Docker daemon to create the service containers, and validates the file before coop up and before every networked box launch. An agent could replace a checked mount folder with a link to another part of your machine before Docker opens it. To prevent that race, co:op holds an exclusive lock while it checks the mounts and asks Docker to start the services, and boxes that can edit the checkout hold a matching shared lock. coop up waits until it can take the exclusive lock, then starts the separate development stack. co:op accepts these service settings: an image inline environment named volumes or repo-relative binds healthcheck depends_on loopback-only published ports co:op refuses settings that give a service access beyond the allowed project container and explains which setting failed. These include: privileged cap_add a host bind like /:/host or /var/run/docker.sock network_mode: host env_file build a port published on 0.0.0.0 a symlink that points outside the allowed project path bind options that relabel host files or change mount propagation A read-only session, such as an investigation or review, can still use service containers, but every service mount of the repository must also be read-only, using :ro or read_only: true. Otherwise the service could change files the agent is not allowed to write. The mount source must already exist, because Compose can't create a host directory for a read-only session. The file-approval rules above still apply. An agent can create .agent/compose.yml for you, but its configuration must pass these checks before co:op starts it. Stop any Compose service that can write to the checkout before starting another service stack. co:op's error names the writable mount and suggests coop down. co:op also refuses mounts nested inside a writable service mount: on restart, Docker could open a path that the service had replaced. co:op automatically starts only configurations within these restrictions. Run other configurations yourself.

heading: Dev servers in your browser
text: When the agent builds a website in the box, you can open it on your machine. List the ports the dev server listens on in .agent/project.yaml: serve: ports: [5173] # what the server binds INSIDE the box Each box for the repo (coop acp, coop run) maps these ports to stable host ports based on the repo's path. The URL stays the same between launches and differs between projects, so one Zed agent definition can serve all of them. When an ACP thread starts, co:op posts a browser link for each port and for the project services it starts. It also names problems it found while starting, such as a saved sign-in that no longer works. Terminal runs print the port links on stderr. The dev server must bind 0.0.0.0 inside the box (vite --host, next dev -H 0.0.0.0 and so on), because a server on the container's localhost isn't reachable through the mapping. In an editor thread, co:op tells you when a server starts, with the command and the link, or warns you when the server is only on localhost. Ports bind to your localhost only, never the LAN. Publishing needs networking: filtered (the default), which publishes the port on the run's gateway, or open. See restricted networking. co:op skips a host port that is already in use and prints a note. COOP_SERVE_URL_<port> still carries the workspace's assigned URL for configuration and discovery. An editor session says so in the thread instead of posting a link, and takes the port when it frees. In an editor session the link always reaches the box the thread is using, including after you switch provider or account. A box restart (a credential switch, a rebuild) takes the dev server down with the old box. The URL stays the same, so run the server again.

heading: Keeping the box current
text: coop update # self-update coop, then prepare this project's box image coop update --self-only # just upgrade the coop binary coop update --box-only # just prepare this project's box image coop update prepares the image for the project's network mode, using the definitions of the co:op version it installed. A filtered project keeps co:op's pinned client base, and an open or offline project gets fresh OS packages. See stable and fresh rebuilds. If GitHub has a newer release, coop update downloads its versioned archive and checksum, verifies the archive and replaces the coop binary atomically. The new binary takes effect on your next coop run. When the binary is not replaced: A dev or source build, or a binary that is already current or newer, skips the self-update with a note and still prepares the image. If coop is installed somewhere it cannot write (a package-manager prefix), the self-update fails with an error that tells you to update co:op with the tool that installed it. coop update still prepares the image, then exits 1. coop update --self-only stops at the error.

heading: A newer co:op repairs its own box
text: If your installed co:op uses a different box definition from the current shared image, the next interactive launch rebuilds that image before starting the agent. This can happen after coop update --self-only or go install. The Checking the Coop box section names both versions and ends with ✓ Box updated. Filtered runs use the client image checked for filtered networking, so they do not trigger this repair. A current image prints nothing. An old image with the same box definition gets a reminder to run coop update under that heading. co:op does not rebuild it without being asked. An image co:op did not build (COOP_IMAGE) is never replaced. If the repair cannot run because Docker is not answering, the launch stops there and says what to start before you repeat the same command.

heading: Stable and fresh rebuilds
text: Command Base image Result coop build (stable) fixed to a specific image digest rebuilding uses the same OS and runtime coop update, filtered project co:op's pinned client base the OS and runtime change only with a co:op release coop update, open or offline project (fresh) uses the current node:24-slim image and rebuilds with --pull --no-cache updates the OS packages and runtime to the newest available versions

heading: Agent clients
text: All standard co:op boxes use the same fixed versions of the agent CLIs and ACP adapters, including plain runs, filtered runs, loops, presets and editor sessions. These are the versions checked for this co:op release, and co:op verifies Grok's binary against its checksum. Each client's own updater is disabled, so the versions change only with co:op. With open or offline networking, you can use other client versions in a custom image selected with COOP_IMAGE or built from an .agent/Dockerfile on another base. Those clients are not covered by the checks for co:op's own image. Filtered runs require co:op's fixed client base and reject images that replace its clients.

heading: Restricted networking: what is supported
text: Choose which network destinations an agent can reach, and review access before a run. Boxes run behind a per-run gateway by default. The box can reach its selected providers and the destinations you approved. Other connections are blocked. Filtering works on the network itself, so changing proxy settings can't bypass the rules. The same rules apply to every tool in the box: the provider CLI, curl, an SDK or a subprocess. The credential broker handles API-key and subscription accounts. It works behind the packet filter and doesn't replace it. coop net shows what a new run in this project can reach, and why. coop net runs lists recorded runs, and coop net --help lists the commands.

heading: Allow one website
text: Add a rule for the site under box.egress_rules in the project's .agent/project.yaml: box: egress: filtered egress_rules: - to: {domain: "api.github.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] Then run coop approve on the host and answer y: NETWORK RULES (+ new) + api.github.com:443 · TLS Approve this access for new runs and running editor sessions? [y/N] y ✓ Approved for new runs and running editor sessions New runs can reach that exact name over HTTPS, but not its subdomains or other ports. Everything else stays blocked: $ coop run -- curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.github.com/ 200 $ coop run -- curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com/ curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com 000 coop net check <url> answers the same question without starting a box. To allow a site for a single run, see access for one run. Asking for access explains how approval works.

heading: Network modes
text: Every box uses filtered networking unless you or the project choose another mode, even outside a co:op project. A plain coop run or coop shell reaches only the destinations you approved, and an agent also reaches its provider. coop init writes box.egress: filtered into new projects and leaves an existing project file unchanged. There are two other modes: open allows all network traffic, and offline turns networking off. The command line, COOP_EGRESS and the project file use the same three words. Where you set the mode decides what it covers: For a single run, use --egress open or --egress offline. The project's network rules don't apply to that run, approved or not, and its Configuring network access section says This project's network rules do not apply to this run. For your runs, set COOP_EGRESS. COOP_EGRESS=offline always keeps a run offline unless you pass --egress. For filtered and open, a project's saved approval outranks COOP_EGRESS, and the run shows a warning. For one project, set box.egress. COOP_EGRESS overrides it, with a warning when that allows more than the project asks for. A project's request for open needs your approval on the host. Once you approve a project, a changed box.egress needs your approval again, with or without COOP_EGRESS, because the approval outranks it. When the mode comes from the default, the run's Configuring network access section starts with Filtered by default. Use --egress open for unrestricted access. Filtered networking needs Docker. On another runtime, such as Apple's container, co:op refuses a run with no mode set. Run it with --egress open or --egress offline, set COOP_EGRESS, or switch to Docker with COOP_RUNTIME=docker. co:op never switches to open networking on its own.

heading: Setting up a host
text: Before your first filtered session, co:op runs five checks to make sure Docker can enforce the network rules. It shows you the results, then starts your session if all five pass. If Docker isn't running or a check fails, co:op explains the problem and won't start the session. Later runs skip these checks while the saved results are still valid. You still need to approve what each project can access on the network. The checks use co:op's pinned gateway and locked client images with the selected Docker daemon, and co:op builds those images if needed. Run coop net setup to do these checks ahead of time. This is useful before an unattended run, after upgrading Docker or co:op, or when troubleshooting network setup: Setting up restricted networking using Docker 29.4.0 on linux/arm64. The gateway and client images are already available and will be reused. Checking filtered access: ✓ approved TLS access to example.com works ✓ unapproved domains are blocked ✓ direct IP connections cannot bypass domain rules ✓ the cloud metadata address is blocked ✓ DNS does not resolve unapproved domains ✓ All 5 checks passed. This host is ready for filtered runs If a check fails, co:op shows the error and the checks that passed before it. The output ends with ✗ this host is not ready for filtered runs and No setup was saved.

heading: Fleet workers and Docker-in-Docker
text: Install a Docker CLI and a matching Buildx plugin that work together through docker build. Buildx alone isn't enough: Debian bookworm's Docker CLI 20.10 doesn't pass that command to the plugin. Docker CLI 27.5.1 with Buildx 0.20.1 is a supported pairing for a Docker-in-Docker (DinD) sidecar running Docker 27.5.1. Filtered runs need a Linux Docker daemon running as root on amd64 or arm64, accessed through a local Unix socket. Rootless Docker and daemons with user-namespace remapping aren't supported. With DinD, mount the worker's state and temporary directories at the same absolute paths in the daemon container. Never mount the Docker socket into the agent's container. Run coop net setup as the worker's OS user, using the same Docker endpoint and network state directory as the worker. Session API requests don't build images or run these setup checks. If setup fails, the worker can't accept filtered jobs. Don't retry them with open networking. Before accepting a job, co:op checks that the saved results still match the daemon, runtime requirements and exact images in use.

heading: Supported today
text: Rule Meaning Enforced by to: {domain: "api.example.com"} · protocol: tls · ports: [443] that exact name over TLS on port 443 the gateway checks the visible SNI and routes to a validated IPv4 address to: {domain: "*.example.com"} · protocol: tls · ports: [443] one label under that name (www.example.com), but never the bare domain and never a.b.example.com the same hostname check applies to DNS requests and the SNI to: {domain: "dns.google"} · protocol: tls · ports: [853, 8443] that name over TLS on those ports, and on no other the gateway redirects only those ports, then checks the original port that the kernel reports to: {ip: "10.42.8.12"} / to: {cidr: "10.42.9.0/24"} · protocol: tcp|udp · ports: [...] raw TCP or UDP to those IPv4 addresses on those ports an nftables rule allows the traffic and keeps its own packet and byte counts to: {ip: ...} / to: {cidr: ...} · protocol: icmp · types: [echo-request] IPv4 ping to those addresses an nftables rule allows echo requests, and conntrack allows the replies to: {service: "db"} · protocol: tcp · ports: [5432] one Compose sidecar that belongs to this project co:op reads the service container's exact IP address from the runtime at launch serve: {ports: [3000]} in .agent/project.yaml the host browser reaches the box's dev server Docker publishes the port on the gateway, and the box shares the gateway's network namespace In a filtered run, COOP_RUN_ARGS and extra runtime arguments accept bind mounts, -e KEY=VALUE and --label KEY=VALUE only. co:op refuses any other flag by name. Its own tracking labels take precedence over your labels with the same key.

heading: Provider access
text: Each agent gets access to the provider endpoints its client needs: Agent Hosts a filtered run reaches coop claude api.anthropic.com, platform.claude.com (the OAuth refresh) and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com (the claude.ai connectors a login has on by default) coop codex chatgpt.com and auth.openai.com. An API-key account uses api.openai.com coop gemini the Google model and Code Assist routes that co:op's Gemini adapter declares for the selected credential type coop grok cli-chat-proxy.grok.com, code.grok.com and auth.x.ai (the OAuth refresh) Provider rules don't include release feeds, package registries, update checks or telemetry (raw.githubusercontent.com, registry.npmjs.org, api.github.com and the Datadog intakes). co:op disables this traffic through each client's settings inside the box, and your host profiles stay unchanged. Updates are also disabled in co:op's images, so clients can't update themselves even when their home folders aren't mounted. Client In the box Update switch in co:op's image Claude runs with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 and DISABLE_UPDATES=1 DISABLE_UPDATES Codex reads a generated config.toml that sets check_for_update_on_startup = false, analytics.enabled = false and the otel exporters to none, on top of your own settings /etc/codex/managed_config.toml, which also turns off Codex's background server and its updater Gemini gets general.enableAutoUpdate, general.enableAutoUpdateNotification and privacy.usageStatisticsEnabled off, plus GEMINI_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false /etc/gemini-cli/settings.json Grok runs with GROK_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false and GROK_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 GROK_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER A session that only answers a prompt should produce no blocked requests from these background features. If the agent or your project requests one of these hosts directly, co:op records the blocked request as usual and never hides it from the report. You can inspect it and approve access.

heading: Provider credentials stay outside the box
text: API keys and OAuth or subscription accounts both use a provider broker for each Docker run, whether networking is open or filtered. The broker accepts requests only for the selected providers and accounts, and the provider folders mounted into the box never contain reusable credentials. The host can refresh credentials during a long run without restarting the client. Removing or replacing an account stops the old run from using it. Clients keep using their original provider URLs. co:op's adapter for each provider lists the origins and routes its client may use. A private loopback listener handles TLS for those origins. It checks each request's path, method and query, then adds the selected account's credentials before forwarding the request. Requests to undeclared routes on those origins are blocked. Only the run itself receives the broker's certificate authority, and co:op never installs it on the host or in a global trust store. The broker still verifies the provider's TLS certificate. Other origins follow the run's open or filtered network rules. A separate container with no Linux capabilities holds the short-lived credential snapshot. The box joins that container's network namespace after co:op inspects the container, but can't read the private snapshot or the CA signing key. When the run stops, co:op removes that container, so nothing can reach the broker. If the host stops renewing or publishing snapshots, they expire and the broker refuses access. Filtered runs keep their approved network rules, and co:op still records which traffic came from the box. Open runs still allow ordinary outbound traffic. The lead and its teammates share one account per provider inside a box. Run teammates in separate boxes if they shouldn't trust one another. A fallback list can include both API-key and subscription accounts. The supported API variables are ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY. co:op refuses alternate token variables, Vertex credentials and XAI_API_KEY instead of exposing them. Gemini's own plain-file OAuth credentials are supported, but an encrypted-only cache with no credential that co:op can import is not. co:op also refuses custom provider base URLs. Offline runs receive no provider keys and don't start a broker. Online provider runs need Docker with an ordinary bridge or a project services network. Host networking, arbitrary joins to another container's network, and Apple's container runtime don't support this setup.

heading: A client's own downloads
text: A client may need to download public files as well as call its model API. For example, Codex fetches its curated plugin store from chatgpt.com and github.com whenever an API-key run starts. These downloads use the broker's download route, which sends no credentials and rejects any that the box supplies. It allows only the exact requests that the provider's adapter lists, including their query strings. For Codex, these are: Host Request lines chatgpt.com GET /backend-api/plugins/featured?platform=codex github.com GET /openai/plugins.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack and POST /openai/plugins.git/git-upload-pack The github.com lines fetch one public repository and never push. The same discovery path with service=git-receive-pack isn't in the list. The broker never turns the public Git download route into general GitHub access. Other GitHub requests still require ordinary network approval in filtered mode.

heading: Filtered runs
text: Bearer tokens for MCP servers stay outside filtered boxes. When a shared server uses bearer_token_env_var, co:op adds a route for it to the run's broker. The MCP configuration inside the box points to that route's loopback listener and uses COOP_MCP_TOKEN_<n> instead of your token. This stand-in works only for that server and run, and the broker adds the real token when it forwards the request. The route allows only the server's exact URL path and the methods MCP uses: POST, GET and DELETE. It waits for long tool calls to finish. The agent can't bypass the broker by connecting directly to that server's host. Your token variables never enter a filtered box, even if that box doesn't load MCP. That covers every variable the default ~/.config/coop/agents/mcp.json or your COOP_MCP_FILE reads a secret from, whichever file is active and even with MCP turned off, because the env file holds those tokens either way. If one of these files is there but co:op can't read it, the launch stops and names the file. A session's ACP adapter receives the stand-in too. If a token is missing, co:op stops the launch, names the server and says to put the token in agents/env. A token variable passed with -e stops the launch too. Tools supplied by a remote session's controller use the same route, restricted to the server's exact path.

heading: Legacy SSE servers
text: Legacy SSE servers need broader access because they choose a message endpoint during each connection. co:op allows GET on the stream's path and POST on any path at the same host. Other hosts and methods are blocked, and the broker still sends only one secret header. The credential still stays outside the box, but a legacy SSE connection lets the box reach more paths on that host than streamable HTTP does. co:op names these servers at launch and explains what to ask their vendors for. Use a server's streamable HTTP URL when it offers one. Some legacy SSE servers return a full endpoint URL instead of a path, and the client then posts directly to that URL, bypassing co:op. Filtered networking blocks the request. Open networking sends only the stand-in, so authentication fails without exposing the real token. To use this server, switch to its streamable HTTP URL.

heading: Offline runs
text: An offline box can't reach remote MCP servers, so co:op removes them from its MCP configuration. The launch reports: "MCP servers that need internet are left out: …". Local command servers remain available, and the token variables stay outside the box, as in a filtered run. An offline remote session's editor adapter also receives only the local servers.

heading: Open runs
text: With open networking, the box connects directly to the internet, so co:op uses a separate helper container to keep supported MCP credentials outside the box. If the MCP configuration includes a remote server with a secret, co:op starts a helper from the gateway image (coop-net broker). It joins the box's network, and co:op adds a hosts entry so the box can find it. The helper runs without privileges (--cap-drop ALL, uid 65532, read-only root, 256 MB). It has the label coop=broker and the box's supervisor labels. The helper exits with the coop process that started it, even after a crash, and box cleanup removes any helper left behind. Inside the box, each brokered MCP server points to http://coop-broker:<port>, where the port is 15580 plus the server's index. The box sends a stand-in token, and the helper replaces it with the real credential and connects only to that server's host. Your token variable stays outside the box. The box talks to the helper over plain HTTP on the container network. If the project has no co:op-managed network, the helper uses Docker's default bridge, which is shared with other containers that have no assigned network. On that bridge, the stand-in token protects access to the credential. It's a random 256-bit value created for the run and accepted only by its own listener for its server's route. co:op controls the helper's hosts entry and rejects any --add-host argument that would replace it. Remote sessions with open networking also use the helper for tools the controller provides. co:op builds the helper image on first use. The MCP helper is separate from the provider broker used in open and filtered runs. It allows exact paths for streamable HTTP and the same-host routes described above for legacy SSE. The following servers still run with their secrets inside the box. co:op names each one at launch: a server whose secret is in two places, or whose secret header is anything other than literal text followed by one variable reference a server whose URL isn't plain https on port 443 every server, when the box has no network to reach a helper on (Apple's container runtime, --network none or --network container:… in your runtime arguments)

heading: Project services
text: A service: rule requests access to one project service and needs your approval. Before a filtered run starts, co:op recreates that service and its dependencies on an internal network owned by the project. They can talk to each other, but have no direct internet connection. With Docker Engine 26 or later, Docker's DNS server on this network resolves only service names. The filtered box sends its own DNS requests only to the gateway. The services reach the gateway through the standard HTTPS proxy variables. The gateway forwards requests only for approved TLS names, after checking the name in the actual ClientHello. Removing the proxy variables disconnects the services from the internet. It doesn't bypass the gateway. Allowed and blocked external requests appear in coop net watch, inspect, blocked and the JSON views, with the name of the Compose service they came from. Direct traffic between services stays on the internal network and isn't reported as external traffic. In filtered mode, you must name the service you need. co:op rejects box.network: true alone, and coop net shows the same refusal with the rules to add. coop init --services adds a rule for each service it sets up, so one coop approve lets the box reach them. For any other Compose file, coop approve lists the services and their ports and asks once whether to add and approve their rules: If you answer yes, it writes the rules under box.egress_rules, keeping the file's comments and order. It also saves each service's definition, so a later edit asks again. If you answer no, nothing changes. A service that declares no TCP port gets no guessed port. You need to finish its rule yourself. With no terminal, the command asks nothing and writes nothing. It shows the rules and box.network: false, and exits non-zero. A filtered run that needs project services waits for every other box in the project to stop before starting those services. Each loop run and editor session gets its own Compose project, network and volumes. A run started directly uses the project's development stack. The box gets COOP_SERVICE_<NAME>_URL with the service's name and port, such as https://keycloak:8443, for each expose port a rule allows. The box reaches only the services co:op starts for it, so it won't start with COOP_AUTO_UP=0 or box.auto_up: false while its approved rules name services. Unset the setting, or remove those rules and run coop approve. Service approval covers both the name and the Compose definition you reviewed, and each launch compares that definition with the current file. Changing db: to use a different image or network setup requires another approval. Changing an unrelated service doesn't. If the definition changed, the launch stops and tells you how to review it. coop net lists the change under ⚠ New runs need your approval as The Compose service "db" changed after its network access was approved.

heading: TLS ports and localhost
text: A tls rule isn't limited to port 443. It lists its ports, such as [443], [853] or [443, 8443], and the gateway redirects only those. It reads the original destination port from the kernel's SO_ORIGINAL_DST record, so the client can't choose a different port after the redirect. A request to an unlisted port is blocked and recorded with its port number. Connecting directly to the gateway's TLS listener is also blocked and counted, because that connection has no original destination port. You can run a test server on 127.0.0.1:3000 and use curl to reach it inside the box. This traffic stays inside the box's network namespace and never reaches your host or the gateway. The exception is Docker's DNS address, 127.0.0.11, which is blocked so the box uses only the gateway for DNS.

heading: Your project's image
text: You can use your own project image in filtered mode if its .agent/Dockerfile starts with ARG COOP_BASE_IMAGE=coop-box / FROM ${COOP_BASE_IMAGE}. Build it on the host with coop build --egress filtered, or with plain coop build when the project's effective network mode is filtered. co:op uses its locked client image as the base and tags the result coop-<repo>-<path hash>-filtered:<hash>. A filtered launch uses only a project image built from files you approved by running coop build. If the image is missing or the clients changed, co:op rebuilds those same files by itself. It works on a private snapshot and compares that snapshot with your approval first. If the build inputs changed, co:op asks you to review and rebuild, and coop update leaves that to you too. Build inputs include copied scripts and file modes, but not the secrets and Git metadata that co:op leaves out of the build. The message names the files that changed, or says that only a build setting or co:op's own client image did. coop build warns when the build context holds many files the Dockerfile never copies, since a change to any of them asks for another build. To keep unrelated edits from requiring a rebuild, list the files this image doesn't build from in .agent/Dockerfile.dockerignore, or in an ignore file named after your configured Dockerfile. Its rules take precedence over the root .dockerignore. The running box still sees excluded files through its repository mount. For a toolchain-only image, exclude everything with ** and add !path/to/input for each file it copies. The Dockerfile and the active ignore file always count as build inputs. A Docker exception can't bring back secrets, Git metadata, generated output or .agent/project.yaml. co:op leaves all of these out. .agent/project.yaml is never a build input, with or without an ignore file. Adding a network rule needs coop approve and no rebuild, and COPY . . can't put that file in an image. co:op refuses a Dockerfile that copies the file by name, so copy another file instead. Pointing box.dockerfile at another Dockerfile still needs a review and a build. Before starting the box, co:op checks the built image itself, because the Dockerfile's FROM line alone can't show what the image contains. Two checks must pass: The locked image's layers must be the first layers of the built image, so the box is that exact image plus your own layers. Every pinned client entry point must match the file in the locked image byte for byte. That covers each launcher, what it execs, and the native binaries it needs. co:op reads them out of a container that it creates and never starts, so nothing from the image runs to describe itself. You can add tools to the image, but you can't replace, wrap or delete a pinned client. The host setup checks cover co:op's own image, and your project image must pass both checks above on every launch. co:op rejects COOP_IMAGE because an arbitrary image hasn't passed those checks. A build gets its tag only after both checks pass. co:op removes an image that fails them, unless another tag or a container still uses it, and a run on the same files says why it was refused. co:op caches what it reads from an image outside every agent mount, tied to the image's ID. The base image uses the non-root box user. To install packages, put USER root before the installation commands and USER node after them. Review the Dockerfile and its copied files before building, because the build runs project instructions with ordinary Docker networking. --egress selects the image to build. It doesn't filter traffic during the build. co:op checks the resulting image and saves approval for its exact inputs outside the agent's mounts. If saving approval fails, the command fails even if Docker finished the build. An agent's edit can't reach a build's ordinary networking, because co:op rebuilds only files you approved. Such a rebuild fetches again whatever the approved Dockerfile fetches. An editor connection with open networking may build a missing image. An open-network run warns when the build inputs have changed, but keeps using the old image until you run coop build --egress open. Offline launches don't build project images automatically. co:op may still prepare its own embedded base, gateway and client images, but those builds don't run instructions from your repository.

text: Requested Message IPv6 address, CIDR, or icmpv6 IPv6 destinations are not supported yet — a filtered box runs on IPv4 only tls on port 53 TLS on port 53 is not allowed here — the gateway takes 53 for DNS; use 443 or another port raw tcp/udp on port 443 or 53 raw tcp to <dest> on port 443 is not allowed — the gateway takes 443 for TLS and DNS; use another port raw tcp on a port a tls rule also names raw tcp to <dest> on port 8443 clashes with a TLS rule on the same port — the gateway takes that port for TLS; use another port a serve port on a port the gateway takes for TLS or DNS port 8443 is one the gateway uses for TLS and DNS — serve on another port in filtered mode ICMP beyond echo-request ICMP N to <dest> is not supported yet — only echo-request is cidr: 0.0.0.0/0 a /0 rule allows everything, which is not filtering — use --egress open if that is what you want to: {provider: …} this release has no optional provider features to approve — an agent's core endpoints are allowed automatically, so drop the provider rule a host, loopback, link-local or metadata range <range> is a protected range (your host, loopback, link-local or cloud metadata) — no rule can allow it a project image not built on the client image this project's .agent/Dockerfile did not build on coop's client image — start it with ARG COOP_BASE_IMAGE=coop-box and FROM ${COOP_BASE_IMAGE} … a project image that changes a pinned client this project's .agent/Dockerfile changes claude's cli client at /opt/coop/bin/claude — a filtered box runs only the clients that coop net setup checked on this host … COOP_IMAGE a filtered box runs coop's own image — unset COOP_IMAGE to start one a runtime other than Docker, including a run with no mode set restricted networking needs docker; <runtime> cannot run the network gateway — run this with --egress open or --egress offline, set COOP_EGRESS, or set COOP_RUNTIME=docker box.network: true with no service: rule <Agent> cannot start because filtered boxes reach project services only through approved network rules, then a complete rule to paste for each Compose service. In a terminal, coop approve offers to add them COOP_AUTO_UP=0 with an approved service: rule a filtered box starts the project services its approved network rules name, and COOP_AUTO_UP=0 says not to start them — unset COOP_AUTO_UP, or drop the service rules from box.egress_rules and run coop approve. With box.auto_up: false instead, it names that setting -v /var/run:/x (or any mount of /run, /proc, /sys, /dev, /, or the Docker socket's directory) a filtered box cannot mount …: it is or holds …, which reaches Docker or the kernel a project file with an unapproved rule, or a changed rule <Agent> cannot start because this project asks for network access that has not been approved · Review it: coop approve a box.egress changed after the project's approval <Agent> cannot start because box.egress: offline in .agent/project.yaml has not been approved · Review it: coop approve. With COOP_EGRESS=open set, it adds , and COOP_EGRESS=open does not override an approval a project file with a rule that coop approve refuses <Agent> cannot start because this project asks for network access that cannot be approved: and the reason above · Change .agent/project.yaml, then review it: coop approve an --egress-rules file inside the project egress rules file <path> is inside <project>, which the box can reach — keep the rules file outside the project --allow-domain or --egress-rules beside --egress open or --egress offline Cannot combine "--egress offline" and "--allow-domain" in "coop run" · --allow-domain only adds to filtered access. Use --egress filtered, or leave out --allow-domain. (exit 2) --allow-domain or --egress-rules on a run that COOP_EGRESS, the project or its approval makes open or offline <Agent> cannot start because --allow-domain only adds to filtered access, and COOP_EGRESS=offline makes this run offline · Use --egress filtered, or leave out --allow-domain. a rules file that is a bare list, or nests its rules under box: --egress-rules takes a file that lists its rules under one top-level egress_rules key, like this:, then a rules file to copy open, in a project with no approval yet <Agent> cannot start because this project asks for unrestricted internet access, which has not been approved · Review it: coop approve an approved Compose service whose definition changed <Agent> cannot start because the Compose service "db" changed since it was approved · Review it: coop approve an approved project directory replaced by another at the same path <Agent> cannot start because the project directory at <path> was replaced since it was approved · Review it: coop approve an approved project whose marker was deleted, as by git clean -x <Agent> cannot start because this project's network approval marker is gone, as after git clean -x · Review it: coop approve an approved project whose marker was written over in place <Agent> cannot start because this project's network approval marker was written over · Review it: coop approve a checkout moved to a new folder with its marker <Agent> cannot start because this checkout has a network approval marker but no approval for its current location · Review it: coop approve If co:op can't enforce a rule, it stops the launch before saving approval or creating a container. It never starts a run with a requested restriction silently removed.

heading: Ranges no rule can reach
text: Some destinations can never be allowed, by a cidr: rule or any other rule: the host's own interface addresses every subnet the container runtime allocates and the gateway address it holds in each one, so sibling containers, other sessions' boxes and the daemon's own address are out of reach the loopback, link-local and metadata ranges co:op reads this list from the daemon at launch and updates it while the box runs.
