When another filtered box creates a network, or a VPN brings an interface up, co:op adds the new subnets, gateways and host addresses to the running box's protected set in one atomic kernel update. Those addresses are blocked as soon as the update takes effect. A network change stops the box only if the update is refused or the protected set would exceed 256 ranges. An address remains blocked after it disappears from the host. An approved CIDR can't override these protected ranges, and packets to protected addresses are still dropped and counted. The only exception is an approved service: rule: it allows the exact container address you approved, without allowing the rest of that subnet.

heading: Serve ports and mounts
text: A published serve port accepts connections only from the host. Other containers on the same bridge can't connect through it. A Docker socket or kernel control directory could let the agent bypass the gateway. For example, one curl request to a Docker socket could start another container outside the filtered network. So filtered runs reject mounts of /var/run, /run, /proc, /sys, /dev, / and the Docker endpoint's socket directory, and the error names the blocked mount. They also reject a mount whose source doesn't exist, which --egress open lets Docker create as an empty folder.

heading: Observed versus counted
text: coop net inspect [<run>] shows network activity for a run, or this project's newest one if you omit the run. The report starts with totals for allowed traffic, then lists every destination the box or its Compose services reached. The rest of the report lists problems: blocked attempts, alerts, missing evidence, parts of the network setup that didn't run normally, and unfinished cleanup. A clean run omits these sections. --json includes every field. At the end of an interactive filtered run, co:op saves the final network record and prints the same report on stderr under Networking stats:. First, it says why the box stopped, as in The Coop box has stopped: main process exited with status 0. When Ctrl-C reached coop, the reason is interrupted by Ctrl-C. What the report shows depends on what co:op could record: For TLS traffic, the gateway records each connection's requested name, resolved address and transferred bytes. It also saves an event when it blocks a name. coop net blocked <host> finds this project's newest run that blocked that host, groups its blocked attempts by cause and counts repeats. Use --run <run> to choose a run, and with it you can supply an exact event ID instead of a host. When no recorded block matches, it says so and exits 1, as grep does. A blocked DNS lookup doesn't record which port the program wanted, so coop net blocked shows a rule for TLS on port 443, labeled as the likely fix. A direct connection to an address the run looked up, such as http:// to a name approved only for TLS or https:// to a port its rule doesn't list, is listed under that name with the address and port beside it, so coop net blocked <host> finds it. For a port other than 80, it shows a rule for TLS on that port, labeled as the likely fix. An address that two looked-up names share is listed as an address. For raw traffic, the kernel counts packets and bytes for each approved address rule. These appear under Raw traffic in coop net inspect, each row named by its rule, such as 10.42.8.0/24:5432 · TCP or 1.1.1.1 · ICMP echo-request, and as address_grants in --json. Raw traffic isn't counted as connections, so a run that sent only raw traffic shows Allowed raw traffic only. Individual hosts within a CIDR aren't recorded or shown. For other blocked packets, the filter counts how many it drops but doesn't record their destinations, so the report shows only a count (N packets were blocked, and Coop did not record where they were going). coop net blocked has no destination record to open, so check the program's own error for the address it wanted. When the report also lists a direct connection, whose packets are part of that count, it reads N packets were dropped in all, direct connections included. An unmeasured metric appears as UNKNOWN, never zero. A total is also UNKNOWN if any part of it wasn't measured. Only traffic co:op can identify as coming from the box or its Compose services appears as Allowed. co:op's own resolver connection and a closing kernel socket with no owner appear only in --json. Other connections that co:op can't tie to either one appear under Other observed endpoints with the reason, and don't count as allowed traffic.

heading: Runs, checks and exports
text: Use any unique prefix of a run's ID to select it. The eight characters shown by coop net runs work with every run command. If a prefix matches more than one run, co:op refuses it and shows the longer prefixes you can use. These commands use the same project as coop run: the Git repository you're in, or the current folder outside Git. coop net runs shows this project's 25 newest runs. When there are more, it shows a count and the --all option. A run that is still going is marked live. Use --all-projects to see runs from every project, labeled by name and path. With --json, the listing has total and more, each run has live, and with --all-projects each run also has project_name and project_path. co:op keeps a finished run's record for 90 days after it ends. If cleanup is still pending, it keeps the record until cleanup finishes. Each run also keeps a copy of the rules it started with, which the --run option below reads. co:op removes the saved copy of a launch's rules only when no retained run record refers to it and no launch has used it for 90 days. It keeps the copy a worker session was created with for the whole session. An editor session that starts no box for 90 days may need to be started again. A copy made by coop net setup is removed along with that check's run record. coop net check <url-or-host> tells you whether the rules would allow a normal new run in this project to reach a destination. It gives one answer and one reason, based on the approved project rules and each agent's provider access. Use --run <run> to check the rules a recorded run started with instead. Neither check sends network traffic. The exit status is the answer: 0: the rules allow the connection 3: the rules block it, or new runs need approval first 1: the check could not finish 2: invalid arguments To check an IP address, also specify --protocol tcp|udp --port <n> (or --icmp) and a run, because the answer depends on the transport and that run's protected ranges. A blocked answer names what no rule covered: the address, its port, or the connection type. coop net export <run> exports the run's final record as JSON. It leaves out destination names and addresses by default, because even a blocked name can contain a secret. Use --include-addresses to include them in the export on your machine. The digest is a checksum of the exported content. It isn't a signature and doesn't make a partial record complete.

heading: Asking for access
text: Add the rule to .agent/project.yaml under box.egress_rules, then ask a human to run coop approve on the host. Editing the repository file requests access but doesn't grant it. co:op stores approval outside the repository, so editing or deleting the file can't widen access, and nothing inside the box can approve its own request. New runs use the approved rules, and a box that's already running keeps the rules it started with. In a filtered editor session (coop acp), each new thread starts with a note naming what the agent can reach and how to allow more. A running editor session can pick up a new approval without reconnecting. Once no prompt is running, co:op starts a box with the new rules, then stops the old box and any processes left in it, and the editor shows a line explaining this. A box started for another reason, such as a crash or provider switch, also gets the new rules. If co:op can't apply the rules, or the new box stops before the switch, the session keeps its previous rules and explains why. After coop net forget, a running session keeps its rules until you reconnect the editor.

heading: Reviewing a request
text: Approval covers the file's exact network mode, rules and the reviewed definition of every service: it names. To change network access, edit the file and review it again. Before saving approval, coop approve checks that the runtime can enforce the rules, just as it does at launch. It refuses unsupported rules, such as an IPv6 destination, rules that clash, such as raw TCP on a port a TLS rule names, and a serve port the gateway takes, so they can't be approved and then fail at every launch. Plain coop approve doesn't allow any file exposure. With mount protection, a launch may refuse hidden files that stay readable under another letter case. To review that permission as well, use coop approve --case-exposure. A run that uses eBPF enforcement protects those files without this approval. See hiding secrets. The review compares the request with the access already approved. Unchanged rules have no marker, additions use + and removals use -. co:op explains any network mode change in plain words, and a request for open gets a red warning because it would allow unrestricted traffic. To confirm, answer Approve this access for new runs and running editor sessions? [y/N]. If the file is already exactly what was approved, coop approve prints No approval needed: this project's requested access has not changed. and grants nothing new. If a filtered box still can't start because the project's services have no network rules, it says that instead and offers to add them. See project services. Provider endpoints aren't shown as access the project requested, because co:op allows the endpoints each agent needs.

heading: Pending requests
text: If the project's request differs from your saved approval, co:op treats it as pending: coop init ends with ⚠ New runs need your approval, the reason, and Review changes: coop approve. Running coop net without a subcommand shows the same comparison under ⚠ New runs need your approval. Every launch stops before starting a box or its main process. It explains why and prints Review it: coop approve. This applies to coop run, a named agent, coop loop, an interactive fork, fork ACP, and a fork review or merge gate. If coop approve would refuse the request, a launch and coop net give its reason and ask you to change .agent/project.yaml first. coop acp connects your editor anyway and runs no agent until you approve. See editors. A withdrawn approval, a replaced project folder or an offline setting still stops it.

heading: Access for one run
text: For one run, use --allow-domain <host> to allow an exact name over TLS on port 443, or pass --egress-rules <path> to add the rules in a file. Both add to the project's approved rules for that run only. A rules file lists its rules under one top-level egress_rules key, the way .agent/project.yaml lists them under box.egress_rules: egress_rules: - to: {domain: "docs.example.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] Keep the file outside the project. co:op refuses a rules file inside a folder mounted into the agent's box, where the agent could write its own rules, and a file with other hard links or one that someone else can change. Both flags only add to filtered access, and co:op refuses them by name on an open or offline run.

heading: The approval follows the directory
text: Approval belongs to the project directory itself. If you move an approved checkout aside and put another checkout at the same path, co:op refuses the next launch until a human reviews it again. coop net reports that access is blocked and names the command to review it. co:op identifies the directory by a hidden marker file with 0600 permissions. The marker is hard-linked to a file in co:op's private state, so the checkout and $XDG_STATE_HOME (or ~/.local/state) must be on the same filesystem, and that filesystem must support hard links. The marker contains identifiers, not credentials. Running git clean -x removes ignored files, including this marker. Run coop approve again to review and restore access. Copying the marker's contents doesn't restore its hard link. If you move a checkout with its marker intact, coop approve can recover it. It verifies the marker against co:op's private hard link, removes the old marker and private link, then asks you to approve the checkout's new path. A copied marker can't inherit the original checkout's access or cancel its approval. If a marker is malformed, inspect it with ls -l -- ./.coop-network-approval. Only after confirming it's stale, remove it inside that checkout with rm -- ./.coop-network-approval, then run coop approve again. Writing the marker in place, as printf … > .coop-network-approval does, also changes co:op's private hard link, so the approval no longer applies. coop approve replaces both once you review the access again, and coop net forget removes them. The box can see the marker, so co:op also checks the paths in runtime mount arguments: You may mount the exact project directory. You may not mount a path inside it that an existing agent could swap before Docker opens the mount, or a writable parent directory that would let the agent replace the project. No mount may expose co:op's private state, even read-only. That includes the paths it will use for network state, forks, execution records and launch locks on a first run, before those paths exist. co:op inspects existing named volumes. When it uses the marker to verify approval, it refuses --volumes-from and custom volume-driver options. To mount a cache, keep it outside the checkout and name its path explicitly so co:op can inspect it.

heading: Forgetting an approval
text: coop net forget removes a project's approval. It shows the saved access, asks you to confirm in the terminal, then removes only that approval record. Run it in the project, or pass --project <path> if the checkout is already gone. Run records, their receipts and this host's setup results stay. Until you approve again, only offline runs of that project start. If the approved path was a symlink, the approval belongs to the directory it pointed to. Once both the symlink and directory are gone, co:op can't find the approval from that path. coop net forget explains this and leaves other projects' approvals alone.

heading: When a run is interrupted
text: The coop process that starts a filtered run manages its gateway containers, volumes and network record. If it dies because of SIGKILL, a crash or a reboot, the run stays cleanup pending until co:op recovers it. If it died after cleanup but before saving the final record, the status is final record missing. co:op attempts recovery automatically: coop net inspect makes one recovery attempt for that run, with a time limit, before reporting its cleanup status. Starting a loop, fork or build checks for runs waiting for cleanup and attempts recovery. Every filtered launch does the same before starting its own box. If recovery succeeds, you don't need to do anything. If it can't finish, co:op reports what prevented it, such as Docker being stopped, a different daemon at the saved endpoint, a resource it couldn't remove, or a resource Docker may still be creating. If Docker never answered a request to create a resource, co:op counts that resource as gone only if it's still missing ten minutes later. coop net inspect shows ⚠ Cleanup incomplete — <the blocker> and what to do next, and co:op retries automatically. To recover runs now: coop net recover # settle every pending run now coop net recover <run> # settle one run now Without a run, coop net recover reports only the runs it cleaned up or couldn't clean up. A run whose own coop process is still running, in this project or another, is left for that process to clean up and isn't listed. Name the run to see why it was left alone. When coop net recover can't finish a run, it prints ⚠ Cleanup incomplete for network run <run>, followed by the causes and what to do next. An unreadable run record doesn't stop recovery of the others: co:op names any records it couldn't read and exits 1. Recovery removes only that run's resources, using their exact names and the run's labels. It never matches a name prefix or runs a general prune. It saves a final receipt marked partial, with the workload outcome supervisor_lost.

heading: Agents, accounts and presets
text: Sign in, choose models and accounts, and configure presets, teammates and instructions. co:op runs four coding agents, with a choice of accounts and models. You can add peers for second opinions, use presets and provide instructions for each agent. For short introductions, see credentials, models, second opinions and presets.

heading: Where agent settings live
text: co:op gives each repository and selected account its own provider folder. The box mounts it where the provider normally keeps its files, so conversation history, saved sessions, settings and indexes stay together. Provider Home in the box Settings inside that home Claude ~/.claude settings.json Codex ~/.codex config.toml Gemini ~/.gemini settings.json Grok ~/.grok config.toml Under ~/.config/coop/agents/<agent>/, co:op keeps these separate folders: Path What it holds credentials/<name>/ the account's credentials and sign-in records, kept only on the host native-homes/<name>/<repository-key>/home/ the provider's history, settings and other files for this repository and account acp-homes/<repository-key>/home/ one repository's editor-session files, kept when you switch accounts profiles/<name>/ what Coop before v11 kept here. Nothing reads or mounts it, and Coop never deletes it co:op sets its own defaults in a new provider folder once. Later changes stay with that repository, and changing the defaults doesn't overwrite an existing folder. A fork co:op created shares its parent's history storage, and unrelated repositories keep separate history.

heading: What each run can see
text: A box gets provider folders only for its lead, named peers and preset roles. Shell, raw-command and maintenance boxes get none. Sign-in runs in a separate sign-in home for the selected provider, with no project mounted. API keys and OAuth access and refresh tokens stay outside coding boxes. Each run has a broker that adds the credentials to requests sent to the selected provider, and the host renews expiring credentials without stopping the run. All agents using the same provider in one box share its selected account. Put agents you don't trust with each other's access in separate boxes.

heading: Blast radius
text: A compromised agent can read and change the history and settings saved for its current repository, and it can use the selected account through the run's broker. A hook it adds to those settings can run again in later boxes for the same repository and account. Keeping repositories separate doesn't protect those local files from the agent or limit what it can spend with the provider. The provider folders co:op mounts don't give the agent access to another repository's provider files. Open networking still lets it send traffic to any destination. To restrict destinations, use filtered networking. To turn networking off, use --egress offline or COOP_EGRESS=offline. Offline runs receive no provider credentials. Manage shared accounts on the host with coop login and coop credentials … rm. Don't use a provider's own login or logout command inside a coding box. If local authentication files don't match the account state co:op expects, it stops the next launch and keeps the files so you can recover them. See migration and recovery.

heading: Sign in
text: Sign in with coop login: coop login claude # interactive login; credentials stay in host-only storage coop login codex # device-code login (the box has no browser for an OAuth redirect) coop login gemini # hidden API-key prompt; stored outside the mounted Gemini home coop login grok # device-code login, like Codex coop claude login does the same as coop login claude, and coop claude@work login signs in to the work account.

heading: API keys
text: Supported API keys work with both open and filtered Docker networking. Put a key in the shared env file, or use the provider's sign-in flow on the host: install -d -m 700 ~/.config/coop/agents touch ~/.config/coop/agents/env chmod 600 ~/.config/coop/agents/env echo 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-…' >> ~/.config/coop/agents/env echo 'OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-…' >> ~/.config/coop/agents/env echo 'GEMINI_API_KEY=AIza…' >> ~/.config/coop/agents/env co:op lets only your user access the credential folder (0700) and its secret files (0600). Provider Supported key Refused alternatives Claude ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN Codex OPENAI_API_KEY CODEX_API_KEY, CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN Gemini GEMINI_API_KEY Vertex GOOGLE_API_KEY Grok none XAI_API_KEY Subscription and OAuth accounts also keep their credentials on the host. Loops, peers, presets, editor sessions and remote sessions all use the broker, so you can switch between API-key and subscription accounts across runs without exposing either account's credentials to the box. The broker needs a private Docker network namespace to keep provider credentials outside the box, so an online provider run can't use host networking, join another container's network or use Apple's container runtime. co:op also refuses custom provider base URLs and credential types it doesn't support. See provider networking.

heading: The env file
text: KEY=value sets a value directly. A bare KEY copies the value from the environment of the process running co:op, and co:op leaves it out if that variable is unset. When a variable appears more than once, the last assignment or successful import wins. A login supplied only through the env file appears as the provider's default credential in coop credentials, and it covers only that default account. To add named accounts, save a separate login for each one. When you run a stored named account, even your default, co:op leaves that provider's token variables out of the run so they can't override the selected login. co:op shares non-credential variables, such as DATABASE_URL and COOP_NO_ASDF, with every box.

heading: What the box receives
text: The box receives only the public authentication values the provider's native client needs and a private connection to the run's broker. Before launch, co:op removes reusable provider keys and tokens from both the user and project environment. It refuses provider credentials passed through the runtime's -e flag, because that would expose them directly to the box. Sign-in boxes also receive none of the existing API keys from the shared env file or the host's account store.

heading: First run
text: On the first run, co:op answers the provider's setup prompts inside the box: Claude's theme, folder-trust and bypass warnings, Codex's "trust this directory?", and Gemini's and Grok's folder trust. You don't need to repeat this setup after signing in. co:op treats the mounted repository as trusted inside the container, where the box provides the sandbox.

heading: Several accounts and failover
text: You can save several accounts for one provider, each with its own name and usage limits. When one account reaches its limit, an unattended run can switch to another account and keep working. coop login claude@work # a second account… coop login claude@personal # …and a third coop credentials # list them and which are signed in coop usage # limits and a 30-day API estimate coop usage codex@work # include history and pricing details for one account

heading: Failover
text: When coop loop (or a coop fork --loop) reaches a rate or usage limit, it switches to the next target. It waits only when every target has reached its limit. A Zed (ACP) session also switches targets, sends your prompt again and updates the toolbar selection. If every account is limited, it waits until the first limit resets. The lead's agent: list, called a ladder, sets the order of models and accounts to try. You don't need to configure a separate account pool: With no preset, the loop rotates the agent's default model across every signed-in account. A bare model (no @account) in a ladder does the same. A pinned model@account runs just that one account. co:op tracks limits for each model and account pair, so claude-opus-5-5@personal stays usable while claude-opus-5-5@work waits for its limit to reset. A ladder tries its fallbacks in the order you write them, and each step can move to a cheaper model, another account, or both. For example, run coop presets init my-ladder, then edit that preset's lead: # .agent/presets/my-ladder/preset.yaml (lead excerpt) lead: # Opus on all accounts, then Fable on work. agent: [claude:claude-opus-5-5, claude:claude-fable-5-1@work] coop loop my-ladder # rotates that ladder; coop presets shows every recipe coop loop claude:opus@work # or a one-off single target, no preset Switching accounts loses no work. Each loop iteration is a fresh run, and the queue and Git carry the progress.

heading: Choose the default account
text: The default account is the login a plain interactive coop claude uses. The first account you sign in to becomes the default, even when you give it a name. Account names have no special meaning, so choose names that help you recognize them. Use coop credentials <agent> <credential> default to set the default, or coop credentials <agent> <credential> rm to remove an account: coop credentials claude personal default # `coop claude` now runs on the personal account

heading: Picking models
text: To choose a model for a run, include it in the target as <agent>:<model>. This works for interactive sessions, loops, forks and editor connections: coop claude:opus # one big-model interactive session coop claude:fable --peer codex --peer gemini # the lead's model (peers keep their own) coop loop claude:haiku # a cheap overnight grind coop fork risky claude:opus # a careful fork on the big model coop acp claude:sonnet # pin an editor entry's model Save the model in a preset if you use it regularly. Each of its roles chooses its own model. Credentials select the account and subscription, not the model. coop models # the model menu per agent coop claude:opus # one run on the big model coop codex/high # default model at high reasoning effort coop claude:opus/xhigh # …at extra-high reasoning effort (low·medium·high·xhigh·max) coop frontier # a standing lead model + roles, from the preset (its lead leads) COOP_<AGENT>_MODEL sets the agent-wide default, for example COOP_CLAUDE_MODEL=fable. Use .agent/loop.yaml to choose a model for each loop step. work.agent selects the model that works on tasks, and signoff.agent lets you use a stronger model for the final review. Choose each fork's target or preset in coop fork <name> <target|preset> --loop. If several settings choose a model, the most specific wins: the target's :model the preset ladder's active entry COOP_<AGENT>_MODEL a model baked into COOP_<AGENT>_CMD the agent CLI's own default

heading: Reasoning effort
text: Set reasoning effort on the same target by adding /effort after the provider or the optional model: coop codex/high, coop codex:gpt-6-astra/high, coop claude:opus/xhigh, coop loop claude:opus/low. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max. co:op refuses known unsupported model-and-effort combinations before starting. It passes any other level to the agent's CLI: Agent Where the level goes Claude --effort Codex model_reasoning_effort Grok --reasoning-effort Gemini its thinking setting (low or high only) Haiku 4.5 doesn't support reasoning-effort settings, and co:op refuses the combination before starting. Use claude:haiku without an effort suffix, or a model that supports the setting, such as claude:opus/low. co:op accepts low or high for Gemini models it can map to the thinking setting, and checks the value before launch. If you've explicitly saved a thinking setting for a model in your own Gemini settings, that setting takes precedence. Effort uses the same priority order as model selection, and you can set both together: a target's :model/effort, COOP_<AGENT>_MODEL and a loop.yaml step's agent: all accept model[/effort]. For example, signoff.agent: [claude:opus/xhigh] uses xhigh effort for final review while you keep the work step at low effort.

heading: Which model runs
text: Each consult peer follows the same model-selection rules and uses its own default when you don't name a model. coop loop shows the model reported by the agent at the start of each iteration. coop models lists the models for each agent. Model IDs change, so co:op passes the ID to the provider's CLI without checking it against a fixed catalog, and the CLI reports its own error for an invalid one.

heading: Second opinions
text: Add read-only peers when you want the lead to get another model's opinion on difficult or risky decisions. The lead decides whether to ask and how to use the answer, and it makes all changes itself. Peers work with interactive runs, loops, forks, ACP and preset consult roles: coop codex --peer claude --peer gemini coop loop claude --peer codex --peer gemini coop acp claude --peer codex Add each peer with --peer <target>, repeating the flag for more. This also works with a codex, gemini or grok lead. The lead can use coop-consult to ask several peers in parallel. A peer may use the lead's provider with another model, for example coop claude:opus@work --peer claude:haiku. It shares the lead's selected account, and other providers use their default account. --peer doesn't accept @account, because one box selects one account per provider. Peers are off by default, and only the peers you name are available. co:op mounts the selected providers' repository homes writable, and the run's broker authenticates the peers' requests. Only the lead gets consultation instructions, so a peer isn't told to consult more peers. Each consultation starts another read-only model run, so include that usage when choosing how many peers to add.

heading: Inside the box
text: Call a preset's consult role by its role name. Several roles can use the same provider while keeping separate models and instructions. Inside the box, use: coop-consult claude --fresh "<prompt>" # new read-only session; never edits coop-consult gemini --continue "<prompt>" # resume the peer's thread; send only the delta A peer has none of the lead's conversation, so the lead writes a self-contained prompt instead of forwarding your message word for word.

heading: Continuity and fallback
text: Use --fresh to start a new consultation or --continue to follow up on the peer's last one. coop-consult manages session IDs for you. If co:op can recover the earlier conversation from a saved transcript, it tells the lead to send just the new information. Otherwise the lead needs to supply the full background. co:op can resume a new session only after it has returned a usable reply. If resuming fails, co:op reports the failure and doesn't reuse the failed ID or make a second paid call on its own. The next --continue starts a new session with the target that last succeeded, using the last complete transcript and your new information. co:op tries the next fallback target after a confirmed rate limit, a permanent failure, or an ordinary failure that happens again on one retry. A target has failed permanently if it can't start, has invalid configuration or can't sign in, and co:op skips it for the rest of the run. A timeout or too much output ends the call with an error and doesn't trigger another paid attempt on a fallback target. Follow-up consultations use the target that last succeeded.

heading: Limits
text: co:op shows the provider's stderr as diagnostics, and it never saves stderr or treats it as the peer's answer. What Cap Provider reply and diagnostic streams unlimited by default. COOP_CONSULT_STREAM_LIMIT sets a limit in bytes Consult time unlimited by default. COOP_CONSULT_TIMEOUT sets a limit in whole seconds stdin 512 KiB Constructed prompts 512 KiB Saved transcripts 512 KiB If output exceeds a limit, co:op doesn't try a fallback target or save a partial reply. If a complete reply is too large for the saved transcript, co:op returns it but can't resume that conversation, so use --fresh for the next call. Only one consultation can use a target at a time, and a second call waits for the first to release its lock. A custom image without flock uses a mkdir lock instead and refuses access when it can't safely acquire that lock.

heading: Token usage in loops
text: Inside coop loop, co:op records each provider's consultation usage in the active run's private, Git-ignored .agent/runs/<run>.peers.jsonl. Each successful consultation adds at most one row with the token counts and cost reported by the provider, and failed consultations add nothing. If the box can't write that file, the first consultation says why its usage wasn't recorded; the reply is unaffected.

heading: The orchestrator pattern
text: Use your strongest model to plan the work, break it into tasks and combine the results. Subagents use the models you assign to them, so routine implementation can run on cheaper models. Peers from other providers give independent opinions. This uses co:op's built-in tools: coop claude:claude-fable-5-1 --peer codex --peer gemini # run it; --peer mounts the named peers Save the lead model and roles in a preset to reuse this setup. Start it with coop <name> or coop loop <name>. In .claude/agents/, assign a larger model to reasoning work and a cheaper model to routine implementation. These are native Claude Code subagents: the lead chooses them from their descriptions, and each turn is billed at the subagent's model. coop init doesn't create these roles, so write your own repository roles or use a preset, which generates its own coop-<role> inside the box. With --peer <target>..., the lead can ask the named peers read-only through coop-consult <peer>, which needs no vendor plugin, keeps one writer per working tree and limits provider access to the accounts selected for the run. For high-stakes decisions, ask a native subagent and a peer to examine the same problem in parallel. Keep their answers separate until both finish, then compare them and decide. Use coop loop claude:claude-fable-5-1 --peer codex --peer gemini for the same setup in an unattended loop. Each iteration gets the subagents defined in the repo and the peers named by --peer. This also works in a fork loop: coop fork <name> claude --loop --peer codex --peer gemini.

heading: Presets
text: A preset saves the model and peer choices you'd otherwise pass with :model and --peer <target>. Store it under .agent/presets/<name>/. It names the lead, the roles it can call and when to use each role. Each role uses one of three modes: Mode What the role is native a subagent running inside the lead's own session consult a read-only advisor called with coop-consult delegate a worker that can edit files, called with coop-delegate An example recipe: lead: # agent: is a TARGET, or a fallback LADDER (model-first, even cross-provider). A bare # provider:model runs on EVERY signed-in account (rotating on rate limit); @account pins # one. On a loop it rotates top-to-bottom (running each rung's agent); a single run uses # the first. The model+account ride agent:. agent: [claude:claude-opus-5-5/xhigh, codex:gpt-6-astra/xhigh] prompt: roles/lead.md # optional Markdown, appended to the generated contract roles: thinker: # deep thinking + review, read-only mode: consult # native would run it in the lead's session: every lead must be claude agent: claude:claude-fable-5-1/max # model + effort ride agent: when: [architecture, debugging, code-review, before-commit] prompt: roles/thinker.md # the persona it answers as critic: # independent critique from another vendor, read-only mode: consult agent: [codex:gpt-6-astra/xhigh, grok:grok-4.5/high] when: [plan-review, security, tradeoffs] fast: # cheap mechanical work, write-capable mode: delegate agent: [gemini:gemini-3.8-flash, codex:gpt-6-luna] when: [boilerplate, bulk-edits, test-scaffolding, repo-survey] commit: never # it edits; the LEAD reviews the diff, gates, commits concurrent: never # delegate runs are serialized

heading: Run a preset
text: Use the preset name where the command expects a target, and co:op runs its lead. A target in that position (<agent>[:model][/effort][@account]) runs the agent directly: coop presets init # scaffold the recipe + starter prompt files, ready to edit coop frontier # interactive lead with the full routing contract coop loop frontier # unattended: lead credentials rotate, roles ride along coop acp frontier # the same preset from an editor An interactive terminal run uses the first lead target in the preset, while ACP keeps the full fallback list.

heading: Where presets live
text: co:op looks for presets in these locations, using the repository copy first: the repo's .agent/presets/<name>/ the per-user global directory ~/.config/coop/presets/, which COOP_PRESETS_DIR overrides A global preset such as frontier works across repositories without symlinks. If a repository has a preset with the same name, co:op uses only that copy and doesn't merge the two. The SOURCE column of coop presets says project or global. coop presets init creates presets in the repository. To create a global preset, write it in the global directory yourself.

heading: What co:op generates
text: co:op reads the YAML and tells the lead which roles are available, when to use them and how to call them. Depending on the role, that means the coop-thinker subagent, coop-consult critic --fresh "…", or a coop-delegate fast <<'EOF' … EOF heredoc. If co:op can't create any required instruction file, helper or role prompt, it stops before starting the provider. A native role runs inside the lead's session, so every lead listed in the preset must use that role's provider. If they don't match, co:op stops before launch and tells you which role to change. It generates native subagents for Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok in each client's own format. The generated coop-<role> uses the role's model, when rules and prompt. It exists only in the box, and .gitignore keeps these generated files out of commits. Set subagent: <name> to use a subagent the lead's client already has. coop presets init creates starter prompts in roles/lead.md, roles/thinker.md, roles/critic.md and roles/fast.md, which you can edit or delete. co:op adds their text to its generated instructions, and that text can't replace the safety rules or the rules for calling roles.

heading: Fallback ladders
text: Consult and delegate roles accept one target or a fallback list. co:op skips providers without credentials and mounts each available provider's repository home in the lead's box, and the run's broker handles authentication. A consult role tries its fallback targets under the rules in Continuity and fallback. Delegates use the stricter fallback rules below.

heading: Delegates
text: Delegates share the working tree and run one at a time, and they must never commit. co:op checks HEAD, Git refs and reflogs before and after each attempt. If a delegate changes Git history, co:op reports an error and keeps the evidence. co:op tries the next delegate target only after a confirmed rate limit, a failure to start or a refused login, and it skips that target for the rest of the run. Before trying another, it checks that the failed attempt changed no Git history or files, including tracked, untracked, staged and ignored files. The only exception is co:op's own run record in .agent/runs. co:op limits the prompt size, output size and duration of each delegate attempt. The standard image includes the flock, setsid and timeout this needs, and a custom image missing them refuses to run the delegate. A delegate can't start another delegate, but it can still ask a configured coop-consult for read-only advice. The lead reviews git diff, runs the configured checks, fixes or reverts changes it doesn't accept, and makes the commit. If co:op refuses a delegate attempt, inspect the result with git status --short, git diff and git diff --cached, plus git log and git reflog if history changed.

heading: Instructions
text: coop init sets up shared instructions for all agents. It links CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md to one AGENTS.md and gives every agent the same project skills source. An existing instruction file stays unchanged if it's a regular file, not a symlink.

heading: Instructions that follow you
text: Put guidance for all your repositories in ~/.config/coop/agents/INSTRUCTIONS.md. Keep project-specific rules in that repo's AGENTS.md. Inside the box, co:op makes the shared file available at each agent's global instruction path: Agent Global instruction path Claude ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Codex ~/.codex/AGENTS.md Gemini ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md Grok ~/.grok/AGENTS.md If the selected repository's provider folder already has its own instruction file, co:op uses it instead of the shared file. Edit that file for a local change, or the shared INSTRUCTIONS.md for repositories with no local override.

heading: Skills and the .agent/ folder
text: coop init creates the agent directories (.claude/, .codex/, .gemini/, .grok/) only for agents you're signed in to. You can choose them explicitly with --agents claude,codex, or use all. You can delete an agent's directory from a repo that doesn't use it. If you later run that agent in a box, co:op copies the workflow skills from .agent/skills into ~/.<agent>/skills inside the box. The copy is writable, but the host source stays unchanged. You need the repository directory again only if you run the agent's own CLI directly on the host. When the repository has an agent directory, co:op uses that committed copy as it is, and the agent can edit it. If the repo already has a real .claude/skills directory but no .agent/skills, coop init keeps that directory as the skills source and adds none of co:op's templates. Existing valid skills links stay unchanged.

heading: Claude settings and hooks
text: coop init keeps fallback Claude settings in .agent/claude/settings.json and hooks in .agent/claude/hooks/. For each run, a Claude box copies whichever of these is missing into ~/.claude. Existing project .claude/settings.json and .claude/hooks/ each take precedence on their own, so having one doesn't disable the fallback for the other. These temporary copies never change the host's .agent/ source.

heading: Editors, MCP and controllers
text: Connect an editor or MCP server and check which actions run on your computer or in the container. Use this reference to connect an editor over ACP, share MCP servers across agents, or run co:op workers for a controller. For a shorter introduction, see the guide's Editors and MCP and remote sessions sections.

heading: Zed and other ACP editors
text: Use Zed or another ACP editor to work with an agent running in a co:op box. You send prompts from the editor's agent panel, and co:op runs the agent in the box and handles account rotation.

heading: Set up Zed
text: Install co:op. The install one-liner puts coop on your PATH and builds an image with the ACP adapters included. Check that your shell can find it: command -v coop # e.g. /Users/you/.local/bin/coop Sign in to the agent you'll use. See Authentication. coop login claude # or codex / gemini / grok Register co:op in Zed. In the agent panel, use Add Custom Agent, or edit settings.json directly: { "agent_servers": { "coop": { "type": "custom", "command": "coop", // absolute path if Zed's PATH lacks ~/.local/bin "args": ["acp"] // automatic startup; choose in the live toolbar }, "coop · second opinion": { "type": "custom", "command": "coop", "args": ["acp", "claude:opus/xhigh", "--peer", "codex"] // named peer; the lead's model/effort ride the target } } } Open the agent panel, pick coop from the dropdown and start a thread. GUI apps don't always inherit your shell's PATH. If Zed can't find coop, use the absolute path from step 1 as command.

heading: Pick the provider, model and account
text: Without a target, co:op checks Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok in that order and starts the first signed-in provider with its default account. You can change the provider or choose a preset in the toolbar. If no provider is signed in, run coop login <agent> and reconnect the editor. To choose the starting model, reasoning effort and account, add a target to args in the form provider[:model][/effort][@account], such as ["acp","claude:opus/xhigh@work"]. Set these in the target, not in the editor's separate defaults. The toolbar shows your target's choices, and you can still change them during the thread.

heading: Remote repositories
text: For a repository on another machine, use Zed Remote Development. Open the repository through Zed's SSH remote workflow, then register command: "coop", args: ["acp", "<target>"] there. The editor, terminal and ACP process then use the same remote filesystem and absolute paths. If the editor must stay local, its custom-agent command can be SSH itself: { "agent_servers": { "coop · remote": { "type": "custom", "command": "ssh", "args": ["-T", "dev@coop-host", "cd /srv/projects/my-repo && exec coop acp claude"] } } } SSH carries the process's input and output, and co:op doesn't open a TCP listener for ACP. Use this setup only if Zed can resolve the same absolute repository paths that the remote ACP process reports. If the machines use different paths, use native Remote Development.

heading: What runs in the box
text: Zed runs coop acp [<target|preset>] in the project directory. That starts the selected provider's ACP adapter in the box, and the adapter talks ACP to the editor over stdio. Provider Adapter in the box Claude @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp Codex @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp Gemini gemini --acp Grok grok agent stdio In a normal writable session, co:op mounts the repository at its real host path, so Zed's absolute file paths resolve correctly. Tool calls don't ask for permission. co:op runs editor sessions in yolo mode, regardless of the provider's settings, and ignores the editor's permission mode setting. The box isolates requests handled inside it, but an agent can also use ACP to ask the editor to access files and terminals on your computer. See the file and terminal restrictions below. Editor threads store the agent's complete native home in ~/.config/coop/agents/<agent>/acp-homes/<repository-key>/home/. Accounts for the same provider share that repository's home, so you can switch accounts during a thread without losing the conversation or exposing another project's threads. Sessions from coop <agent> and coop loop use separate storage.

heading: The toolbar
text: A plain session shows the Preset, Provider and Account menus: Changing accounts or other choices within the same provider keeps the conversation. Changing providers creates a new session. co:op tries to carry over the message text and one-line descriptions of tool use, but not tool payloads. If you switch during a turn, co:op sends the current prompt again to the new target. The model menu starts with the target's :model or your configured default, and you can change it. With a preset active, the toolbar shows only the Preset menu. The preset's fallback list chooses the provider, model, effort, account and roles, and co:op doesn't apply saved Provider and Account choices from the editor. Select None to choose a provider or account yourself. Both menus return: Provider shows the provider currently in use, and Account is set to Auto.

heading: Usage limits
text: If a provider reports a usage limit during a turn, co:op hides the error, switches to your next signed-in account and sends the prompt again, updating the account dropdown to match. If no account is available, it posts Waiting for account "<name>" on <Provider> to reset its usage limit at <Mon 15:04 MST> (in MM:SS). Your message will send automatically. and sends your prompt when the limit resets.

heading: Restarts
text: A box can stop during coop build or coop update, when it runs out of memory, or when Docker restarts. co:op always keeps the editor connected and starts another box, even for a thread that hasn't received a message yet.

heading: Dev servers
text: Set serve.ports in .agent/project.yaml to publish the box's ports. The thread shows the stable http://localhost:<port> URLs you can open and tells you when a server starts. After a switch, the URLs reach the box the thread is using.

heading: Tracing a session
text: To record a session's ACP traffic, run touch ~/.config/coop/acp-debug or set COOP_ACP_TRACE=1 in the agent server's environment. Each coop acp server then appends traffic between the editor and box to ~/.local/state/coop/acp-trace-<pid>.log. Creating the file also turns tracing on for servers that are already running, so you can use it after a problem appears. The trace contains prompts and file contents, so treat it as sensitive. See Troubleshooting.

heading: Filtered networking
text: With filtered networking, the editor offers only compatible providers, and only presets that can run in full under those network rules. Provider Filtered ACP works with Claude its own supported credentials, or an API key Codex its own supported credentials, or an API key Gemini an AI Studio API key or importable plain OAuth account, but not Vertex Grok its OAuth login co:op refuses a Vertex GOOGLE_API_KEY in every network mode. Its broker keeps API keys and native OAuth grants outside the box. Switching providers never widens the session's network access. If you explicitly ask for an unsupported provider or preset, the request fails before launch.

heading: Forks
text: To work in a fork from the editor, start the adapter with coop fork <name> acp. The agent edits the throwaway clone, not your working tree, and you review and land the result locally without pushing the fork. co:op doesn't copy uncommitted, Git-ignored secrets into the fork, but secrets already in Git history can remain. The command starts the agent the fork was created with. Name a target to start another, as in coop fork <name> acp claude:opus. Configure this command with the parent project open in Zed, and co:op maps that directory to the fork inside the box. If the editor is open on an unrelated directory, co:op refuses the session. The fork, provider and account stay fixed, so co:op hides the usual ACP Provider and Preset menus. You can still use any model and effort choices the adapter offers.

heading: Services and custom images
text: With open networking, run coop up for the repo's .agent/compose.yml, and the ACP box joins the same network. With filtered networking, request and approve access to each service in the project's network rules, and co:op starts those services on a separate network for the editor session. A custom image must include the ACP adapters. If you build on co:op's box with FROM ${COOP_BASE_IMAGE}, as coop init sets up, the image already has them. If you use another base image, install them as shown in box.md. For filtered runs, the image must inherit co:op's client base and keep its client versions. Without the required adapter, coop acp fails with an error such as codex-acp: not found.

heading: When the project box is not ready
text: With filtered networking, your editor connects even if the project's box can't start yet. The thread says why, and anything you send waits. The agent doesn't run until the box is ready, so it never works without your project's tools. If your build files haven't changed since you last ran coop build, co:op rebuilds the box by itself. If they're new or changed, co:op waits for you, because an agent can edit them and a build runs them with ordinary networking. Review them, then run coop build --egress filtered in the project. Or send /build in the thread: co:op saves the files and shows where they are on this computer, and /build with the code it gives builds exactly those saved files. The code works once, for ten minutes. If the project has services and no network rules for them, the thread says to run coop approve, which lists the services and offers to add their rules. Or set box.network: false to start without services. If the project asks for network access you haven't approved, the thread says to run coop approve. No agent runs until you approve. If .agent/project.yaml doesn't load, the thread says what's wrong and where. No agent runs until you fix the file, and the session moves on by itself once you do. Anything new the file asks for still waits for coop approve. If the box exits as it starts for any other reason, such as a service that changed since you approved it, the thread says so and the agent log has the reason. co:op tries again every 30 seconds and whenever the project changes. If the box starts but doesn't answer within a minute, co:op stops it, says so in the thread and keeps trying. The time before it starts has its own limit of 5 minutes, not counting time the box reports waiting for another box. At that limit, the thread says the box took too long and co:op keeps trying. When the box can start, the session moves onto it and sends what was waiting. You can cancel a waiting message as usual. You don't need to reconnect, with one exception: a session started with filtered networking can't move to a project that ends up with unrestricted access or no network at all, so the thread asks you to reconnect. A message you sent is not delivered, so send it again after you reconnect. If even the waiting box can't start, as happens when Docker has stopped, the session ends and the thread says why. A session you start with --egress offline doesn't wait on a broken .agent/project.yaml, because the waiting box would have a network. The editor's log says what's wrong.

heading: Files and terminals on your computer
text: ACP lets an agent ask the editor to work on your computer directly, outside the box. Requests such as fs/read_text_file, fs/write_text_file and terminal/* run through the editor, and a login button can run a command there. A filtered session blocks these requests. co:op doesn't tell the agent the editor can handle them, refuses any such request from the box, hides the login buttons and refuses to open a link the box chose. The agent can still ask you a question in the editor. It works on the project inside the box as usual, so it sees what's saved on disk, not your unsaved edits. Zed loads an image in an agent's message by itself. A remote image would send data to an address outside the network rules, and a project path can be a symlink the box made, which Zed follows on your computer. A filtered session blocks both: co:op turns any image in what the box writes into a plain link, which you have to click. Only an image carried in the message as image data still shows. In a code block, a Markdown image and a line that starts like a Markdown link definition, such as [key: string]: number;, show a backslash. An open or offline session forwards these requests to Zed without filtering them, so your editor's file and terminal restrictions are part of the security boundary. A prompt-injected agent could ask the editor to read or write an absolute path outside the repo on your computer. In a test, Gemini's adapter wrote project files this way when the editor offered it, while Claude's and Codex's adapters did their work inside the box. coop claude and coop loop don't have this editor channel.

heading: MCP servers
text: Define MCP servers in one shared file for all agents. coop init creates an empty ~/.config/coop/agents/mcp.json using the standard { "mcpServers": { ... } } format. It connects no servers until you add them: { "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@playwright/mcp@latest", "--headless", "--no-sandbox"] }, "github": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"], "env": { "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "ghp_replace_with_your_token" } }, "sentry": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp", "bearer_token_env_var": "SENTRY_TOKEN" } } }

heading: Where the file lives
text: Set COOP_MCP_FILE to the shared file's absolute path. The default is ~/.config/coop/agents/mcp.json. If you set COOP_MCP_FILE to a path with no file, co:op names the path and won't start the run. Keep the file outside repositories, companion repositories, agent credential homes and ACP session stores. co:op mounts those directories in full, which would expose the file to the box, so it refuses a COOP_MCP_FILE in any of them before launch, even if the file is empty or doesn't exist yet. The file must also: be a regular file, not a symlink or special file be 4 MiB or smaller have a canonical path without .. To keep token variables out of filtered and offline boxes, co:op reads the default mcp.json and the file COOP_MCP_FILE names, even when another file is active or MCP is turned off. Such a launch stops if one of these files is there but can't be read, or if it, or the file it links to, sits in a directory co:op mounts in full. Gemini's native settings.json must follow the same file rules. co:op reads it on every Gemini launch, Codex's native config.toml on every Codex launch, and Grok's native config when the shared file is active. If one of these files is unsafe or can't be read, co:op stops that launch.

heading: How each agent gets them
text: At launch, coop passes the shared server definitions to each agent in its native format: Agent Where the servers go Claude --mcp-config Gemini merged into its settings.json Codex, Grok converted to their provider-specific [mcp_servers.*] tables in config.toml co:op mounts the generated configs read-only over the existing ones inside the box and leaves your source files unchanged. When the shared file is active, it's the only source of MCP server definitions, and co:op leaves out the native Codex and Grok [mcp_servers.*] tables. co:op refuses dotted, quoted or inline mcp_servers entries in your native TOML before launch, so remove them or move them into the shared file. Remote sessions use the same mcp.json without extra setup. co:op checks it before changing any session state, and the adapter gets only the copy it checked. If the active file is unsafe or ambiguous, the turn stops before its child process starts.

heading: Tokens and headers
text: Every agent passes a command server's env block (github above) to that server unchanged. The values are literal strings, so $VAR is not expanded. To keep a token out of mcp.json, point bearer_token_env_var at a variable (sentry above), and put the value in the env file: echo 'SENTRY_TOKEN=…' >> ~/.config/coop/agents/env co:op reads the value from this file, not from your shell. Every agent supports an HTTP server's headers. Claude and Grok turn bearer_token_env_var into an Authorization header using the environment variable's value. For Codex, a literal value becomes a static header, and a value containing exactly one ${VARIABLE} becomes an environment-variable reference, which keeps the secret out of the generated config. Codex can't represent a mixed value such as Bearer ${TOKEN}, so use bearer_token_env_var for that form.

heading: SSE servers
text: The agents handle a legacy SSE server ("type": "sse") differently: Agent What happens Grok Grok supports legacy SSE, and co:op passes the declaration through. Claude, Gemini They receive the declaration and decide for themselves. Codex co:op stops before launch and names the unsupported server. The Codex refusal applies wherever Codex takes part, including as a --peer of another lead.

heading: Filtered runs
text: With --egress filtered, header values must be literal for every agent. co:op builds the approved network policy from those literal values, so it rejects environment references such as ${…} before launch. In a filtered run, co:op's credential broker keeps the bearer_token_env_var token outside the box and sends it to the server. The box gets a modified config that points to a loopback listener and uses a replacement variable, COOP_MCP_TOKEN_<n>. That replacement works only for this server during this run. The token variables in co:op's env file never reach a filtered box, even if that box doesn't load MCP. That covers every variable a shared file names in bearer_token_env_var or in a header, such as SENTRY_TOKEN above. It covers the default mcp.json and the file COOP_MCP_FILE names, whichever file is active and even with MCP turned off, because the env file holds their tokens either way. co:op also stops a launch that passes one of these variables with -e. The ACP adapter receives only the replacement value, not the real token. A legacy SSE server with a bearer token needs a broader allowed route: GET on its stream path and POST on any clean path at the same host. The token still stays outside the box, and co:op reports this compatibility mode at launch. Prefer a streamable HTTP URL when the server provides one, because that limits the route to an exact path.

heading: Open runs
text: For supported MCP servers, an open run also keeps secrets outside the box. co:op starts a small, unprivileged helper container on the box's network and removes it when the run ends. Like the filtered broker, the helper holds each server's credential and accepts only a replacement value valid for that run. The box's config points to coop-broker and uses COOP_MCP_TOKEN_<n>. The box talks to the helper over plain HTTP on its container network, or on the default bridge if the project has no network of its own. The replacement value protects access to the credential on that network. At launch, co:op lists the servers the helper covers. If the helper can't handle a server through one route, the server still works but its secret stays inside the box. co:op reports the server's name and reason at launch. This happens for: a server whose secret is in two places, or whose secret header is anything other than literal text followed by one variable reference a URL that is not plain https on port 443 every server, when the box has no network of its own to reach a helper on (Apple's container runtime, --network none, --network container:…) Remote sessions with open networking use the same helper and the same fallbacks.

heading: Offline runs
text: An offline run (--egress offline) omits all remote MCP servers because it can't reach them, and reports this at launch. Local command servers still work. The token variables stay outside the box, as they do in a filtered run.

heading: Playwright
text: The image includes Chromium's system libraries. On first use, the example downloads the Playwright package and browser, then keeps the browser in the cache volume. In a filtered run, you must approve the download destinations and any sites the browser needs to visit. If a download is blocked, review the reported destination before granting access. The browser runs with --headless --no-sandbox and relies on the box for isolation.

heading: Controllers and workers
text: A controller is your platform that assigns jobs to co:op workers. Start a worker, which connects out to the controller, on the controller's VM or a separate VM: coop sessions connect --controller https://controller.example --token-file /run/secrets/coop-token The controller supplies jobs with fixed repositories, context, model targets, network settings and execution limits. co:op authenticates the controller, fetches complete Git/LFS working trees and authorized submodules, runs the models in isolation and saves session state between runs. You don't need a local policy catalog or worker configuration file. Any controller can use the same protocol, and Ryker is one example. A private Unix API manages sessions, turns in first-in-first-out order, inspection, checkpoints, review, publication, cancellation, budgets and explicit cleanup. It stays on the host, doesn't listen on TCP and doesn't enter a model sandbox. After each turn, co:op removes the box unless the job uses a warm-idle timeout to keep it ready. If cleanup fails, it retries in the background. A parked session alone doesn't confirm that its containers are gone. Companion repositories are read-only snapshots of exact pinned versions. With a fresh grant limited to the repository, the trusted host can push a fixed, reviewed candidate and open a draft PR. The model never receives the GitHub credential. coop sessions doctor --json checks the service that connect started. Before you upgrade a worker, stop it and run coop sessions check with the new build. See Upgrading a worker. If an old database has duplicate prompts in retry receipts, stop the worker and run: coop sessions compact --backup /safe/path/session-before-compact.sqlite Choose a new backup file outside the state root and treat it as sensitive. Compaction preserves the original turns and prompts. Follow the API's backup and recovery instructions. The worker API reference has the full detail. Its Connect section covers the worker command.

heading: Usage estimates and provider reports
text: Connect your provider's billing reports and compare reported costs with local usage estimates. coop usage shows account limits first, then estimates what your recorded activity would cost at API prices. It reads co:op histories and supported native CLI histories on this computer, and doesn't include browser or mobile conversations or histories on other computers. Deleted histories and unknown model prices can leave gaps. Provider Default history home Override Claude ~/.claude CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR Codex ~/.codex CODEX_HOME Gemini ~/.gemini GEMINI_CLI_HOME/.gemini Grok ~/.grok GROK_HOME If you set an override, co:op scans both it and the default location when they differ. It doesn't change either folder or its sign-ins, and it counts copied requests only once. co:op assigns a request to an account only when it finds the request in exactly one co:op account. Other native history appears as Unassigned local usage, because signing in today can't show which account made an old request. Shared editor histories appear as Unassigned editor usage. If copies point to conflicting accounts, the request stays unassigned instead of going to your currently selected account. Provider subtotals and Total count unassigned history once. ≈$.../30d estimates the activity's value at standard API prices, including activity covered by a subscription. It doesn't show what you paid. Use coop usage codex@personal (or another provider/account) to see which history and prices the estimate includes. Incomplete coverage shows as partial, and missing or unpriced history never counts as zero. Saved co:op turn summaries have no prices, so the native-history totals leave them out. co:op caches the token records it parses under usage-cache in ~/.local/state/coop, so later checks read only the files that changed. The cache holds no conversation text. A finished check of every provider removes the records of deleted files.

heading: Account limits
text: Limits come from the provider and cover the whole account. A dimmed reset time shows the time left and the date in UTC. Claude and Codex also show available resets and their reported expiry dates when the provider supplies them. Checking usage never redeems a reset. Credits appear in the provider's own units, not dollars. co:op checks the limits of the accounts it manages using credentials that stay on the host, and it sends no model prompt. If an account is busy, wait for its run to finish and try again. API-key and Vertex accounts may have priced token history even when they have no subscription limits to report.

heading: Connect an API billing source
text: To enable provider reports, create ~/.config/coop/usage-reports.json, or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/coop/usage-reports.json if you set the XDG config home. The file must be a regular file, not a symlink, and can define one reporting source per provider. name labels the source and doesn't select a co:op account. { "reports": [ { "provider": "codex", "name": "work", "organization": "org-example", "key_env": "COOP_REPORT_OPENAI_KEY" }, { "provider": "claude", "name": "work", "key_env": "COOP_REPORT_CLAUDE_KEY" }, { "provider": "grok", "name": "work", "team": "your-team-id", "key_env": "COOP_REPORT_XAI_KEY" } ] } Set the named environment variables in the host shell where you run co:op. Don't put the keys in this JSON file, your project or agents/env, which is forwarded into boxes. Reporting keys can have broader permissions than model API keys, so grant only the access needed for reports. co:op keeps these keys out of agent homes and containers, and its error messages don't include the key or the provider's response body. OpenAI: use an organization Admin API key. organization selects the organization sent to the Costs API. Anthropic: use an organization Admin API key. The key determines the organization. Its cost report excludes Priority Tier charges, so co:op marks this source as partial. xAI: use a separate Management API key authorized to read the configured team's billing usage. Don't use an inference key. The report reads billing usage, not a prepaid balance. These sources report API usage for an organization or team, which can include other applications and devices in it. They don't include personal subscriptions or ChatGPT or Claude web activity.

heading: Google billing exports
text: For Google reports, set up a standard Cloud Billing export. The host's gcloud account needs access to that export and permission to create BigQuery query jobs in the selected project. If the configured email isn't signed in, run gcloud auth login. This sign-in is separate from your Gemini CLI sign-in. co:op gets a fresh short-lived access token through gcloud auth print-access-token <email> --quiet. It doesn't copy a Google refresh credential. { "reports": [ { "provider": "gemini", "name": "work", "project": "my-gemini-project", "billing_table": "billing-project.billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_example", "sku_ids": ["your-gemini-api-sku-id"], "location": "US", "gcloud_account": "billing@example.com", "maximum_bytes_billed": 104857600 } ] } billing_table names the export table as project.dataset.table. In your billing export, find the exact SKU IDs for the Gemini or Vertex API charges you want to report, and replace the example SKU list with those IDs. co:op uses a fixed query with your chosen project and SKU IDs as parameters. The query includes their billing credits and accepts only USD billing. It doesn't include unrelated Vertex AI or cloud services. If the query is incomplete, rows are missing or the currency is unsupported, co:op shows the report as unavailable. It doesn't report those missing amounts as zero. Queries can cost money. Set maximum_bytes_billed to limit how much data you can be charged for. The largest limit co:op allows is 1 GiB. Google rejects a query that exceeds the limit without charging for that query. co:op requests cached results, but a query may still cost money. You must create the export and set up its permissions yourself. co:op doesn't create it, change permissions or enable billing. The report stays partial because the export may lack some usage or older records, and your SKU list may leave out charges.

heading: Reading the reports
text: Provider reports appear in a separate section without an approximation sign. These amounts come from the provider's usage reports and aren't a final invoice. Each report covers 30 completed UTC days and excludes the end date. Local estimates use a rolling 30-day window instead. Checked shows when co:op fetched the report, beside the report's dates and scope. The provider may still report requests late or revise costs. co:op marks reports with excluded usage or missing data as partial. Denied access, a malformed or truncated report and an unsupported currency show the source as unavailable, never as zero. A failed source stays visible. If one configured source fails, co:op marks the reported subtotal as partial too. If none returns a usable report, it shows no reported spending subtotal. co:op keeps reported API spend separate from local estimates because they can cover the same requests and measure different things. A provider command such as coop usage codex filters the reports. An account command such as coop usage codex@personal doesn't request an organization report or assign its bill to that login.

heading: The loop
text: Set up a task queue for an agent to work through on its own, with decisions and a final review. coop loop works through your task queue with a fresh agent for each task. When the queue is empty, a reviewer checks the completed work and reopens anything unfinished. Tasks that need your decision wait for you. Start with the loop guide, or use this page for the details. coop init # scaffold AGENTS.md, the .agent/ working folder, and the hooks coop tasks add "..." # add a task (a folder under .agent/tasks/00_todo/) coop loop claude # disposable agents work the queue until it's done, then sign off coop loop codex # …or name claude, codex, gemini, grok, or a preset A task is a folder under .agent/tasks/. Its state is the directory it sits in: 00_todo/, 10_in_progress/, 50_blocked/ or 99_done/. The numeric prefix sorts ls in lifecycle order, and coop tasks shows the clean names. Before starting an agent, the loop claims the next task on the host or resumes one left in 10_in_progress/, and the agent works only on that task. The loop keeps going while it can claim work from 00_todo/ or 10_in_progress/. A task that must not land before another one can wait for it. The agent hands it back with tasks_wait, or you add waits_on: <task-id> to its task.md frontmatter. The task stays in 00_todo/ and the loop skips it until the other task is in 99_done/, then works it. If the other task is missing or blocked, the loop blocks the waiting task too, with a decision that says why. If a commit lands after the agent hands a task back, the loop refuses the wait and stops, unless the commit carries another task's Coop-Task trailer. The task returns to 10_in_progress/ with the commit kept. coop tasks ls shows what each task waits for. Choose an agent (claude, codex, gemini or grok) or a preset that defines the lead agent. To run a custom command for each task, set work.command in .agent/loop.yaml. It replaces the whole iteration command. When the model reaches a rate or usage limit, the loop tries the next configured target. If every target is limited, it waits with a countdown until one can run, then retries the same task. A rate limit doesn't count as a failed task attempt. Add --preflight to check the queue before work starts. This pass unblocks tasks in 50_blocked/ when their decision.md has an answer. It leaves backlog tasks parked with coop tasks park alone, does no task work and makes no commits. Preflight is off by default. A task its worker committed before blocking it waits for your answer to coop tasks unblock <id> "<answer>", which names that commit and lets the next worker close the task without a new commit.

heading: Exit codes
text: A cron job or CI can act on the loop's exit code without parsing its output: Exit code Meaning 0 Final review and enabled final checks passed, or a successful --max-tasks pause before final review. 1 A failure, an unverified final pass, or work still left to do. 2 A usage error. 3 The loop stopped with a task blocked on a human decision, including one the review kept reopening past the round limit. Resolve it with coop tasks decisions, then run the loop again. 130 The run was interrupted before the final verdict. A successful --max-tasks pause exits 0, but the work still needs review. Run the same command without the limit to finish that review. The resumed review uses the Coop-Task: <id> trailer to find each task's commit among the commits made since the run started. You can sign those commits between runs. If any commit seen by a previous review has changed, including a repair commit that was on top of the branch, co:op reviews the task again. If it finds no matching commit or more than one, it stops before review and lists the task and commits.

heading: Task locks and claims
text: While an agent works on a task, co:op holds a lock on the host under ~/.local/state/coop/task-leases/, so another loop skips that task and can work on an independent one. coop tasks watch shows how long the task has been worked, how long its heartbeat has been quiet, that its loop waits out a usage limit, or that its worker is gone or you stopped it, without run IDs or PIDs. A missing heartbeat can help you spot a stalled worker, but it doesn't release the task. The loop takes over as soon as the operating system's lock becomes available, never because a timeout has passed. It can also resume an in-progress task that no co:op process, such as a running coop loop, has locked. coop tasks claim <id> records you as the owner and exits, without keeping a lock open. The loop leaves your task alone and shows the owner and the coop tasks release <id> command. Your claim never expires: only an explicit release, block, unblock or done clears it. coop tasks claim <id> --force takes over a claim that another running process holds. It ends that process's coop tasks lease, and that process can no longer complete, block, release or lease the task, or claim it back without --force, from the host or from a box. Stop every running co:op process, such as coop loop, before a major-version upgrade. Processes from different major versions can't share a task queue.

heading: Completion records
text: When a task completes, co:op stores a small receipt on the host's persistent task lock file, so other loops can recognize the completed folder without trusting task metadata the agent can edit. Before starting a box that can write, including a review box, co:op also records a fingerprint of each done folder in a host-only journal. If co:op crashes, the next loop uses the journal to undo any completion that had no authorized owner. Tasks completed outside a supervised box remain part of the ordinary task history.

heading: Sweeps and commit hooks
text: The /sweep skill has a Stop hook that keeps an active sweep running while it has tasks to work on, without holding other sessions open. coop init sets it up in new projects. A repo set up by an older co:op needs a manual update. init installs a fast commit check for Claude. For other committers, it installs a Git pre-commit check at .githooks/pre-commit and sets core.hooksPath, so the format check runs for everyone, including Codex, Gemini and a plain git commit. Git tracks the hook files, but core.hooksPath is local, so run coop init in each new clone to enable them there. The tracked .githooks/prepare-commit-msg hook also calls co:op's box-attribution hook when that hook is mounted. On a normal host, the tracked hook does nothing. init leaves an existing custom core.hooksPath unchanged. Copy both tracked hooks into your active hook directory, or have your existing hooks call them. If you already have a prepare-commit-msg, keep your file and copy the tracked hook's call to the co:op hook into it. To skip the format check for one commit, use git commit --no-verify.

heading: Final review
text: When the queue empties, a fresh final review (the signoff) checks each task the run completed: every acceptance criterion and subtask is met the change follows AGENTS.md and .agent/kb/rules, with no scope creep the failure path is tested the change is polished, with docs and the CHANGELOG updated the bookkeeping is right The worker records its final checks in the task's state.md, which co:op finalizes before review.
