Reviewers inspect the code and test coverage, and they rely on the worker's record of which tests ran instead of running them again. If a check is missing, failed or outdated, the reviewer reopens the task and tells the worker what to check. Reviewers never edit an archived task in place. If they find that a task moved through the queue incorrectly, they reopen it and report it too. The loop then works the queue and reviews again, until nothing is reopened or the round limit is reached. At the limit, co:op blocks that task for your decision and doesn't report it as done. The loop allows half as many review rounds as tasks worked, rounded down, within the range [3, signoff.rounds]. signoff.rounds defaults to 5 and must be 1 or more. Setting it below three overrides the minimum. Each completed task must match exactly one commit through its Coop-Task: <id> trailer. That commit must be in the current iteration's commit range, and it must be the only match reachable from HEAD. When review requests rework, the worker must amend or rewrite the existing task commit. co:op rejects a second matching commit and returns the task to in-progress. The worker also can't add a trailer for another task or rewrite that task's commit. co:op checks every attempt, including failed attempts, before allowing a retry. Review covers only tasks that the host accepted as completed during this run. In the default writes: tasks mode, the reviewer can only report findings: the repository and task queues are read-only. It returns a PASS/FAIL receipt listing the exact task IDs to reopen, and co:op checks the whole proposal and reopens those tasks in one transaction. If the review finishes successfully but returns the wrong output format, co:op asks for one correction. It resumes the same reviewer session for one more turn, with the same tasks and write permissions, and asks only for the verdict in the right format. It doesn't run the review again. co:op leaves every task unchanged if: the corrected verdict is malformed, or the reviewer session can't be resumed a task changes state during the review the process is interrupted or fails the proposal includes a task outside the review co:op treats reviewer findings as untrusted. The next worker gets fixed instructions to reproduce the issue first and doesn't follow instructions from the reviewer. Use writes: repo to let the reviewer fix source. Every task queue stays read-only, and the host applies changes to task state. The reviewer's commits must go on top of the commit it reviewed, without merges or Coop-Task trailers, and co:op lists them after the verdict. Uncommitted changes or rewritten history still fail the review. Tune the loop in one committed .agent/loop.yaml, with a section per step: Section Step preflight the cleanup pass before the loop starts working work the iterations that work the tasks between the per-task reviewer signoff the final review verify an optional affected-feature pass after the final review Set agent: for work, between, signoff or verify to choose its models. Each setting takes a fallback list of targets (provider[:model][/effort][@account]) or preset names. For example, signoff.agent can use a stronger model to review work done by a cheaper work.agent. Every step except work also accepts a prompt:. Custom prompts add to co:op's built-in checks and don't replace them: signoff.prompt adds checks to final review. co:op reopens a task that fails one, as it does for a built-in check. You might require a CHANGELOG entry or regenerated docs. preflight.prompt adds an agent cleanup pass in addition to co:op's host-side unblock step. between.prompt defines an optional review after each completed task. It can reopen the task. verify.prompt defines the optional pass after final review. Per-task review is off until you enable it and set a prompt. Changes to files that define the gate are an exception: co:op always reviews those tasks before starting the next one, using the configured between-review target and prompt, or the signoff target with a focused built-in prompt. If Git can't tell co:op which files changed, the loop stops, because it can't assume the gate was untouched. Run the continuation command it prints to review that task before starting other work. Final review also stops if co:op can't read the run's changes. co:op automatically reviews changes to Makefiles, CI, hooks and its own config. If your gate also depends on wrapper scripts or ordinary source files, list their exact repo-relative paths under gate_sources: in .agent/project.yaml. The loop keeps the list it read at startup, so a task can't remove itself from review. Restart the loop to apply a deliberate change to the list. Settings live in the same file: signoff.rounds, preflight.enabled, verify.enabled and work.command. Every field is optional, and without the file co:op uses the built-in defaults. coop init creates a fully commented starter file.

heading: The .agent/ folder
text: init creates a folder for instructions and working notes that any supported agent can use. The agent reads it when it starts and after its conversation is compacted. Git ignores the local working state and tracks the shared knowledge and rules (kb/, including kb/rules/), workflows (skills/, presets/), fallback Claude settings (claude/), project.yaml, loop.yaml, compose.yml, Dockerfile and tasks/README.md. Path What it's for tasks/ The work queue, one folder per task. Each folder carries its own spec.md, log.md, state.md and decision.md as needed, and coop tasks moves it between states. the backlog Unscheduled ideas stored as task folders in tasks/xx_backlog/ (coop backlog). The loop and Stop hook ignore them. When an idea is ready, coop backlog promote <id> moves it into tasks/00_todo/. kb/ Committed notes explaining subsystems, how they interact, and problems that are hard to spot from the code alone. kb/rules/ Committed rules that tell agents how to work in the project. Corrections become rules here. claude/ Fallback user-level Claude settings and hooks for repos without matching project .claude/ artifacts. Committed. project.yaml Committed project settings: subprojects:, serve: ports, box policy (box:), the merge gate:, and extra gate_sources: to review when changed. The box: policy sets egress, egress_rules:, resource caps and auto_up/network. Explicit COOP_* environment or config settings override box: and gate:. This file can tighten security settings but cannot relax them by itself. Egress can require filtered or offline, but open needs human approval through coop approve. The file cannot set no_new_privileges. On a fresh setup, init also installs generic workflow skills into .agent/skills/ and links the selected agents to it: Skill What it's for /spec writing a spec for a multi-file change /work carrying out that change step by step against the gate /sweep working through every task in .agent/tasks/ /investigate finding the root cause of a failure /verify-api checking anything you're unsure of before you call it /review-board a thorough multi-hat review before landing Edit them freely. init won't overwrite a skill you've changed. When init adopts an existing real .claude/skills/ instead, it leaves that project-owned set unchanged and links the other selected agents to it.

heading: Monorepos
text: When one repo holds several components, each with its own work, list them once in the top-level .agent/project.yaml: # .agent/project.yaml — committed with the repo subprojects: [runner, packs, portal, mcp] co:op then combines every member's .agent/tasks automatically: coop tasks lists them under a header for each queue one coop loop works through them all coop prompt counts across them the id commands (claim, done and the rest) find a task in whichever queue holds it An explicit COOP_TASKS or --tasks overrides automatic discovery. Each member keeps a queue for its own work, and the root queue holds changes that span members. Run coop init at the root to find member folders and write project.yaml. It looks for .agent/ folders at any depth, skipping hidden and build folders, and creates a task queue for each member. Members share the root's AGENTS.md, .agent/skills/, .agent/kb/ and box. A member can also commit its own .agent/kb/rules/ when it needs additional rules. Use coop tasks queues when a script, such as the sweep queue guard, needs the resolved queue paths.

heading: Parallel forks
text: Run several models at once, each looping unattended in its own fork. Point them all at the same queue in your project, called the canonical queue. The host assigns the tasks, so each task is claimed exactly once: coop fork perf codex --loop -d # each worker claims a different canonical task coop fork deps gemini --loop -d coop fork docs claude --loop -d coop tasks watch # canonical queue + assignments + every active sandbox coop fork ls # worker state, sandbox activity, candidate/task progress, diff, cost coop fork logs -f # tail every fork at once (compose-style, prefixed) coop fork stop perf # halt one; coop fork logs perf -f to watch just it Without --tasks, a fork takes the queues COOP_TASKS names, as coop loop does. Without either, it takes work from the repo's .agent/tasks and then every monorepo member's queue, in project.yaml order. Use --tasks <path> to choose a queue, and repeat it for more: like coop loop, the fork takes them in the order you give them. A fork's --tasks queue can be an absolute path outside the project, and the fork uses the original queues without copying them or changing their paths. Nothing else takes a queue outside the project: COOP_TASKS names queues inside it, and coop loop, coop tasks and coop backlog refuse to run in a folder outside a Git repository. The fork receives only its assigned task under .coop/task-executions/. Restarting the same fork generation resumes that task, and another fork can't claim it. A fork recreated under the same name is a new generation. -d (--detach) runs the worker in the background and saves its output in a private log. Read it with coop fork logs <name>. When the fork finishes its available work, review and land it as you would a pull request, then git push. Add more agents only while you can keep up with reviewing their work. coop fork merge --all merges forks in sequence. It rebases each fork onto the result of the previous merge and re-runs the configured gate (gate: in .agent/project.yaml, or COOP_GATE). The merge stops at the first conflict or failed gate and leaves the remaining forks untouched. To split work between forks, point them at the same queue. The host gives each task to one fork. Use separate queues only for parts of the project that already own separate work. --tasks selects an existing queue and doesn't divide it. If you run agents at the same time, give them different accounts to avoid competing for the same subscription limits. A preset can define a rotation across providers and accounts. Agents running at the same time also run their full gates at the same time, which can overload the host until tests time out. To limit that, tell your agents to run the full gate as coop-gate-slot make check (or put coop-gate-slot in front of your own gate command). Every box has this helper. At most two gates run at once on one host; another one prints Waiting for another gate to finish and starts when a slot is free, so its timeouts start only then. The coop fork merge gate takes a slot the same way. A gate inside another gate runs in the outer gate's slot, so a gate: command that already starts with coop-gate-slot doesn't wait for a second one. Boxes share the slots through their common ~/.cache volume on Docker and OrbStack. Apple container runs each box in its own VM, and sharing slots there hasn't been tested, so don't count on the limit there. A stale or crashed worker shows as cleanup in coop fork ls. Run coop fork stop <name> to clean it up. If co:op started the worker on another operating system, such as a Linux container that shares the folder, the listing says so. Stop that worker on the system where it started, because co:op can't check it from here. stop removes only that fork's containers, even if another repository has a fork with the same name. Running it twice is safe. Remove an unused fork with coop fork rm <name>. --yes skips the confirmation prompt. --force may stop a detached worker and discard uncommitted or unmerged Git work, the reviewed candidate and pending proposals. It also returns the fork's assigned tasks to their original queue.

heading: Forks
text: Work in a separate copy of your project. Review the changes and checks before merging them. A fork is a temporary local clone of your repo where an agent can work. You review its changes and decide whether to merge them. The forks guide has a short overview of the workflow. An ordinary fork keeps the agent's edits out of your checkout while it works, but you still need to trust what it writes. Git can share object files between the clone and your repo, and Git or editor settings the agent writes can run code when you open the fork on your machine. Use --isolated to give the fork independent Git storage and to check changes before they enter your checkout. Several forks can run at once. A fork's origin points to a local path, not your upstream server. Secrets already in Git history can still be in the clone. At creation, Coop also copies present services.require_real_files and regular files in the same directories that Compose binds, such as a generated key's certificate. Other ignored files stay out. These are independent copies; reopening a fork leaves them unchanged, and existing files in the clone take precedence. Open a fork, let the agent work, review its changes, then merge them: coop fork perf codex # open: clone into ../<repo>-forks/perf, run codex there coop fork perf # re-enter: continues codex's last session by default coop fork ls # list your forks (branch, changes, state, last activity) coop fork review perf # review: the dossier, then the diff coop fork merge perf # land: rebase onto your branch, then close the fork coop fork rm perf # or discard it (confirms first; inspect task/Git impact before --force) coop fork <name> creates a fork or reopens an existing one. Add an agent, as in coop fork perf codex, or a target such as codex:gpt-6-astra@work to choose the model and account too. You can also name a preset, as in coop fork perf frontier, and the preset's lead runs the fork. A fork inherits your Git identity, signing-key setting and global gitignore from the parent repo. At creation, Coop also snapshots the parent's network, service, project-build and coop approve --case-exposure file approvals. They keep the same approved inputs and restrictions; changing the fork's rules, Compose file or build files still needs approval there. A fork refused for new network access names the command that reviews it, COOP_REPO=<fork folder> coop approve, and one refused for new build files names COOP_REPO=<fork folder> coop build --egress filtered. You can run both from the project. Later parent approvals do not update an existing fork, and a fork recreated with --fresh takes the parent's approvals again. Coop can build a separate fork image from unchanged approved files without asking again. Approved external or explicitly named service volumes still refer to the same Docker volumes. Coop refuses to copy approvals whose parent identity or stored records are invalid. A network approval withdrawn at a fork's path stays withdrawn even if you recreate that fork; run coop approve in the fork to grant access again. Removing a fork removes the approvals it holds, and leaves the parent's alone. Point a fork at a task queue and it works the queue unattended: coop fork api codex --loop -d # loops the repo's task queue(s); -d detaches — tail with coop fork logs api -f The loop explains how iterations work. Parallel forks shows how to run several at once. A refused loop appears as stopped in coop fork ls, with the reason beneath it. A fork whose box must wait for other boxes before it can start its services appears as waiting to start services, with the boxes it waits for beneath it. When a task needs your decision, it waits in coop tasks decisions while the fork goes on with its other tasks. The fork stops for the decision only when nothing else is left. Answer it from the project with coop tasks unblock <id> "<answer>" or coop tasks decisions -i: the fork picks the task up on its next pass, and a stopped fork resumes with coop fork <name> --loop -d. An answer typed into decision.md by hand still needs coop tasks unblock <id> to send the task back, and a stopped fork says which of its tasks have one. unblock also finds a task in a queue the fork was given with --tasks, and run in the fork's own checkout, it answers the task in the project. A fork loop makes its reviewed work ready to merge only when it has no other task to take. To merge each task once it's reviewed, add --stop-after-review. The fork stops after a task passes review, before it takes another, and coop fork ls shows it as ready to merge. Merge it and let the merge delete the fork, then run the same command again for the next task: coop fork api codex -d --stop-after-review # stops once a task passes review coop fork merge api --yes # merges the reviewed work and deletes the fork coop fork api codex -d --stop-after-review # a new fork takes the next task

heading: Isolated-write forks
text: coop fork research codex --isolated coop fork research # the host remembers isolation coop fork review research --stat coop fork merge research --yes An isolated fork keeps its own Git metadata and object files. co:op prevents the box from mounting your parent checkout or its Git storage, including through another path, a service or a volume that co:op inspects. The agent can still create commits and branches and run rebase inside the fork. Isolation stays enabled when you reopen the fork, run a detached loop or connect through ACP. You can't convert an existing ordinary fork, so you must create a new isolated one. Ordinary forks and runs that write directly to your checkout don't get this isolation.

heading: What an isolated fork copies
text: co:op recreates each initialized, unchanged local submodule from its exact commit, with independent storage, and never copies the submodule's raw Git metadata. coop fork review and coop fork merge refuse an isolated fork whose commits change a submodule commit or .gitmodules, so make those changes in your own checkout. co:op copies Git LFS files from Git's default cache in the common directory and verifies them without network access. It refuses missing or corrupt files and a custom lfs.storage.

heading: Storage you share with the fork
text: Isolation doesn't make shared storage private. Other processes can still change provider folders, caches or service data that you choose to share with the fork, so use private storage or read-only sources if you don't trust those processes. co:op must be able to inspect the files in mounts you add, service mounts and existing volumes. If a path exists only on the Docker daemon's machine, or co:op can't read it on the host, co:op refuses the mount. Use a separate bind mount whose contents co:op can inspect. co:op's own private volumes are exempt only when co:op can identify them exactly. Dependency and toolchain caches you enable are shared storage you choose to trust. co:op checks their exact local volume-driver configuration, but it can't promise that daemon contents it can't read are safe or independent. It refuses custom cache drivers and caches backed by bind mounts. This cache exception doesn't apply to other extra volumes or service volumes.

heading: Reviewing an isolated fork
text: When you review an isolated fork, co:op copies its committed history into private storage and rebases the copy onto the parent commit it recorded. This leaves your checkout, the fork's workspace and the parent's Git refs unchanged, so you can review even while your parent checkout has uncommitted changes. review --open and COOP_REVIEW_CMD show a private copy of the committed files. co:op prints its path and the command that removes it, and deleting the fork removes it too. Edits to a preview are never included in the merge. Use only an editor, difftool or review command you trust to run on your host. coop fork open opens the agent's actual workspace instead of a private review copy, and co:op warns that Git or editor metadata in that workspace may run code on your machine.

heading: Merging an isolated fork
text: Before merging, your checkout must be clean and on a branch. co:op also checks the exact Git index and tracked-file contents, and hidden index flags or an index.lock it can't account for stop the merge. Incoming files can't overwrite untracked or ignored files in your checkout. co:op never merges untracked files from the fork, including Git metadata for a new child repository. co:op inspects every incoming commit, including changes that disappear from the final diff. It refuses the following, and --force cannot bypass the refusal: unsafe paths or file modes changes to nested Git sources files that can automatically run code on your host new or changed npm install lifecycle scripts possible credentials that a commit adds oversized files You can still review and merge build files that run only when someone explicitly invokes them. Configured checks run on a separate disposable clone, which has the same restrictions on mounting the parent checkout. If the rebase fails, co:op prints the path of the fork it kept and a commit that must remain unchanged. Keep that commit and its earlier history intact, fix only the later commits, then review again. If signing failed, check your trusted signing settings first. Don't run Git's printed recovery commands in your fork, because they refer to the temporary clone co:op has already discarded. If you keep the fork after merging, the next merge starts after the original fork commit that was already merged. A reviewed result with no code changes can still complete its assigned tasks. merge --all skips a fork only when it has no new commits and no active task records to finish. co:op completes tasks from the exact source it reviewed.

heading: When a merge is interrupted
text: If you cancel a merge or co:op refuses it before it starts, the parent's files, index and refs stay unchanged and nothing is left to resume, so the next merge asks again and runs the checks again. Once co:op starts changing the checkout, it records each step in a journal, and an interruption can leave the checkout partly updated. Keep the exact reviewed changes and the journal, then rerun coop fork merge <name>. co:op can resume only if the checkout exactly matches its original clean state or the complete merged state recorded for that merge. If it finds unrelated edits, a partly updated checkout, a changed branch or an index.lock it can't account for, recovery stops so you can resolve the mismatch. Never reset, stash, delete a lock you cannot identify, or remove and recreate the fork to bypass this check.

heading: Re-entry resumes the session
text: A fork remembers the agent you created it with. After coop fork perf codex, coop fork perf re-enters with codex and never silently falls back to claude. Pass an agent to switch. coop fork ls shows each fork's agent. Reopening a fork also resumes the last conversation. co:op saves a session ID for each fork, provider and account in the fork's git-excluded .coop/ folder, and uses it to resume the exact session for the active account and the fork's directory inside the box. If the saved ID is missing or the provider no longer has that session, co:op starts a new one. It doesn't choose another conversation just because it's the newest in that directory. Switching providers or accounts starts or resumes that provider and account's own session, and doesn't copy a conversation between providers. co:op allows only one of its interactive Codex processes at a time for each account and working directory inside the box. A second process stops with an error you can retry, so co:op can't record the wrong session ID. Codex processes started outside co:op don't respect this lock, so while co:op sets up a new fork session, don't start another Codex process for the same account and working directory. Flag What it does --new Starts a new session for the selected provider and account. The fork's files stay. --fresh Recreates the whole fork while keeping its selected provider. It asks before deleting anything. Without an interactive terminal, it requires --yes. On coop fork rm and --fresh, --force can: stop the detached worker discard unmerged or dirty Git work return the fork's assigned tasks to the project's queue discard the exact set of changes prepared for review discard pending task proposals from the fork Blocked tasks and proposals already imported into the project's queue stay there. Check coop fork ls and coop fork review before discarding a fork. Land it explains the different effect of --force on coop fork merge.

heading: Review
text: coop fork review <name> shows a review summary before the patch: the commits the agent's latest task log.md, clearly labeled as the agent's own account of its work findings from the same policy scan that coop fork merge uses changed files, starting with config and instructions, then code ordered by amount changed, then tests and docs. Each file shows +N -N. whether a check command is configured to run before merging Then the diff opens in your pager. The counts and the diff cover committed fork changes only. If the fork has uncommitted or untracked edits, co:op warns you. Open the fork, commit the work you want, then review again. Uncommitted files are not merged. These flags change how you review: Flag What it does --stat shows the review summary only and skips the diff --tool opens each changed file in your GUI difftool --open opens your editor. Isolated forks use a private preview of the committed files. --gate rebases a temporary clone, then runs the parent's configured check command in a box with that clone mounted. Ignored build output can be written there, but changes to HEAD or tracked files fail the check. --gate exits 0 when the checks pass, or after a clean rebase when no check command is configured. It exits 1 when the checks fail or the rebase conflicts. The parent and fork refs, branches and worktrees stay unchanged, and co:op always removes the temporary clone. You can combine --gate with --stat or --tool, but not with --open, because an editor can return before its review window closes. To review in your editor's source control panel, run coop fork open <name>. It opens the fork directory with the first of these that's set: COOP_EDITOR, a co:op-only override git config --global core.editor, your normal Git editor (co:op reads only the global value) a GUI editor detected on PATH: cursor, code, zed, idea, subl $VISUAL or $EDITOR Automatic detection uses the order in step 3, so if both code and zed are installed, it chooses code. Set one of the first two options to choose your editor explicitly: git config --global core.editor "zed --wait" # your standard git editor (git commit uses it too) export COOP_EDITOR="zed" # coop-only; overrides core.editor co:op runs the editor command as written, so with core.editor = "zed --wait" your terminal waits until you close the window. To return at once, set COOP_EDITOR without --wait, like COOP_EDITOR=zed. --tool runs git difftool, which opens each changed file in your diff.tool. co:op uses only the global diff.tool and its command. Register a tool once: # VS Code git config --global diff.tool vscode git config --global difftool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait --diff "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"' # Zed git config --global diff.tool zed git config --global difftool.zed.cmd 'zed --wait --diff "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"' JetBrains, Meld, Beyond Compare, vimdiff and others work the same way. git difftool --tool-help lists the tools git already knows. Set COOP_REVIEW_CMD to run a TUI or review script. co:op runs it with sh -c and provides $COOP_FORK_PATH, $COOP_FORK_NAME and $COOP_REVIEW_REF in the environment. For an ordinary fork, the working directory is the parent repo. With --gate, it is the temporary clone instead, and co:op removes the clone when the command exits. For an isolated fork, the working directory is a private copy of the parent commit, which keeps HEAD...$COOP_REVIEW_REF usable for comparisons, and $COOP_FORK_PATH points to a separate copy of the fork's committed changes. Neither path is your parent checkout or the agent's workspace. co:op prints both paths. Remove them after the review tool has finished, even if it returned control to your terminal earlier. export COOP_REVIEW_CMD='cd "$COOP_FORK_PATH" && lazygit'

heading: Land it
text: coop fork merge <name> rebases the fork's commits onto your current branch, then advances the branch to include them, with no merge commit. The rebase runs on your host, so if you sign commits (commit.gpgsign=true), co:op signs the merged commits with your key even though the box created them unsigned. You then run git push yourself. Set a check command for merges with gate: make check in .agent/project.yaml. COOP_GATE="make check" overrides it on your machine. Every merge runs the command in the box against the rebased files. If it fails, co:op stops the merge and your branch stays unchanged. You still review the changes yourself. co:op checks for oversized files and changes to files the box hides. This includes secret-looking filenames and paths matched by a .coopignore, including one above the project. It also flags additions, edits, removals and renames of a .coopignore, because these change what future boxes can see. The scan checks the lines the fork adds for credential patterns from AWS, OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, Slack and other providers, and for random-looking values assigned to secret-named keys, even if the file's name doesn't look secret. A credential your branch already has doesn't hold up a fork that edits its file. co:op refuses to merge while your own working tree has uncommitted changes. co:op asks before merging, then offers to delete the fork after the merge. In a non-interactive shell, such as CI or a pipe, you must confirm up front, or co:op refuses to run the merge. Flag What it does --yes, -y Confirms the merge and the fork's removal up front, which a non-interactive shell needs. In an interactive shell, it skips the prompts. --force Ordinary forks only. Overrides the risky-file policy, but not the check command. Isolated forks cannot bypass the policy. --all Merges all forks in sequence. See parallel forks. A fork loop takes work from the selected task queues. The host assigns each task to one fork generation, which lasts until you remove or recreate the fork, and places only the assigned task in the fork. It never mounts the whole queue there. The agent works on that copy of the task, including its state, artifacts, reviews and final signoff. In the task's original queue, the task stays in_progress while the fork is reviewing or ready. After final signoff and signing, co:op records one merge candidate for that fork generation: the exact HEAD commit, file tree and completed task assignments. Before merging, it checks that candidate again, rebases it and runs the configured checks, then updates the parent and completes only the tasks recorded in that candidate. A journal lets co:op resume these steps after an interruption. A Coop-Task trailer helps with consistency checks and search, but it cannot complete a task on its own. If a fork can't reach a candidate, for example because its box keeps failing a check your project passes, you can bring its commit to your branch yourself, such as with git cherry-pick. Then run coop tasks done <id> --from-fork in your terminal. It needs exactly one commit on your branch with that task's Coop-Task trailer and a stopped fork with no candidate waiting to merge. If your branch already had that commit when the fork took the task, such as a loop's commit whose completion was refused, your branch must also have every commit the fork made since then. co:op adds the tasks the fork found to your queue, completes the task with a note in its log, and releases the fork's assignment without deleting the fork. A later merge of the fork skips each commit you brought over unchanged. If the final candidate review finds a gap, co:op names the affected tasks and returns them to work in the same fork before reviewing the complete candidate again. Missing handoff records can be repaired without another code commit. A repeated finding after an unchanged-history repair, or a task whose rework cannot be safely authorized, waits for your decision with the finding recorded. After a stop or crash, the same fork generation can resume its assigned tasks. rm, --fresh and the worker API's session discard refuse to proceed while the fork still owns assigned tasks, a merge candidate, task proposals or cleanup state. rm and --fresh proceed only with --force, which records how those assignments are handled. coop tasks watch shows the project's task states and every box, including when the status of the process that controls the fork loop is stale or cannot be determined.

heading: Evaluations
text: Run repeatable checks to compare changes to models, presets and loops. Keep the results for review. coop eval runs the same tasks repeatedly, then an independent verifier grades the finished work. Use it to check whether changing a model, preset, loop recipe or co:op build improves the result. The website guide walks through a first run.

heading: Try it
text: Preview the shipped core suite. The preview launches no container or provider and spends nothing: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m --dry-run A dry run checks the plan, not whether your credentials, runtime or image are ready. For a real run, sign in with coop login codex. You also need a working container runtime and a current co:op box image. If the image is missing, run coop build --egress open from a directory without a project Dockerfile. Building may download dependencies. Then run: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m coop eval inspect A real run uses your provider account and may spend credits. Change one thing and run the same suite again. Find the run IDs with coop eval runs, then compare them with coop eval compare <before-id> <after-id>. co:op takes the order from your arguments, not from timestamps. Inspect and compare show a short fingerprint of each configuration and its co:op build, so you can spot a preset or recipe that changed while keeping the same name. coop help eval run lists every option, including these: Flag What it does --timeout 35m Limits the whole command from the moment it starts. At the limit, preparation, trials and grading stop, though cleanup and saving the final record may finish afterward. It limits time, not spending. --repeat 3 Runs each case three times. --jobs 2 Allows two agent trials at once. Each case also has its own timeout in suite.yaml, and a larger --timeout doesn't raise it. More configurations or repeats mean more paid work. Install cloc if you want change-size figures. Without it, grading and verdicts still work, and co:op labels the measurement as missing.

heading: Choose what to evaluate
text: core has three small coding tasks for one agent, with independent checks that catch near misses. Choose a provider target such as codex:gpt-6.1-sol/xhigh. queue sends ten tasks through the real coop loop, including review and signoff. Use it to compare presets or loop recipes. Each trial works through its tasks in order and can take hours. For example, coop eval run queue frontier --timeout 2h uses your existing frontier preset. Add --loop-config .agent/loop.yaml to test your project's recipe. coop eval init ./evals/my-suite creates a custom suite from a working greeting example. Edit suite.yaml, files/greeting/ and the separate verifiers/greeting/verify.sh. The verifier's README explains grading. suite.yaml includes a commented example for a loop. examples/evals/maintenance/ is an example of a custom comparison, with three independent maintenance loops for shell, Python and Node. It isn't an official benchmark score, and coop eval ls doesn't list it as a starter. Each target or preset after the suite is a separate configuration, not a fallback. Presets need a loop suite such as queue, and core and other single-agent suites accept targets only. This command previews two configurations: coop eval run core codex:gpt-6.1-sol codex:gpt-6.1-sol/xhigh --timeout 70m --dry-run

heading: Runtime profiles for custom agent cases
text: For an agent case that needs its own tools, use a trusted runtime profile, which gives the case a dedicated image that you build yourself in place of the shared image. Add these four fields to the case: runtime: profile: /absolute/path/to/clean-profile workdir: /app agent_timeout: 15m verifier_timeout: 15m Set the case's timeout long enough to cover preparation, the agent's work and verification. Loop suites don't support runtime profiles. Keep the profile outside both the suite and co:op's evaluation state. It must contain no Git metadata, symlinks or special files. Its project Dockerfile defaults to .agent/Dockerfile and must inherit co:op's client image. The profile can't add project environment variables, services, published ports or extra network access. Review the files used to build the profile, then run coop build --egress filtered from the profile directory before you start the evaluation. Evaluations never build a profile themselves. The build uses ordinary host networking, not the filtered network of the candidate (the agent being evaluated). Profile cases always use the coop-adapted-offline-profile-v1 protocol, which fixes these settings: Setting Value Working directory /app CPU 1 Memory 2 GiB PIDs 128 Storage declared as 10 GiB, but co:op doesn't enforce the quota or measure usage Candidate network only the core endpoints co:op maintains for its provider, through filtered networking Grader the same immutable image, with no network or credentials These settings adapt the workload to co:op's runtime and don't show that it runs under the same conditions as an official benchmark. Exclude cases that depend on a disk quota or on running out of disk space. co:op saves a private copy of the profile and records its digest, image and platform before work starts. This saved copy doesn't approve a build. The original profile must stay available and unchanged for both the agent phase and the verifier phase, and if you rebuild a different image after preparation, co:op refuses to start the candidate. The saved profile counts toward the suite's 2 GiB and 200,000-entry limit. A dry run doesn't look up the image, so the workload fingerprint it shows isn't final.

heading: Understand a result
text: coop eval inspect shows the latest run, or an older one if you add its run ID. It shows why trials didn't pass and where to find the saved JSON records and work. See coop help eval inspect for explanations of the results. Result Meaning failed The independent verifier rejected the work. error Execution or grading didn't produce a verdict, so grading is incomplete. It doesn't mean the model failed the task. A timeout, or a trial that never started Grading is incomplete here too. A loop trial starts when its loop launches its first box. If the loop stops before that, for example because the image is missing or the account isn't signed in, the trial is an error, not a graded failure. For a real run, exit code 0 means every trial has a grade, even if some tasks failed. If grading is incomplete, the command exits 1 and saves the results so you can inspect what happened. A dry run exits 0 after showing the plan. Code-size changes can help you review the work, but they aren't a quality score. To measure what changed between two runs: Choose two different runs. Run the same tasks, with the same number of repeats for each task. Test one configuration, such as a model or preset, in each run. co:op also checks the saved workload IDs, which identify the tasks and how they run and are graded. Both runs must have an ID, and the IDs must match. If any of these requirements aren't met, co:op shows each run's results separately. coop eval compare checks the saved plan for each run. A missing trial stays pending. If a trial is recorded twice or wasn't part of the plan, co:op refuses to compare the results. For each task, co:op reports the change only after every repeat in both runs has a pass or fail grade. The overall change and its uncertainty range appear only when all tasks are fully graded in both runs. The report shows the pass rate after the change minus the pass rate before it, in percentage points, counting tasks and repeats separately. It also gives a 95% uncertainty range, which applies only to the tasks you tested and assumes each trial runs independently. The range uses a conservative Hoeffding bound, sqrt(log(40)/(cases*repeats)), and stays between −100 and +100 percentage points. If you plan to make a decision from the comparison, run each task at least three times. Before you start, write down how much improvement would matter and how you'll decide. co:op doesn't save those rules or choose a winner for you. If a trial doesn't pass, co:op keeps the candidate's original workspace for inspection and removes the writable copy used for grading. The grader receives only a cleaned copy of the workspace, and the trial details list any symlinks that point outside the workspace and any special files left out of that copy. If a provider refuses a sign-in or reports a quota limit, check coop credentials <agent> before starting another paid run. For a timeout, check both the case's timeout in suite.yaml and the run's --timeout. A run with no final summary may still be running or may have been interrupted. You can inspect it, but you can't compare or resume it. To try again, start a new run yourself. Recorded diagnostics may contain private provider output, so review them before you share them. Each trial gets a private workspace without the source repository's Git history. The model can't access the hidden verifiers, which run afterward in a separate container with no credentials or network access. co:op excludes your MCP servers and COOP_RUN_ARGS from trials, because they could change the task setup without co:op recording the change. Use co:op-managed logins for provider credentials. The results describe the workload you tested. They don't prove equal performance across providers, and they aren't a public benchmark ranking. co:op turns off the native client's web search and fetch tools for every evaluation candidate, including consultations and delegated work that co:op manages. Terminal, file and editing tools stay available. This relies on the client obeying the setting, and it won't stop a model from making its own authenticated provider requests. Regular co:op runs keep their normal web tools. Before trials start, co:op saves private copies of the suite's named inputs and hidden verifiers. The run uses those copies, so later edits to the source can't change its tasks or the workload ID used for comparisons. The saved suite must fit within 2 GiB and 200,000 entries, or co:op refuses the run before any provider work begins.

heading: Coop CLI reference
text: Look up co:op commands and options, with examples of how to use them. coop help --all prints this reference in your terminal, followed by a page for each preset you can run in the current project. coop: run coding agents in an isolated box for your project. Usage: coop <command> [<args>...] THE BOX: an isolated environment for running commands in this project coop run -- <command> run a command in the box coop shell open a shell in the box RUN AGENTS: work with a coding agent or a team of agents coop <claude|codex|gemini|grok> start Claude, Codex, Gemini, or Grok coop <preset> run agents together using a preset coop <target> --peer <target>... start with read-only peer agents A target is an agent, optionally with a model, effort and account: codex:gpt-6-astra/xhigh@work ACCOUNTS, MODELS & PRESETS: choose the accounts and models your agents use coop login <agent> sign in to an agent coop credentials [<agent>] show your signed-in accounts coop models [<agent>] show available models coop usage [<agent>] show limits and a 30-day API estimate coop presets [<name>] show your presets TASKS: each task is a folder in .agent/tasks/ coop tasks ls show tasks grouped by status coop tasks watch follow task progress coop tasks add "<title>" add a task coop tasks decisions show tasks waiting for your decision coop backlog save ideas for later coop context [<path>...] show instructions and docs for your files LOOPS: work through tasks automatically; configure the steps in .agent/loop.yaml coop loop [<target|preset>] run agents until the queue is done EVALUATIONS: check whether a model, preset or loop change helped coop eval run repeatable checks and compare results FORKS: work in separate project copies, then review and merge the changes coop fork <name> <target|preset> start an agent in a new fork coop fork ls show this project's forks coop fork review <name> review a fork's changes coop fork merge <name> merge a fork's changes into this branch coop fork merge --all merge all forks into this branch coop fork logs [<name>] show loop logs for one or all forks coop fork rm <name> delete a fork coop fork stop <name> stop a fork's background loop coop fork open <name> open a fork in your editor coop fork path <name> print a fork's directory path SERVICES: databases and other services defined in .agent/compose.yml coop init --services choose services to add coop up start services coop down stop services SECURITY & ISOLATION: control access, check isolation, and protect secrets coop doctor check that the box's isolation works coop approve review and approve requested project access coop net manage this project's network access coop check-secrets check project files for exposed secrets coop sign sign unpushed commits with your host key SETUP & MAINTENANCE: set up projects and manage Coop on this machine coop init set up Coop in this project coop build rebuild the box coop update update Coop and the box coop version show the installed Coop version INTEGRATIONS: use Coop with other tools and your shell coop help acp connect Coop to your editor coop help sessions let other apps start and manage agents coop help prompt add Coop status to your shell prompt or tmux coop help completion enable tab completion in Bash or Zsh Help and examples: coop help <command> Full reference: coop help --all Documentation: https://coop.dryga.com/docs.html

heading: coop run: run a command in the box
text: Usage: coop run [<options>] -- <command> [<args>...] OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file Put Coop options before --. Everything after it belongs to your command. Without --, Coop options end where your command starts. EXAMPLES coop run -- npm test coop run --egress open -- curl https://example.com coop run --egress offline -- git status NETWORK ACCESS filtered allow only what approved network rules permit (default) open allow unrestricted internet access offline block internet access Without --egress, the box is filtered unless the project's network setting or COOP_EGRESS chooses another mode. With --egress open or offline, the project's network rules do not apply to that run. RULES FILE The file uses an egress_rules key, like box.egress_rules in .agent/project.yaml: egress_rules: - to: {domain: "docs.example.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] Keep the file outside the project, where the agent cannot edit it. Coop refuses a file inside the project. For more details see: coop help net

heading: coop shell: open a shell in the box
text: Usage: coop shell [<options>] OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file EXAMPLES coop shell coop shell --egress open coop shell --egress offline USING THE SHELL The shell opens in your project inside the box. Type exit or press Ctrl-D to return to your host. NETWORK ACCESS filtered allow only what approved network rules permit (default) open allow unrestricted internet access offline block internet access Without --egress, the box is filtered unless the project's network setting or COOP_EGRESS chooses another mode. With --egress open or offline, the project's network rules do not apply to that run. For more details see: coop help net

heading: coop claude: run Claude in the box
text: Usage: coop claude[:<model>][/<effort>][@<account>] [<options>] [-- <claude-args>...] OPTIONS --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable -p "<prompt>" run one prompt and exit -- pass all remaining arguments directly to Claude NETWORK OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file EXAMPLES coop claude coop claude:opus coop claude:opus/high@work coop claude -p "fix the failing test" coop claude -- --help MODELS AND ACCOUNTS coop models claude list Claude models coop credentials claude list Claude accounts coop login claude sign in to Claude For a guide to using multiple models and providers together: coop help presets

heading: coop codex: run Codex in the box
text: Usage: coop codex[:<model>][/<effort>][@<account>] [<options>] [-- <codex-args>...] OPTIONS --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable -p "<prompt>" run one prompt and exit -- pass all remaining arguments directly to Codex NETWORK OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file EXAMPLES coop codex coop codex:gpt-6-astra coop codex:gpt-6-astra/high@work coop codex -p "fix the failing test" coop codex -- --help MODELS AND ACCOUNTS coop models codex list Codex models coop credentials codex list Codex accounts coop login codex sign in to Codex For a guide to using multiple models and providers together: coop help presets

heading: coop gemini: run Gemini in the box
text: Usage: coop gemini[:<model>][/<effort>][@<account>] [<options>] [-- <gemini-args>...] OPTIONS --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable -p "<prompt>" run one prompt and exit -- pass all remaining arguments directly to Gemini NETWORK OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file EXAMPLES coop gemini coop gemini:gemini-3.8-flash coop gemini:gemini-3.8-flash/high@work coop gemini -p "fix the failing test" coop gemini -- --help MODELS AND ACCOUNTS coop models gemini list Gemini models coop credentials gemini list Gemini accounts coop login gemini sign in to Gemini For a guide to using multiple models and providers together: coop help presets

heading: coop grok: run Grok in the box
text: Usage: coop grok[:<model>][/<effort>][@<account>] [<options>] [-- <grok-args>...] OPTIONS --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable -p "<prompt>" run one prompt and exit -- pass all remaining arguments directly to Grok NETWORK OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file EXAMPLES coop grok coop grok:grok-4.5 coop grok:grok-4.5/high@work coop grok -p "fix the failing test" coop grok -- --help MODELS AND ACCOUNTS coop models grok list Grok models coop credentials grok list Grok accounts coop login grok sign in to Grok For a guide to using multiple models and providers together: coop help presets

heading: coop login: sign in to an agent
text: Usage: coop login <agent>[@<account>] AGENTS claude codex gemini grok EXAMPLES coop login claude coop login codex@work ACCOUNTS Without @account, signs in to the agent's default account. Use a name such as @work to keep a separate login. An agent's first account becomes its default, named or not. Show accounts: coop credentials Start an agent: coop claude

heading: coop credentials: show and manage your agent accounts
text: Usage: coop credentials show all accounts coop credentials <agent> show one agent's accounts coop credentials <agent> <account> show an account coop credentials <agent> <account> default use it by default coop credentials <agent> <account> rm remove it USE AN ACCOUNT coop claude@work coop login claude@work The list marks the default account with "default". Account removal options: coop help credentials rm Models and automatic rotation: coop help models

heading: coop credentials <agent> <account> default: choose the default account
text: Usage: coop credentials <agent> <account> default New runs try this account first. Add @account to use only one account. EXAMPLES coop credentials codex work default Accounts: coop credentials codex

heading: coop credentials <agent> <account> rm: remove a saved account
text: Usage: coop credentials <agent> <account> rm [--yes] OPTIONS -y, --yes skip confirmation Removes the saved login and its ordinary repository history. Account-independent editor conversations are kept. Choose another default before removing the current default account, unless it is the last one. EXAMPLES coop credentials codex old-work rm

heading: coop credentials <agent> <account>: show an account
text: Usage: coop credentials <agent> <account> EXAMPLES coop credentials codex personal Use by default: coop help credentials default Remove account: coop help credentials rm

heading: coop models: list models available to each agent
text: Usage: coop models [claude|codex|gemini|grok] [--refresh] LIST MODELS coop models all agents coop models claude Claude only coop models claude --refresh refresh Claude models list now USE A MODEL Put :model after the agent name. This works anywhere Coop accepts a target. coop claude:opus coop loop claude:haiku coop fork risky claude:opus --loop You can use any model accepted by the agent, even if it is not listed. SET REASONING EFFORT Add /effort after the model, or after the agent to keep its default model. coop codex:gpt-6-astra/high coop codex/high Claude, Codex, and Grok pass the level to their own CLI. Gemini takes low or high as its thinking setting, on models Coop can map. A thinking setting you pin on one model in your Gemini settings still wins. CHOOSE AN ACCOUNT Add @account after the model. A --peer target takes no @account: peers use the run's accounts. coop claude:opus@work coop credentials FULL SYNTAX A target is an agent, optionally with a model, effort and account: coop <agent>:<model>/<effort>@<account> coop codex:gpt-6-astra/high@personal SET A DEFAULT MODEL export COOP_CLAUDE_MODEL=opus AUTOMATIC ROTATION Loops and presets can try models in order when one is rate-limited. Leave off @account to let Coop also try another signed-in account. Add @account when you want to use only that account. coop loop claude:opus coop loop claude:opus@work For more details see: coop help presets coop help loop

heading: coop usage: show limits and a 30-day API estimate
text: Usage: coop usage [<agent>[@<account>]] Shows your accounts' limits, then a 30-day estimate (≈$.../30d) of what your recorded activity would cost at standard API prices, subscription use included. The estimate reads Coop and native CLI history on this computer and is not a bill. Name an account to see the history and prices it uses. EXAMPLES coop usage coop usage codex coop usage codex@work PROVIDER REPORTS To see your provider's own API spend beside the estimate, add a billing source for it to ~/.config/coop/usage-reports.json. Coop reads no billing API until you do. Keep reporting keys in host environment variables, never in that file, the project or agents/env. EXIT STATUS 0 any usable history, quota or configured report; failures stay visible 1 no usable history, quota or configured report 2 invalid selector or arguments Credentials: coop credentials Guide: https://coop.dryga.com/usage-reports.html

heading: coop presets init: create a preset you can edit
text: Usage: coop presets init [<name>] Creates the frontier template in .agent/presets/. The default name is frontier. Existing presets are left unchanged. A name uses lowercase letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', and starts with a letter or digit. It cannot be a Coop command or an agent name, because coop <name> runs those instead. EXAMPLES coop presets init coop presets init review Learn how presets work: coop help presets

heading: coop presets: configure multiple models and providers to work together
text: Usage: coop presets list presets coop presets <name> show a preset coop presets init [<name>] create a preset (default: frontier) coop help <name> explain a preset CREATE A PRESET coop presets init coop presets init review RUN A PRESET coop frontier start the lead agent interactively coop loop frontier work through tasks with this preset coop acp frontier use this preset in your editor coop fork risky frontier --loop work through tasks in a fork HOW TO DEFINE A PRESET A preset is a YAML file that defines: - One lead agent. - Optional roles for focused work. - Optional prompt extensions. When you run a preset, Coop starts the lead and tells it which roles are available and when to use them. Each role runs with its configured agent, model, mode, and prompt. The lead combines their work into the final result. Syntax: agent: presets use Coop's standard model, effort, account, and automatic-rotation syntax. For details, see: coop help models mode: controls how a role works native runs inside the lead agent's session consult provides read-only advice from another agent delegate edits files for the lead, one at a time; never commits when: tells the lead when to use a role prompt: adds custom instructions to Coop's generated instructions for the lead or role Every lead in the preset must use a native role's provider; otherwise Coop stops before it starts and names the role to change. Where presets live: Project .agent/presets/<name>/preset.yaml Global ~/.config/coop/presets/<name>/preset.yaml A project preset overrides a global preset with the same name.

heading: coop tasks: manage work in .agent/tasks/
text: Usage: coop tasks [--tasks <path>]... [<command>] WORK ls list tasks (also the default) add "<title>" create a task claim <id> start working on a task release <id> return a task to todo with its handoff notes block <id> ask for a decision before continuing unblock <id> ["<answer>"] record a decision and return the task to todo park <id> ["<reason>"] set a todo or blocked task aside in the backlog done <id> move completed work to the archive REVIEW watch watch task progress decisions [-i] show questions waiting for your answer lint check task files for missing or inconsistent information MANAGE lease <id> reserve a task while an agent works outside a loop path <id> print a task's folder path queues print the configured queue paths rm <id> delete a task TASK STATES todo ready for an agent in progress being worked on blocked waiting for a decision done completed and archived GET STARTED coop tasks add "Fix login retries" coop loop claude A task folder holds its instructions, progress and decisions. Most commands accept a full task ID or a unique part of it. FOR AI AGENTS Create a task with its instructions and checklist: coop tasks add "Fix login retries" \ --context "An expired session retries forever." \ --acceptance "An expired session returns to sign-in." \ --approach "Stop retrying after an authentication failure." \ --subtask "Test an expired session." Block a task with a complete decision request: coop tasks block choose-storage \ --question "Where should uploads be stored?" \ --why "Uploads outgrew one disk, and moving them later means a migration." \ --option "A — Local disk: simplest, tied to one machine." \ --option "B — Object storage: shared across machines." \ --recommendation "B — production runs on more than one machine." Get its folder without parsing a listing: coop tasks path <id> Before releasing a task, update its state.md with a complete handoff. PROJECTS Coop includes queues listed in .agent/project.yaml. Use --tasks <path> to select a queue; repeat it to include several. A queue must be inside the project; only a fork loop takes one outside it. With subprojects, coop tasks add uses the subproject you run it in. Elsewhere, choose one with --project <name>. Command options: coop help tasks <command>

heading: coop tasks ls: list tasks and their progress
text: Usage: coop tasks ls [--tasks <path>]... [<options>] OPTIONS --todo show tasks ready to start --in-progress show tasks being worked on --blocked show tasks waiting for a decision --done show completed tasks --all show the full completed archive Combine state options to show more than one state. By default, completed tasks are limited to the five most recent. EXAMPLES coop tasks ls --in-progress --blocked coop tasks ls --done --all coop tasks ls --tasks web/.agent/tasks

heading: coop tasks add: create a task for you or an agent
text: Usage: coop tasks add "<title>" [<options>] OPTIONS --project <name> choose root or a subproject, as listed in project.yaml or by its last folder name; inside a subproject's folder, add uses that subproject --tasks <path> choose one task queue --context <text> explain the problem and why it matters --acceptance <text> describe what must be true when finished --approach <text> describe how to tackle the work --subtask <text> add a checklist item; repeat for more items New tasks use the task.md Template in the selected queue's README.md, including its checklist. Each subproject uses its own README.md. --subtask replaces the <…> step placeholder and keeps the default checklist items. Without the text options, Coop creates a template for you to fill in. If you use any text option, include --context, --acceptance and --approach. Repeat a text option to add another paragraph. The first task in a new task queue sets the queue up: its README.md, and .gitignore lines that keep its task folders out of Git. EXAMPLES coop tasks add "Fix login retries" coop tasks add --project web "Fix login retries" coop tasks add "Fix login retries" \ --context "An expired session retries forever." \ --acceptance "An expired session returns to sign-in." \ --approach "Stop retrying after an authentication failure." \ --subtask "Test an expired session."

heading: coop tasks claim: take responsibility for a task
text: Usage: coop tasks claim <id> [--tasks <path>]... [<options>] OPTIONS --as <label> name the person or agent working on it --pid <n> bind the claim to an existing process --force take over a claim held by another live process Moves a todo task to in progress. An agent's claim normally follows its process. A claim made at a terminal stays until you release or finish it. Taking over with --force ends the other process's lease, and that process can no longer finish, block or release the task. A blocked task must return to todo first, through coop tasks unblock, even when its decision is answered. Completed tasks stay in the archive. EXAMPLES coop tasks claim login-retries coop tasks claim login-retries --as codex --pid 812 Hand it back: coop tasks release <id>

heading: coop tasks release: return a task to the queue for another agent
text: Usage: coop tasks release <id> [--tasks <path>]... Before releasing, update state.md with the work completed, checks run and anything another agent needs to continue. Returns the task to todo and removes your claim. Progress and handoff notes are kept. A task being worked on by another process or assigned to a fork cannot be released. EXAMPLES coop tasks release login-retries

heading: coop tasks lease: reserve a task while work is running
text: Usage: coop tasks lease <id> [--tasks <path>]... [<options>] [-- <command>...] OPTIONS --as <label> name the working agent --pid <n> hold the reservation while this process is alive -- run a command and release the reservation when it exits Claim the task first. Other loops skip it while this reservation is held. Without a command, Coop follows your agent's process or the task's claimant. With no process to follow, it waits until the task moves or you press Ctrl-C. EXAMPLES coop tasks lease login-retries -- make check coop tasks lease login-retries --as codex --pid 812

heading: coop tasks block: pause a task that needs a decision
text: Usage: coop tasks block <id> [--tasks <path>]... [<options>] OPTIONS --question <text> ask the question that needs an answer, on one line --why <text> say what happened and why the task cannot go on --option <text> describe a choice and its tradeoff; repeat for more choices --recommendation <text> recommend a choice and explain why Without these options, creates decision.md for you to fill in. If you use any of them, include a question, why, at least one option, and a recommendation. Existing answers and decision notes are never overwritten. FOR AI AGENTS coop tasks block choose-storage \ --question "Where should uploads be stored?" \ --why "Uploads outgrew one disk, and moving them later means a migration." \ --option "A — Local disk: simplest, tied to one machine." \ --option "B — Object storage: shared across machines." \ --recommendation "B — production runs on more than one machine." ANSWER A QUESTION coop tasks unblock choose-storage "Use object storage."

heading: coop tasks unblock: record a decision and return a task to todo
text: Usage: coop tasks unblock <id> ["<answer>"] [--tasks <path>]... Provide your answer here, or fill in Resolution in decision.md first. Coop keeps the decision with the task so the next agent can continue. Without --tasks, it also looks in the queues your forks work from. In a fork's own checkout, it answers the task in the fork's project. EXAMPLES coop tasks unblock login-retries "Return to sign-in after the first failure." Questions waiting for you: coop tasks decisions -i

heading: coop tasks park: set a todo or blocked task aside in the backlog
text: Usage: coop tasks park <id> ["<reason>"] [--tasks <path>]... Moves the task to the backlog with its folder and log, so nothing picks it up or returns it to todo on its own. Your reason is saved in the task's log. For a blocked task this answers its decision with "not now"; the decision stays open. Release a task in progress before you park it. coop backlog promote brings it back, blocked while its decision is open. EXAMPLES coop tasks park login-retries "After the release." coop tasks park choose-storage "Not this quarter." Questions waiting for you: coop tasks decisions -i

heading: coop tasks done: move completed work to the archive
text: Usage: coop tasks done <id> [--tasks <path>]... [<options>] OPTIONS --force close it even though its checklist is unfinished --from-fork complete a fork's task whose commit is already on this branch Finish the checks and commit the task's work first. The task must have at least one checklist item, with every item checked. Its state.md must not keep the template's <…> text in Done so far or Traps. Leave required checks open if they failed, could not run, or have not run. Coop moves the task to done and removes its temporary files. The task's instructions, progress and saved evidence stay in the archive. --force is for a person at a terminal who has checked the work. Coop leaves the checklist as it is and notes what was open in the task's log. Agents never use it. A fork's task completes when you merge the fork. If you brought the commit with its Coop-Task trailer to this branch yourself, --from-fork completes the task, notes that in its log and keeps the stopped fork. A later merge skips that commit if you brought it over unchanged. It also needs a person at a terminal. EXAMPLES coop tasks done login-retries

heading: coop tasks path: print a task's folder path
text: Usage: coop tasks path <id> [--tasks <path>]... EXAMPLES coop tasks path login-retries

heading: coop tasks queues: print task queue paths
text: Usage: coop tasks queues [--tasks <path>]... Prints one absolute path per line. By default, includes the project's queues. EXAMPLES coop tasks queues

heading: coop tasks decisions: show questions waiting for your answer
text: Usage: coop tasks decisions [--tasks <path>]... [-i] OPTIONS -i, --interactive read and answer each question interactively Forks ready to merge follow the questions, with the commands that review and merge them. With -i, :r reviews a fork and :m merges it. EXAMPLES coop tasks decisions coop tasks decisions -i coop tasks unblock login-retries "Return to sign-in after the first failure."

heading: coop tasks lint: check task files for missing or inconsistent information
text: Usage: coop tasks lint [--tasks <path>]... Checks the task folders, frontmatter, required sections, decisions and waits. It also names tasks that still hold the template's <…> text. The loop still works such a task: its agent fills the text in first. A finished task is named when its state.md keeps template text. Returns a nonzero exit status when it finds a problem. EXAMPLES coop tasks lint

heading: coop tasks rm: permanently delete task folders
text: Usage: coop tasks rm <id> [--tasks <path>]... [--yes] coop tasks rm --all-done [--tasks <path>]... [--yes] OPTIONS --all-done delete every completed task in the selected queues -y, --yes skip confirmation Deletes task instructions, progress and saved evidence. Git commits remain. To archive finished work, use coop tasks done instead. EXAMPLES coop tasks rm abandoned-task coop tasks rm --all-done

heading: coop tasks watch: watch task progress
text: Usage: coop tasks watch [--tasks <path>]... [--json] OPTIONS --json print one snapshot for scripts Problems that need attention show too. The live view closes when the queue is done and its activity has stopped. Press Ctrl-C to leave the view. In a pipe, Coop prints one static snapshot. EXAMPLES coop tasks watch coop tasks watch --tasks web/.agent/tasks

heading: coop backlog: save ideas that need more planning
text: Usage: coop backlog [--tasks <path>]... [<command>] COMMANDS ls list ideas (also the default) add "<title>" save an idea promote <id> move an idea to the task queue rm <id> delete an idea Backlog items live in .agent/tasks/xx_backlog/. Agents leave them alone until you promote them. Put work that is ready to start directly in coop tasks. EXAMPLES coop backlog add "Redesign account permissions" coop backlog promote account-permissions Command options: coop help backlog <command>

heading: coop backlog ls: list saved ideas
text: Usage: coop backlog ls [--tasks <path>]... By default, includes every configured project queue. Repeat --tasks to select several queues. EXAMPLES coop backlog ls --tasks web/.agent/tasks

heading: coop backlog add: save an idea for later
text: Usage: coop backlog add "<title>" [<options>] OPTIONS --tasks <path> choose one task queue --context <text> explain the problem and why it matters --acceptance <text> describe the intended result --approach <text> describe a possible approach --subtask <text> add a checklist item; repeat for more items Without the text options, Coop creates a template for you to fill in. If you use any text option, include --context, --acceptance and --approach. Repeat a text option to add another paragraph. EXAMPLES coop backlog add "Redesign account permissions" coop backlog add "Redesign account permissions" --tasks web/.agent/tasks Ready to start: coop backlog promote <id>

heading: coop backlog promote: move an idea to the task queue
text: Usage: coop backlog promote <id> [--tasks <path>]... Fill in its problem, completion criteria and approach before promoting it. The task becomes todo, where an agent or loop can pick it up. A parked task with an open decision comes back blocked, with its question. EXAMPLES coop backlog promote account-permissions

heading: coop backlog rm: permanently delete a saved idea
text: Usage: coop backlog rm <id> [--tasks <path>]... [--yes] OPTIONS -y, --yes skip confirmation Deletes the idea's folder, including its notes and saved files. EXAMPLES coop backlog rm account-permissions

heading: coop context: show the instructions relevant to your work
text: Usage: coop context [<path>...] [<options>] OPTIONS --changed use files changed in Git --task <id> use paths listed in a task's frontmatter --tasks <path> choose a queue for --task; repeat for more queues --rendered print the selected files' contents --json print the selection for scripts Coop includes shared agent instructions and any matching context routes. Use paths relative to the repository root, even inside a subproject. Inside a subproject, its path and its own AGENTS.md are included. You can combine explicit paths, --changed and --task. Choose either --rendered or --json for the output format. EXAMPLES coop context web/src/app.ts coop context --changed coop context --task login-retries --rendered CONFIGURE ROUTES: .agent/project.yaml context: routes: - paths: ["web/**"] include: [.agent/kb/web.md] This includes .agent/kb/web.md when the selected work is under web/.

heading: coop loop: let agents work through your task queue
text: Usage: coop loop [<target|preset>] [<options>] HOW IT WORKS A fresh agent works on each task, then a final review checks the work and can reopen tasks. Coop continues until it passes or needs your decision. Tasks run in folder order; priority: high or priority: low in a task.md's frontmatter moves it ahead or back. OPTIONS --tasks <path> choose a task queue; repeat for more queues --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable --review-task <id> add a completed task with a valid completion record to the final review; repeat to add more --max-tasks <n> pause after N tasks finish or become blocked --preflight before starting, resolve answered decisions and release stale claims --no-preflight skip that preparation --no-mcp run without configured MCP servers --debug-on-fail open a box shell after a failure; retry when you exit --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file --max-tasks pauses before the final review. The limit must be positive. --debug-on-fail opens a shell only when running in a terminal. EXAMPLES coop loop claude coop loop frontier coop loop codex --max-tasks 1 STOP AND CONTINUE Press Ctrl-C to finish the current attempt and its required review, then stop. Press it again to stop immediately. Run the same command to continue. Without a terminal, SIGINT does the same. SIGTERM and SIGHUP stop immediately. For a background fork loop: coop fork stop <name> CONFIGURE STEPS: .agent/loop.yaml preflight optional preparation before starting work the agent that works on each task between optional review after each task signoff final review of completed work verify optional checks after the final review Set work.agent to choose the default when no target or preset is given. Review steps can each use their own agent and prompt. Signoff prompts add to Coop's built-in review. Between and verify prompts define those checks and are required when enabled. Changes to this file apply when you restart the loop. Step options: preflight enabled, prompt work agent, command between enabled, agent, prompt, writes signoff agent, prompt, rounds, writes verify enabled, agent, prompt, writes agent: accepts a list of targets or presets. See coop help models. writes: tasks keeps reviews read-only; repo lets reviewers edit source files. mcp: false disables MCP servers for every step. NETWORK ACCESS The run's approved access covers its work and review agents for the entire loop. See coop help net for rules and approvals. EXIT STATUS 0 review and enabled final checks passed, or the task limit was reached 1 the run failed or could not start, final checks failed, or work remains, including work another agent holds 2 rejected input, such as an unknown option, target or preset 3 stopped for a decision 130 interrupted before the final verdict

heading: coop eval: check whether a model, preset or loop change helped
text: Usage: coop eval <command> Run repeatable tasks, grade the work independently, then compare before and after. Real runs use your provider account and may spend credits. A preview spends none. TRY IT 1. Preview three small coding tasks; nothing launches: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m --dry-run 2. Run them with your signed-in account and built Coop box: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m 3. Read the result, including any errors: coop eval inspect RUN AND COMPARE coop eval run <suite> <target|preset>... run a suite; --timeout for real runs coop eval runs find runs and their outcomes coop eval inspect [<run-id>] read a run's results and causes coop eval compare <before-id> <after-id> compare two runs without spending Change your model, preset, loop recipe or Coop build, run the same suite again, then use the two IDs from coop eval runs. Errors are not model-quality failures; inspect their causes before rerunning. Incomplete grading has no definitive winner. CHOOSE A SUITE coop eval ls list the shipped starter suites coop eval init <dir> create an editable custom suite core Three single-agent tasks. Use provider targets, not presets. queue A real loop over ten tasks that takes hours. Use targets or presets. For options and prerequisites see: coop help eval run Guide: https://coop.dryga.com/docs.html#evals

heading: coop eval run: preview or run a repeatable evaluation
text: Usage: coop eval run <suite> <target|preset>... --timeout <duration> [<options>] Each target (<agent>[:<model>][/<effort>][@<account>]) or preset is a separate configuration, not a fallback. Presets need a loop suite such as queue. Real runs use your accounts and may spend credits. Dry runs are free. OPTIONS --timeout <duration> time limit for the whole run; required for a real run --dry-run print the plan without launching containers or providers --repeat <n> trials per case and configuration (default: 1) --jobs <n> concurrent trials (default: 1) --loop-config <path> use this loop recipe instead of the loop suite's recipe EXAMPLES coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m --dry-run coop eval run core codex:gpt-6.1-sol codex:gpt-6.1-sol/xhigh --timeout 70m coop eval run queue frontier --timeout 2h coop eval run queue frontier --loop-config .agent/loop.yaml --dry-run coop eval run ./evals/my-suite/suite.yaml codex --repeat 3 --timeout 60m BEFORE A REAL RUN Sign in with coop login <agent> and have the current Coop box image. If it is missing, run coop build --egress open in a folder without a project Dockerfile. A dry run checks the plan, not your sign-in or image. TRIALS Each trial works in a private copy without source history. The model never sees the hidden verifier, which grades afterwards without credentials or network. Trials run without your MCP servers, COOP_RUN_ARGS or the clients' own web search and fetch tools.
