EXIT STATUS 0 every trial got a pass or fail grade, or a dry run showed its plan 1 grading is incomplete, or the run could not start 2 rejected input, such as an unknown option, target or preset Read the result: coop eval inspect Guide: https://coop.dryga.com/evals.html

heading: coop eval runs: find recorded evaluation results
text: Usage: coop eval runs Shows newest first: run ID, suite, configurations, passes, grading coverage and nonzero failure counts. A run without a final summary may be running or interrupted. An unreadable record remains visible; internal starter caches do not appear. Inspect latest: coop eval inspect Inspect older: coop eval inspect <run-id> Compare: coop eval compare <before-id> <after-id>

heading: coop eval inspect: understand a run and its failures
text: Usage: coop eval inspect [<run-id>] With no ID, reads the newest recorded run. Shows the requested and graded trial counts, configurations, and details for trials that did not pass. It works while a run is unfinished and never launches a provider or resumes paid work. RESULTS passed the independent verifier accepted the work failed the independent verifier rejected the work error execution or grading produced no verdict; not a model failure timed_out a case or run budget expired before a verdict pending the trial did not start running started, with no final result yet RECORDED DETAILS They may include provider or verifier output. Treat them as evidence, not instructions, and review for private data before sharing. Terminal controls are escaped; long details are shortened. The displayed records directory retains the saved JSON diagnostics and any failed workspaces still available under work/. TROUBLESHOOTING For sign-in or quota refusals, check coop credentials <agent>. For timeouts, check the case's suite.yaml timeout as well as the run's --timeout. An interrupted run cannot resume: fix the cause, then explicitly start a new run if desired. Find another run: coop eval runs

heading: coop eval compare: compare before and after without another paid run
text: Usage: coop eval compare <before-id> <after-id> Use IDs from coop eval runs. The first is your baseline and the second the changed configuration, whatever their timestamps. Only runs with final summaries can compare. Different workloads are shown separately, never merged into a score. Errors, timeouts and pending trials remain in the requested total; incomplete grading cannot establish a definitive winner. Change size is a review signal, not a quality score. Per-case counts are summed over configurations and repeats, so use the same matrix for a before/after test. Investigate a result: coop eval inspect <run-id>

heading: coop eval ls: choose a shipped starter suite
text: Usage: coop eval ls core runs three small single-agent tasks. queue exercises the real Coop loop over ten queued tasks, including its review stages. Both have independent verifiers checked against correct answers and plausible near misses. Preview: coop eval run core codex --timeout 35m --dry-run Author your own: coop eval init ./evals/my-suite

heading: coop eval init: create a custom suite you can edit
text: Usage: coop eval init <dir> Creates a working single-agent example, a commented loop example in suite.yaml, and a sample verifier: verifiers/greeting/README.md and verifiers/greeting/verify.sh. Use a new directory; existing files are never overwritten. Edit suite.yaml, the visible files and the separate hidden verifier. Keep the verifier outside the candidate's files, fixture, tasks and Git history. The verifier README explains grading and exit codes. A preview does not run or check your verifier; test it against good answers and near misses. EXAMPLES coop eval init ./evals/my-suite coop eval run ./evals/my-suite/suite.yaml codex --timeout 12m --dry-run

heading: coop fork: let an agent work in a separate copy of your project
text: Usage: coop fork <name> [<target|preset>] [<options>] coop fork <command> [<args>...] START WORK coop fork myfork claude create a fork and start Claude coop fork myfork continue an existing fork's session coop fork myfork frontier use a preset coop fork myfork claude -d work through tasks in the background REVIEW AND MERGE ls show forks and their progress review <name> review a fork's changes merge <name> merge its commits into your current branch merge --all merge eligible forks one at a time MANAGE logs [<name>] show one fork's logs, or all forks stop <name> stop a fork's background loop open <name> open a fork in your editor path <name> print its folder path rm <name> delete a fork SESSION OPTIONS --isolated create independent Git storage and require reviewed publication -c, --continue continue the last session (default when reopening) --new start a new conversation in the existing fork --fresh delete the fork and its service data, then recreate it -f, --force with --fresh, stop active work and discard unmerged changes -y, --yes with --fresh, skip confirmation An isolated fork stays that way when reopened, looped or used over ACP. Existing forks are not converted, and isolation is off by default. Review it with coop fork review; --force cannot bypass its policy. NETWORK OPTIONS --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file LOOP OPTIONS --loop work through the project's task queue -d, --detach run the loop in the background (implies --loop) -t, --tasks <path> choose a task queue, even one outside the project; repeat for more queues --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable --stop-after-review stop once a task passes review, ready to merge Each fork receives one project task at a time. Its task is completed in the project queue when you merge the reviewed work. Stopping keeps it resumable. EDITOR INTEGRATION coop fork <name> acp use an existing fork from an ACP editor Model and account syntax: coop help models Command options: coop help fork <command>

heading: coop fork <name> acp: use an existing fork from an ACP editor
text: Usage: coop fork <name> acp [<target>] [<options>] OPTIONS --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file Without a target, Coop starts the fork's agent with its default model and account; choose another model or effort in your editor. Open the parent project in your editor; Coop maps it to the fork. The fork, provider and account stay fixed. EXAMPLES coop fork myfork acp coop fork myfork acp claude:opus Create the fork first: coop fork myfork claude Editor setup: coop help acp

heading: coop fork ls: show forks and their progress
text: Usage: coop fork ls [--json] OPTIONS --json print workspace details for scripts Shows each fork's agent, activity, tasks, changes and reported cost. EXAMPLES coop fork ls

heading: coop fork review: inspect a fork before merging
text: Usage: coop fork review <name> [<options>] OPTIONS --stat show a change summary instead of the full diff --tool open the diff with your global Git diff tool --open open the fork in your editor --gate test the fork after rebasing a temporary copy onto your current branch Shows commits, the agent's task notes and changes that need your attention. Counts and diffs include committed changes only. Uncommitted fork work gets a warning; open the fork, commit intended files, then review again. --gate leaves the fork and your working tree unchanged. It cannot be used with --open. Coop reviews an isolated fork's saved private commits even when your main checkout has uncommitted changes. --open and COOP_REVIEW_CMD use a saved private preview, separate from the agent's workspace. Preview edits are never merged. Coop prints the preview folders; delete them when you finish. EXAMPLES coop fork review myfork coop fork review myfork --stat --gate Merge after review: coop fork merge myfork

heading: coop fork merge: bring a fork's commits into your current branch
text: Usage: coop fork merge <name> [<options>] coop fork merge --all [<options>] OPTIONS --all merge eligible forks one at a time -f, --force allow changes otherwise blocked by the merge policy -y, --yes confirm merging and removal without prompting Review the diff first. Your working tree must be clean and the fork stopped. Coop rebases the commits, runs configured project checks and merges the result. --force does not bypass those checks. For isolated forks, --force cannot bypass risky-file or nested-Git policy. Coop saves the exact changes to merge before updating your checkout. If the merge is interrupted, keep its journal and saved private files, then rerun merge. If the checkout is only partly updated or changed by another process, Coop stops for recovery. Do not reset, stash, delete an index.lock you cannot identify, or recreate or remove the fork. After merging, Coop asks before deleting a clean fork. With --all, one prompt covers the batch and removal. Forks with uncommitted work are kept. Removing a fork also removes its service containers and Docker volumes. EXAMPLES coop fork review myfork coop fork merge myfork coop fork merge --all

heading: coop fork rm: delete a fork and its local work
text: Usage: coop fork rm <name> [<options>] OPTIONS -f, --force stop active work and discard uncommitted or unmerged changes -y, --yes skip confirmation Deleting a fork removes its files and local session data, plus its service containers and Docker volumes. Assigned tasks return to the project queue. Proposed tasks that have not been imported are discarded; tasks already imported into the project are kept. EXAMPLES coop fork rm myfork coop fork rm myfork --force

heading: coop fork stop: stop a fork's background loop
text: Usage: coop fork stop <name> Stops the worker and its running boxes. The fork's work and assigned task stay available so you can continue it later. EXAMPLES coop fork stop myfork coop fork myfork claude --loop

heading: coop fork logs: show a fork's loop output
text: Usage: coop fork logs [<name>] [--follow] OPTIONS -f, --follow keep showing new output Without a name, includes all forks and labels each line with its fork name. Press Ctrl-C to leave the log view; the loop keeps running. EXAMPLES coop fork logs myfork coop fork logs myfork --follow coop fork logs --follow

heading: coop fork path: print a fork's folder path
text: Usage: coop fork path <name> EXAMPLES coop fork path myfork

heading: coop fork open: open a fork in your editor
text: Usage: coop fork open <name> Uses COOP_EDITOR, your global Git editor or an available editor. EXAMPLES coop fork open myfork

heading: coop up: start this project's services
text: Usage: coop up Starts the services in .agent/compose.yml, or the file box.compose names in .agent/project.yaml, and waits until they are ready. Agents reach each service by its Compose name. Running it again is safe. Requires Docker with Compose support. APPROVALS Coop asks at a terminal before a service may read a hidden secret file through a read-only bind, or use an external or custom-named Docker volume. Declining stops startup. Until you approve, the file stays hidden. Automatic, filtered and non-terminal starts refuse such volumes even after approval. An approval covers this checkout's exact Compose file and the service's local image, so any change asks again. Add services: coop init --services Stop services: coop down Guide: https://coop.dryga.com/box.html#project-services

heading: coop down: stop this project's services
text: Usage: coop down [--delete-volumes] [--yes] Stops and removes this project's Compose containers and networks. Uses .agent/compose.yml, or the configured Compose path. OPTIONS --delete-volumes also permanently delete service volumes and their data -y, --yes skip the volume-deletion confirmation Coop names the volumes before asking; press Enter to cancel. Without a terminal, deletion requires --yes. External volumes and files mounted from the project are kept. Start again: coop up

heading: coop doctor: check that the box's isolation works
text: Usage: coop doctor Runs checks in a temporary project and reports what passed, failed, or could not be checked. Your files and credentials are not the test data. Checks secret hiding, host access, privileges, offline networking, task access, credential isolation, settings permissions, and fork handoff. Uses this project's ordinary built image, or the shared image if available. If neither exists, uses Alpine and names the checks it cannot perform. Run coop build --egress open, then coop doctor to test the Coop image. Filtered images are separate and are verified when a filtered run starts. Requires Git and a running container runtime. Honors COOP_RUNTIME. Lists abandoned boxes but does not remove them.

heading: coop approve: review and approve this project's requested access
text: Usage: coop approve [--case-exposure] Shows what .agent/project.yaml asks for, compared with your last approval. Confirm the changes to allow new runs to use them. If nothing changed, there is nothing to approve. If a filtered box is stuck because the project's services have no rules, it lists the services and their ports and offers to add and approve the rules. OPTIONS --case-exposure additionally review file exposure with mount protection Use it only when a launch refuses hidden files that stay readable under another letter case. Approval covers those paths and their future contents for agents and services; new paths need approval again. Runs with eBPF protection keep those files hidden without this approval. Running boxes keep the rules they started with. A running editor session (coop acp) that has network rules moves to a new box with these rules between prompts. Run this command in your terminal. See current access: coop net

heading: coop net: control network access and see what happened
text: Usage: coop net [<command>] ACCESS: control what new runs can reach coop net show this project's current access coop approve review and approve requested access coop net check <url> check access coop net forget withdraw this project's network approval RUNS: inspect recorded network activity coop net runs show recent runs coop net inspect [<run>] show connections and blocked access coop net blocked <host> find blocked connections and how to allow them coop net watch [<run>] follow network activity coop net export <run> export a shareable record REPAIR: normally automatic coop net setup prepare or recheck this host now coop net recover [<run>] retry interrupted cleanup now HOW TO ADD A NETWORK RULE 1. Add it under box.egress_rules in .agent/project.yaml: box: egress: filtered egress_rules: - to: {domain: "docs.example.com"} protocol: tls ports: [443] 2. Review and approve the changes: coop approve Command options: coop help net <command>

heading: coop net runs: show recorded network runs
text: Usage: coop net runs [--all | --all-projects] [--json] OPTIONS --all show every run for this project --all-projects show every project's runs on this host --json print the records for scripts By default, shows this project's 25 newest runs. Use a run's ID or a unique prefix with other network commands. EXAMPLES coop net runs coop net runs --all-projects Inspect a run: coop net inspect e644f07a

heading: coop net inspect: show a run's connections and blocked traffic
text: Usage: coop net inspect [<run>] [--json] OPTIONS --json print the full technical record Without a run ID, shows this project's newest recorded run. EXAMPLES coop net inspect coop net inspect e644f07a

heading: coop net check: check whether network rules allow a connection
text: Usage: coop net check <url-or-host> [<options>] coop net check <ip> --run <run> --protocol <tcp|udp> --port <n> coop net check <ip> --run <run> --icmp OPTIONS --run <run> use that run's rules --port <n> choose a port; defaults to the URL's port or 443 --protocol <tcp|udp> choose the connection type for an IP address --icmp check an ICMP echo request to an IP address --json print the answer for scripts Without --run, checks this project's approved access for a new run. Hostnames use TLS. IP addresses require a recorded run and connection type. EXAMPLES coop net check https://example.com coop net check example.com --run e644f07a EXIT STATUS 0 the rules allow the connection 1 the check could not finish 2 invalid arguments 3 the rules block the connection, or new runs need approval first

heading: coop net blocked: find blocked connections and how to allow them
text: Usage: coop net blocked <host> [--run <run>] [--json] OPTIONS --run <run> look only in this run --json print the evidence for scripts Without --run, finds the newest matching block in this project's runs. Shows a rule you can copy when the record proves the remote address and port. A blocked DNS lookup records no port, so it shows TLS on port 443 as the likely fix. An exact event ID can replace the host when --run is supplied. EXAMPLES coop net blocked registry.npmjs.org coop net blocked registry.npmjs.org --run e644f07a EXIT STATUS 0 a recorded block was found 1 no recorded block matched, or the search could not finish 2 invalid arguments

heading: coop net watch: follow a run's network activity
text: Usage: coop net watch [<run>] [--json] OPTIONS --json stream one JSON record per update Without an ID, selects this project's only unfinished run. Shows new connections, blocks and problems, then the final report. Press Ctrl-C to stop watching. The run continues. EXAMPLES coop net watch e644f07a

heading: coop net export: export a run's network record
text: Usage: coop net export <run> [--include-addresses] OPTIONS --include-addresses include remote hostnames and IP addresses Writes JSON to stdout. The run must have a final record. EXAMPLES coop net export e644f07a > network-record.json

heading: coop net forget: withdraw this project's network approval
text: Usage: coop net forget [--project <path>] Use this when you no longer trust an approval saved on this machine. To change network rules, edit .agent/project.yaml and run coop approve. New runs wait for approval again. The project file is not changed. Existing boxes, recorded runs, and this host's network setup are kept. Run this command in your terminal. OPTIONS --project <path> choose another project by its folder, even a deleted one Restore approval: coop approve

heading: coop net setup: prepare this host for filtered networking
text: Usage: coop net setup Prepares the network images and checks that allowed access works and blocked access stays blocked. Coop does this automatically when a filtered run needs it. Run it yourself to check or prepare the host ahead of time. Requires Docker to be running.

heading: coop net recover: clean up interrupted network runs
text: Usage: coop net recover [<run>] Removes containers and temporary volumes left by an interrupted run. Without an ID, checks every run waiting for cleanup on this host and reports the ones it cleaned up or could not. Running boxes and resources Coop cannot safely identify are left alone. Coop normally retries this cleanup automatically. EXAMPLES coop net recover e644f07a

heading: coop check-secrets: check project files for exposed secrets
text: Usage: coop check-secrets [--include-ignored] Checks tracked and untracked files, plus Coop's task files and notes. Possible secrets are reported by file and line; their values stay hidden. Returns a nonzero status if possible secrets remain or the scan cannot finish. OPTIONS --include-ignored also check other Git-ignored files the box can read FALSE POSITIVES Add the entries printed by a scan to .coopsecretsignore in your project root. Each entry needs a reason. You can edit many entries together in that file. IDs stay the same when line numbers change. A changed value or file path, or a removed entry, is checked again. .coopsecretsignore skips exact findings in this check. .coopignore hides files from the box.

heading: coop sign: sign this branch's unpushed commits with your host key
text: Usage: coop sign [--from <ref>] OPTIONS --from <ref> sign commits after this Git reference EXAMPLES coop sign coop sign --from origin/main HOW IT WORKS By default, Coop signs commits after the branch's upstream reference. Without an upstream, use --from with the last commit you pushed. Signing changes the IDs of the first unsigned commit and the commits after it. It never rewrites a commit the upstream already has, and it preserves the committed files and your working changes. It stops at a merge among the commits it would rewrite; a signed merge below them stays as it is. Coop uses your host's Git signing settings. AUTOMATIC SIGNING When commit.gpgsign is enabled, Coop signs commits after ordinary agent runs and loop cycles. Fork commits are signed when you merge the fork.

heading: coop init: set up Coop in this project
text: Usage: coop init [<options>] You can run coop init again at any time. Coop keeps your existing project files and adds anything missing. COOP SETS UP - Shared instructions and skills for all your AI agents. - A file-based task system. Agents can pick up work, save progress, and hand it to another agent or session. - Commit checks. Coop verifies formatting for the languages it detects or you choose. - Project settings for sandboxed runs, including filtered internet access. - An optional starter Docker Compose file for supporting services; you can extend it with anything else your project needs. OPTIONS --agents <list> set up Claude, Codex, Gemini, Grok, or all default: agents you are signed in to --services [<list>] add Postgres, Redis, or both --stack asdf install tools from .tool-versions in the Coop box Without options, Coop detects what it can and asks before initializing Git, adding formatting checks, or adding Postgres or Redis.

heading: coop build: build the Coop box image
text: Usage: coop build [--egress <mode>] Builds the shared image, or this project's image when it has a box Dockerfile (.agent/Dockerfile, or box.dockerfile in .agent/project.yaml). Run it after changing that Dockerfile or .tool-versions. Requires a running container runtime. Your home folder is never a project, so from there use --egress open, which builds the shared image. OPTIONS --egress <mode> prepare the image for filtered, open or offline networking default: this project's network mode Running this approves the build files for filtered launches. If only Coop's image changed, those same files rebuild by themselves; if you change them, build again. The build itself uses ordinary networking in every mode: review the Dockerfile and the files it copies first. New runs use the rebuilt image, and editor sessions on the replaced image restart. Fresh rebuild: coop update --box-only Guide: https://coop.dryga.com/box.html#builds-and-network-modes

heading: coop update: update Coop and rebuild the box image
text: Usage: coop update [--self-only | --box-only | --check] Updates the Coop binary when a newer release is available, then prepares the image for this project's effective network mode using the installed version's image definitions. Filtered projects rebuild the files you approved with coop build; new or changed build files wait for coop build. Open and offline images refresh base-image components. Agent CLIs and editor adapters remain pinned. Downloaded releases are checked before replacing the binary. Project builds use ordinary networking. From your home folder, which is never a project, it prepares the shared image. OPTIONS --self-only update only the Coop binary; no container runtime needed --box-only prepare only this project's effective box image --check report available updates and local build records; change nothing Choose at most one option. Only building the box needs a running container runtime. HOW IT WORKS Development builds and binaries newer than the latest release are kept. A binary that cannot be replaced is an error; update it with the tool that installed it. The box rebuild can still finish independently. New runs use the rebuilt image. Supervised editor sessions that run the replaced image restart and reconnect. Other running boxes use the old image until their next start. An unchanged image restarts nothing. Coop checks for new releases once a day during terminal use. Set COOP_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to turn off those notices.

heading: coop version: print the installed Coop version
text: Usage: coop version ALIASES coop -v coop --version

heading: coop acp: connect your editor to an agent running in a Coop box
text: Usage: coop acp [<target|preset>] [<options>] EDITOR SETUP Set the editor's agent command to coop and its arguments to: ["acp"] ["acp", "claude"] ["acp", "codex:gpt-6-astra/high@personal"] ["acp", "frontier"] Your editor must support ACP, the Agent Client Protocol. Without an agent or preset, Coop starts the first signed-in provider in Claude, Codex, Gemini, Grok order, using its default account. This does not pin the choice: use the editor's selectors after connecting. No providers signed in? Run coop login <agent>, then reconnect your editor. OPTIONS --peer <target> start a read-only peer agent (no @account); repeatable --egress <mode> network access: filtered (default), open or offline --allow-domain <host> allow TLS to this exact host on port 443; repeatable --egress-rules <path> add the network rules in this file SWITCHING AGENTS Use the editor's Provider and Account controls to change who runs the session. A preset chooses its agents automatically. Select None in Preset to choose a provider or account yourself. Switching providers carries the conversation into a new agent session. Account changes keep the conversation with the same provider. With filtered networking, only compatible providers and presets are offered. Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok support it. Gemini needs a Google sign-in or a Gemini API key, not Vertex AI. Switching never changes this session's network rules. PROJECT BOX With filtered networking the editor connects even when this project's box cannot start yet. Messages are held, the thread says why, and the session moves onto the box once it is ready. Approved build files rebuild by themselves. New or changed ones need coop build, or /build in the thread, which shows where Coop saved them and gives a code that builds exactly those files. Unapproved network access needs coop approve, and a broken .agent/project.yaml needs fixing. A box that exits as it starts, or does not answer within a minute, is tried again every 30 seconds; the agent log says why. TROUBLESHOOTING Set COOP_ACP_TRACE=1 in your editor's agent environment to record a trace. Trace files are saved as ~/.local/state/coop/acp-trace-<pid>.log and may contain your prompts and file contents. COOP_ACP_WARM=0 disables background boxes kept ready for provider switching. COOP_ACP_CARRY_TOKENS sets the conversation size carried between providers. After replacing the Coop binary, send SIGHUP to the specific ACP process to reload it. SIGINT and SIGTERM stop it. For more details see: coop help models coop help presets coop help net

heading: coop sessions: let other applications start and manage agents
text: Usage: coop sessions <command> COMMANDS connect connect this machine to a controller doctor check whether the local service is ready check see whether this build can use the session data as it is quiescence inspect queued and running work before a restart compact back up session data and reduce its disk usage CONNECT THIS MACHINE coop sessions connect --controller https://controller.example \ --token-file /path/to/token The controller supplies each session's code, context, and execution settings. Leave this command running; it starts the local service automatically. Command options: coop help sessions <command>

heading: coop sessions doctor: check the local session service
text: Usage: coop sessions doctor [<options>] The command succeeds when the service responds and is ready for sessions. OPTIONS --socket <path> check this Unix socket --json print the result as JSON EXAMPLES coop sessions doctor coop sessions doctor --socket /path/to/control.sock

heading: coop sessions check: see whether this build can use the session data as it is
text: Usage: coop sessions check [--state <path>] OPTIONS --state <path> check this session-data directory EXAMPLES coop sessions check coop sessions check --state /var/lib/coop/sessions BEFORE UPGRADING A WORKER Stop the session service, then run this command with the new coop build. It reads the session data and changes nothing. EXIT STATUS 0 this build uses the data as it is, or a started service holds none yet 1 the check could not finish: the service is still running, there is no session data at the path, or some data can't be read 2 invalid arguments 3 this build would convert the data; older builds can't open it afterwards 4 this build can't use the data: it is too old or too new DEFAULT SESSION DATA ~/.local/state/coop/sessions

heading: coop sessions quiescence: inspect queued and running work before a restart
text: Usage: coop sessions quiescence [--state <path>] [--json] Before restarting a worker, drain new submissions at the controller, then run this to see whether queued or running work remains. It reads the running service's data, including its write-ahead log, and never migrates it. Zero counts still need a graceful service shutdown to finish cleanup. OPTIONS --state <path> read this session-data directory --json print the snapshot as JSON EXIT STATUS 0 no queued or running work remains in the session store 1 the store is unavailable, damaged or uses an unsupported schema 2 invalid arguments 3 work remains DEFAULT SESSION DATA ~/.local/state/coop/sessions Guide: https://coop.dryga.com/session-api.html#restart-and-recovery

heading: coop sessions compact: back up session data and reduce its disk usage
text: Usage: coop sessions compact --backup <path> [--state <path>] OPTIONS --backup <path> save a verified database backup to a new file --state <path> use this session-data directory EXAMPLES coop sessions compact --backup /path/to/session-backup.sqlite BEFORE RUNNING Stop the session service. Choose a new backup file outside the session-data directory. Its parent directory must already exist. The backup contains private session data. Keep it protected. DEFAULT SESSION DATA ~/.local/state/coop/sessions

heading: coop sessions connect: run a worker for a remote controller
text: Usage: coop sessions connect --controller <https-url> [<options>] OPTIONS --controller <https-url> controller to trust and connect to --token-file <path> enrollment token (only needed on first connection) --state <path> private worker data directory --ca-file <path> CA bundle for a controller's private TLS certificate DEFAULT STORAGE ~/.local/state/coop/sessions RUNNING The controller supplies each session's code, context, and execution settings. No local policy file or worker configuration file is needed. Coop exchanges the enrollment token for worker credentials it can renew, then removes the token. Leave this command running. Connection failures are retried automatically. Press Ctrl-C to disconnect and stop the local service it started. On restart, use the same controller and state directory; omit --token-file.

heading: coop prompt: print a short project status for your shell or tmux
text: Usage: coop prompt OUTPUT Shows task counts, forks, running fork loops, and an unsigned-commit marker. Empty counts are omitted. When there is nothing to show, it prints nothing. EXAMPLE OUTPUT 2 todo · 1 in progress · 1 blocked · 3 forks (2 running) · unsigned commit TMUX Add this to ~/.tmux.conf: set -g status-right '#(cd "#{pane_current_path}" && coop prompt)' SHELL PROMPTS Run coop prompt from your prompt's custom-command configuration.

heading: coop completion: print shell integration for Bash or Zsh
text: Usage: coop completion <bash|zsh> BASH Save the completion script: mkdir -p ~/.config/coop coop completion bash > ~/.config/coop/completion.bash Add this to ~/.bashrc: source ~/.config/coop/completion.bash ZSH Save the integration script: mkdir -p ~/.config/coop coop completion zsh > ~/.config/coop/completion.zsh Add this after compinit in ~/.zshrc: source ~/.config/coop/completion.zsh This also stops Zsh from suggesting corrections to Coop arguments such as claude and codex. WHAT IT COMPLETES Commands, options, agents, models, accounts, presets, forks, and task IDs.

heading: Configuration
text: Find project settings, environment variables, configuration files and exit codes. co:op reads its settings from environment variables, from ~/.config/coop/coop.conf, and from the committed .agent/project.yaml. The website guide covers the settings you're most likely to change.

heading: Environment variables
text: Set these in your shell or in coop.conf. On/off settings take 1/true/yes/on or 0/false/no/off in any letter case, and co:op rejects any other value.

heading: Box and runtime
text: Variable Default What it does COOP_HOME $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/coop, or ~/.config/coop Absolute path of co:op's settings folder, which holds accounts and coop.conf. Use it to keep them out of a sync service, and set it for your editor too. co:op doesn't move your files. COOP_RUNTIME auto (Docker preferred) Picks the runtime: docker or container. COOP_IMAGE auto Forces a specific image, overriding .agent/Dockerfile detection. COOP_BASE_IMAGE coop-box The shared base image. coop-box selects co:op's own image, with a coop-box:<definition> tag for each box definition. COOP_REPO the nearest folder with .git Chooses the repo instead of detecting it from the current directory. co:op follows links, but refuses a link that leads to your home folder or any folder above it. With this unset outside a repository, the current folder is the project, unless it's your home folder or above, which co:op refuses. Set to your home folder, it works for commands such as coop tasks, but no box starts there. COOP_WORKDIR the repo's real path Where the repo mounts in the box, as an absolute path. COOP_HOME_IN_BOX /home/node Where provider homes and instructions mount in the box. COOP_RUN_ARGS unset Extra arguments for the container runtime. Filtered runs accept only bind mounts, -e KEY=VALUE and --label KEY=VALUE. COOP_BOX 1 in every box Lets a process detect that it's running inside a co:op box. COOP_PIDS 4096 Limits the number of processes in the box. 0, unlimited or empty turns it off. COOP_MEMORY, COOP_CPUS unset Limits the box's memory and CPUs, for example 4g and 2. COOP_NO_NEW_PRIVILEGES 1 Runs the box with --security-opt no-new-privileges. Filtered boxes always run with it, so 0 applies only with --egress open or offline. COOP_ALLOW_CASE_EXPOSED_SECRETS off On a Mac, lets one run start when mount protection can't hide every letter-case spelling of a long filename. The box or a service could then read a secret through a name such as .ENV.PRODUCTION. To remember this access for file paths you've reviewed, use coop approve --case-exposure. Runs protected by eBPF keep these files hidden and need neither. See hiding secrets. COOP_HOMES 1 Mounts each selected agent's repository home into the box. 0 keeps those homes out. Agents sign in through their homes, so with 0 an agent runs only offline, and co:op refuses presets, peers and fork sessions. COOP_EGRESS filtered Chooses how the box can use the network. See the choices below and networking. COOP_NO_ASDF off Skips installing the tools pinned in .tool-versions when the box starts. Set it in agents/env, not your host shell. COOP_NETWORK 1 Joins the services network. COOP_CACHE 1 Mounts the cache volume. COOP_AUTO_UP 1 Starts the .agent/compose.yml services for working boxes: all of them for an open box, and the ones its approved network rules name for a filtered box. Set 0 to manage development services yourself with coop up and coop down. A filtered box whose approved rules name services then won't start, because it reaches only the services co:op starts for it. COOP_SERVICES_NET auto The services network to join, so parallel forks can share one database. Choose one of these values for COOP_EGRESS: filtered allows the AI provider and domains you've approved. This is the default, and it needs Docker. open allows full outbound traffic. offline disables the box's network (--network none). The box can't send the repo, secrets or credentials over the network. Installs and model API calls stop working too, so you must choose this setting explicitly. An --egress flag overrides COOP_EGRESS, and COOP_EGRESS=offline always keeps a run offline unless you pass that flag. For filtered and open, a project's saved coop approve decision overrides COOP_EGRESS, and the run warns. A box.egress changed after that decision waits for coop approve, with or without COOP_EGRESS. COOP_EGRESS itself overrides box.egress in .agent/project.yaml, and the run and coop net warn when that allows more than the project asks for. The resource and privilege limits (COOP_PIDS, COOP_MEMORY, COOP_CPUS and COOP_NO_NEW_PRIVILEGES) apply on Docker, and co:op skips them with Apple's container CLI. On Docker, co:op also removes all Linux capabilities (--cap-drop ALL). Even if a repo's .agent/Dockerfile sets USER root, the container process doesn't get powers such as CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, CAP_NET_RAW or CAP_MKNOD.

heading: Agents and config
text: Variable Default What it does COOP_CONFIG_DIR ~/.config/coop/agents Absolute path of the folder for each agent's credentials and settings. COOP_CONF ~/.config/coop/coop.conf Environment only. Reads coop.conf from this absolute path, which must name a readable regular file. NO_COLOR unset Environment only. Any value, even an empty one, turns off ANSI color everywhere (no-color.org). COOP_<AGENT>_CMD, like COOP_CLAUDE_CMD the agent's autonomous command Overrides an agent's base command. COOP_<AGENT>_MODEL, like COOP_CLAUDE_MODEL the CLI's default The agent-wide default model, everywhere that agent runs. See picking models. COOP_CONSULT_TIMEOUT 0 (unlimited) How long coop-consult waits for each peer, in seconds. See below. COOP_CONSULT_STREAM_LIMIT 0 (unlimited) The most output, in bytes, coop-consult accepts from a peer's reply or diagnostics. It discards a larger reply. Set it in agents/env. See limits. COOP_PRESETS_DIR ~/.config/coop/presets Absolute path of the folder for global presets. See where presets live. COOP_MCP_FILE ~/.config/coop/agents/mcp.json Absolute path of the file that defines MCP servers. If you set it, the file must exist. It must be a regular file of at most 4 MiB, outside any directory co:op mounts in full. COOP_SHELL bash The shell coop shell opens. COOP_NO_UPDATE_CHECK off Turns off the once-a-day "a newer coop/box is available" check. By default, a peer can take as long as it needs. In a loop, the lead's own limits still apply: 2 hours for one tool call and 48 hours for one attempt. Set COOP_CONSULT_TIMEOUT to a whole number of seconds (max 86400) to add a timeout. If a peer doesn't answer in time, co:op skips it and the lead uses the replies that arrived. A timeout can't tell a slow answer from a stalled peer. If it interrupts a peer that was still working, that answer is lost and needs a retry.

heading: Forks and loop
text: Variable Default What it does COOP_GATE unset The check command, such as make check, that runs in the box during a local fork merge or during review with --gate. Controller-job reviews use the check in the submitted job instead. COOP_EDITOR detected The editor for coop fork review --open. COOP_REVIEW_CMD unset A full override for coop fork review, run with sh -c. COOP_TASKS derived The task queue directories for coop tasks and the loop, separated by spaces. Each must be inside the project. If unset, co:op uses the queues listed in .agent/project.yaml for a monorepo, or .agent/tasks otherwise. For one run, --tasks replaces this choice and doesn't add to it. COOP_CAFFEINATE 1 On a Mac, uses caffeinate to prevent idle sleep while the loop runs. 0 or false turns it off. COOP_ACP_WARM 1 Environment only. Keeps a box ready for each other editor ACP provider you're signed in to, so switching to that provider's default model skips box startup. Set 0 or false to save memory. COOP_ACP_CARRY_TOKENS 200000 How much of an editor conversation, in tokens of about 4 bytes, co:op carries to a new provider when you switch, dropping the oldest messages first. COOP_ACP_TRACE unset Environment only. Set it to any value in the editor's agent environment to record each coop acp server's traffic. See tracing a session. COOP_SPINNER 1 Environment only. Animates the Box Run beside progress bars and the Corner Run (◰ ◳ ◲ ◱) in task rows. Set 0 or false to freeze them and stop frequent loop-screen redraws. COOP_STREAM_TRACE off Saves each streaming loop attempt's raw provider JSONL and rendered output under .agent/runs/<run>.streams/. You configure loop behavior in .agent/loop.yaml. See the loop for the whole file. Key What it does work.command Sets the command for each work iteration. work.agent, between.agent, signoff.agent Choose the agents for work, per-task review and final review. signoff.rounds Limits the number of final review rounds. preflight.enabled Runs the queue cleanup pass by default in this repository. The --preflight flag turns on the same cleanup for one run.

heading: Command-valued settings
text: co:op splits COOP_GATE, COOP_RUN_ARGS and the COOP_<AGENT>_CMD overrides into argv. Single and double quotes group text into one argument, and \ escapes a character. It doesn't run these settings through a shell, so it doesn't expand wildcard paths or $VAR values. For example, COOP_GATE='bash -lc "make check && make lint"' produces three arguments, with the quoted text as one of them. co:op passes a bare &&, | or $VAR literally, so wrap commands that need those shell features in bash -lc "…". COOP_REVIEW_CMD is the exception: co:op runs it through sh -c.

heading: coop.conf
text: ~/.config/coop/coop.conf takes the same settings as KEY=VALUE lines. The environment wins over the file. The default file is optional, but a file you name with COOP_CONF must exist. If co:op can't read the file, the error names the path. If a line is malformed, repeats a setting or names a setting co:op doesn't read, the error names the path and line. Setting the same variable in the environment doesn't let a broken file pass. Every command except coop version stops until you fix the file. co:op reads COOP_HOME, COOP_CONF, NO_COLOR, COOP_ACP_WARM, COOP_ACP_TRACE and COOP_SPINNER only from the process environment, so you can't set them inside coop.conf. The box reads COOP_NO_ASDF and COOP_CONSULT_STREAM_LIMIT, so they belong in agents/env.

heading: What can sync
text: ~/.config/coop holds your settings and accounts, so you can sync it across machines with Dropbox or a similar service. If two machines refresh the same single-use sign-in, one of them can get signed out. If that happens, run coop login on that machine. Records that belong to one machine, such as each run's generated files, image records, usage caches, ACP traces, network approvals and Git views, live in $XDG_STATE_HOME/coop, or in ~/.local/state/coop when XDG_STATE_HOME isn't set. They never need syncing. Of an account, only agents/<agent>/credentials/<account>/authority.json needs to sync. Its other files are journals and locks for one machine. With Dropbox, put these rules in rules.dropboxignore at the Dropbox root, and coop doctor notes that the folder syncs by them. Some records stay in ~/.local/state/coop whatever XDG_STATE_HOME says. Every co:op process on this machine has to find the same ones, including a process your editor starts without your shell's variables: Service approvals, the files co:op hides from services, and the records it uses to clean up after a run that stopped without cleaning up. An approval you give in one shell applies in every other. Fork records, and the locks that stop two launches from starting a project's services at once. Locks kept in two places couldn't stop anything. Task leases, so two loops never work the same task. The worker's session store and its control socket, where a worker keeps the identity it reconnects with. Use --state to choose another folder. co:op also writes a .gitignore in ~/.config/coop if there is none, so a dotfiles repository keeps only shared settings. Accounts and agents/env stay out of Git. Optional provider usage reports use a separate host-only ~/.config/coop/usage-reports.json. co:op never adds their API spend to local usage estimates. Reporting keys belong in host environment variables, not coop.conf, project files or agents/env.

heading: Project settings: .agent/project.yaml
text: .agent/project.yaml is the committed per-project config. Key What it holds subprojects: A monorepo's members. See monorepos. serve: The dev server ports co:op publishes. See the dev server in your browser. box: The box policy: the dockerfile and compose paths, env defaults, egress and egress_rules:, resource caps (memory, cpus, pids), auto_up and network. services: require_real_files:, the hidden files your services need to read. Listing a file grants no access. See secret files in services. gate: The merge gate: the check command that coop fork merge runs in the box. gate_sources: The exact paths of project-specific files that define the gate. The loop always reviews changes to them. review: Services and environment for review checks only. See review checks. context: The routes for path-routed context. Explicit COOP_* settings in your environment or coop.conf override box: and gate:. Because the project settings file is committed and read on the host, it may tighten security restrictions but can't relax them on its own: egress can choose filtered or offline without approval. open is a request that a human approves with coop approve. You can't set no_new_privileges here.

heading: Review checks
text: review: applies only to the check that coop fork review --gate or a controller review runs: review: compose: .agent/review-compose.yml # services the check needs, such as a test database env: DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@db:5432/app_test review.env values are literal strings, set only in the check's box. Names beginning with COOP_ are reserved. A controller review with open networking starts the services in review.compose before the check, then removes them and their volumes. coop fork review --gate doesn't start them. COOP_REVIEW_BASE names the commit the changes are compared against, so a check can look only at what changed, for example git diff --name-only "$COOP_REVIEW_BASE"...HEAD. co:op sets it for the project checks that coop fork merge and coop fork review --gate run, for controller reviews, and in loop worker boxes. A worker gets the commit its task started from, so a check still covers the task's changes once they are committed, including after a retry or after a review reopened the task. A worker may also have work it hasn't committed: git diff --name-only "$COOP_REVIEW_BASE" compares the base with the working tree, and git ls-files --others --exclude-standard lists new files. co:op sets COOP_REVIEW=1 only for a review (coop fork review --gate or a controller review), so a script can tell a review from a merge check.

heading: Path-routed context
text: Use coop context to give an agent the committed docs relevant to the files it's working on, without loading every rule and knowledge-base note for a small change. co:op always includes the complete AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, then adds documents whose configured path patterns match. # .agent/project.yaml context: routes: - paths: [portal/**, "**/*.ex"] # * within a segment, ** across segments include: [.agent/kb/portal.md] # repo-relative docs to add when a path matches coop context --changed # scope = the paths git reports changed coop context --task <id> # scope = a task's declared `paths:` frontmatter coop context portal/lib/user.ex # scope = explicit repo-relative paths coop context --changed --json # same, as data (files + the route that selected each) coop context --changed --rendered # the compiled content itself, canonical first co:op chooses paths from your arguments, Git's changed files, the task's declared paths or the current subproject, and never guesses them from a prompt. Paths are relative to the repository root, even when you run it inside a subproject. When the work is inside a subproject, co:op adds that subproject's own AGENTS.md after the root's, and its .agent/kb/rules/README.md after the root's when a route includes that. It reports an error if a route includes a missing document or a path outside the repo. Routes come from the committed project.yaml, so a fork uses its parent's routes but matches them against paths in its own tree.

heading: Exit codes
text: Commands use these exit codes so CI and scripts can check the result without parsing messages. Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 A failure, or findings, like coop check-secrets on a hit. Answering no to a confirmation also exits 1: nothing changed. coop net blocked exits 1 when no recorded block matches, as grep does. 2 A usage error: an unknown command or flag, or bad arguments. 3 coop loop stopped with a task blocked on a human decision. coop net check found that the rules block the connection, or that new runs need approval first. coop sessions check found data this build would convert. coop sessions quiescence found queued or running work. 4 coop sessions check only: this build can't use the session data. 130 coop loop only: Ctrl-C interrupted it before the final verdict. If final verification is enabled and fails, coop loop keeps the completed work and exits with 1, or 3 if the only work left is blocked. An intentional --max-tasks N pause exits successfully but leaves final review pending. See the loop's exit codes, and upgrading a worker for coop sessions check.

heading: JSON output
text: Most commands that change state report success or failure through exit codes, not through --json. Read-only commands offer JSON when other tools need the current state. The two main views are: coop tasks watch --json is the standard snapshot of the project's tasks and activity. coop fork ls --json lists workspace URLs and fork status. coop context, the coop net views and coop sessions doctor also accept --json. coop net export always writes JSON.

heading: co:op worker API
text: Connect a worker and manage sessions, turns, evidence and publication through the worker API. A trusted controller supplies the code, context and execution settings, and co:op runs models in isolation and keeps their workspaces. The worker can share a VM with its controller or run on a separate VM. Ryker uses this protocol, but it can serve other products and has no Ryker-specific terms.

heading: Connect
text: coop sessions connect --controller https://controller.example --token-file /run/secrets/coop-token This is the only command that starts a worker. It starts a private local service, the daemon, and a connector that sends requests to your controller, so you don't need to open an inbound TCP port. The worker has no JSON file or local policy YAML. Add --state <path> to choose where the worker stores its private data, and --ca-file <path> to trust a private TLS CA. Public HTTPS uses the system trust store. The single-use token identifies the worker to the controller. co:op saves a renewable identity in the state directory, then removes the token file. To reconnect, use the same controller and state directory without --token-file. The saved identity works only with the original controller. The default state directory is ~/.local/state/coop/sessions, whatever XDG_STATE_HOME says, so every co:op process on the machine finds the same worker. The daemon listens on the internal Unix socket at <state>/control.sock. Each connector starts its own daemon and refuses to reuse a running one, so stop the existing connection before reconnecting. To run several workers at once, give each a separate --state directory. Use a process supervisor to keep the worker running. Ctrl-C stops both the connector and the daemon it started. A worker needs Git, Git LFS and a supported container runtime. The bundled worker image includes Git LFS. On a native worker, install git-lfs with your package manager. Jobs use the worker's base image (COOP_BASE_IMAGE) unless the controller grants a project runtime. That grant can select a project Dockerfile and an isolated Compose test stack. The worker builds the toolchain from its private frozen source and gives Work and review the same image. Filtered jobs use co:op's locked client image and refuse custom controller toolchains. A normal-mode job also installs the tools listed in the repository's .tool-versions when its box starts. Before the worker accepts filtered jobs, run coop net setup as the worker's OS user, using the same Docker endpoint and network state directory. This prepares and checks the networking setup. The session API requires those checks to stay valid but doesn't build the networking images itself. Installing Docker or accepting JobSpec version 2 isn't enough to show that the worker can enforce filtered networking. To check the local session service: coop sessions doctor coop sessions doctor --socket /var/lib/coop-sessions/control.sock --json The local socket and state are private to the worker's OS account. Never mount the socket into a model's box or expose it through an unauthenticated proxy. Connecting out to a controller doesn't by itself prove that the controller can be trusted, so co:op verifies the TLS connection before it sends an enrollment token or accepts work.

heading: Session authority
text: Your controller supplies one job, which sets the session's source, model targets, repository access, network access and resource limits. co:op checks and saves it before creating a workspace. Retries must use that same configuration, and restarts use the saved copy. Repository instructions and model output can't grant more access. co:op doesn't resume model work for a session whose authorization it can't verify. co:op saves a stable ID for each session store in session.sqlite. When it reserves a fork, it records which store and session own that specific instance of the fork, and moving the database with --state preserves the store ID and ownership. Only the session service that owns the fork can discard it, after checking its journal, the session's link to the fork and the workspace safety conditions. coop fork rm --force can't bypass these checks. Old fork reservations without a store ID remain visible, but ordinary fork removal can't delete them, and a matching session ID in another store isn't enough to prove who owns them. You can read these sessions, but recovering them requires an explicit procedure with the service stopped. co:op doesn't assign them to a new owner automatically or delete them because they're old. The worker fetches repository data directly from GitHub using short-lived credentials that your controller grants for that repository. The model receives the complete working tree, with verified LFS files and every explicitly authorized submodule, including nested ones. Tokens never enter the model's mounts, repository configuration or exported results. If objects are missing, a submodule is unauthorized or an LFS pointer format is unsupported, creation fails instead of leaving an incomplete tree.

heading: Workspace storage
text: Each hello message can carry a storage object that reports disk space on the volume holding the worker's fork workspaces. The connector reads it from the daemon's GET /v1/storage endpoint and forwards it unchanged. { "version": 1, "measured_at": "2026-09-11T04:05:06Z", "capacity_bytes": 536870912000, "free_bytes": 107374182400, "reserve_bytes": 26843545600, "high_watermark_bytes": 510027366400, "low_watermark_bytes": 483183820800, "disposable_bytes": 8589934592, "protected_bytes": 21474836480, "unattributed_bytes": null, "allocation": "open", "refusal_reason": null } disposable_bytes is the disk space a discard could still free. protected_bytes is the disk space the worker must keep, including the repository data shared by forks through hard links. A null unattributed_bytes means the worker couldn't identify what uses some of the space, or couldn't finish measuring. Treat it as unknown, never as zero. allocation is refused when the worker won't accept a new workspace, and refusal_reason says whether the cause is reserve_exhausted or protected_storage_exceeds_budget. The worker can still handle existing workspaces and clean them up. The high and low watermarks limit used disk space, and the reserve is the space that must stay free. By default, co:op calculates all three from the volume's measured capacity: It reserves 5% of the volume. It stops accepting new workspaces when free space falls to that reserve or below. It accepts new workspaces again only when twice that reserve is free. If the worker can't measure its volume, it leaves out the storage object and keeps polling. A workspace with no recorded session binding or no uncommitted changes can look unused, but another session store or an unfinished create operation may own it. co:op marks such a workspace as protected in /v1/storage and leaves it for manual inspection. Automatic cleanup only finishes removals that an authorized discard has already started. Before deleting a workspace, co:op moves it into a private staging directory belonging to its owner, so cleanup can resume an interrupted removal. Discard reports success only after the data has been removed.

heading: Restart and recovery
text: Stop the connector with SIGINT or SIGTERM. Across restarts, keep the identity file, the entire journal directory and the same worker and workspace configuration. A restart loads the existing identity and doesn't enroll again. Certificate renewal is automatic over mutual TLS. At startup, co:op locks the state directory and removes unpublished source staging data, temporary transfer files and host-only Git credential files. It keeps published sources and response bodies saved in the journal. Configure the service manager to stop the worker's whole process group or cgroup. Killing only the parent can leave a Git or LFS child running. That child may keep deleted files open, so their disk space isn't freed until it exits. co:op records each command in the journal before running it. After a restart, it resends finished results that the controller hasn't acknowledged. If the controller sends a completed command again, co:op returns the saved result without running it again. It refuses to reuse a command ID with a different payload. The controller can acknowledge an asynchronous create request while the session is still being created, and the journal keeps the original operation ID until co:op can link the resulting session's activity to it. An event cursor advances only when the controller acknowledges the exact events, so co:op resends unacknowledged events and doesn't resend acknowledged ones. When you move or back up a worker, keep the entire journal. The commands directory alone isn't enough. A review may continue after its request loses the connection, and the saved delivery result stays uncertain even if the review later finishes. Look up the operation with GET /v1/operations?key=<original-key>. Once it succeeds, fetch the saved review report. Neither request runs the check again. If the daemon or controller is unavailable, the connector reports the problem and retries. It doesn't run work locally or delete saved results to get past the failure. If the saved identity is malformed or expired, the worker stops connecting and doesn't enroll again automatically, even when an enrollment token is available. Check file ownership, trusted certificates, the clock and the controller's renewal status, then follow the controller operator's identity-recovery procedure. Don't delete the identity or journal as a routine reconnect fix. Before you restart or replace a worker, stop new submissions at the controller, then run coop sessions quiescence to see whether queued or running work remains: It reads every committed turn and operation, including the running service's write-ahead log, so it needs that service's existing database, WAL and index files. It never migrates session data. When you inspect the data from a new container image, mount the data read-only. That also stops SQLite from creating sidecar files if the service stops during the inspection. Zero counts mean no queued or running work remains. Still shut the service down gracefully so it can finish its runtime cleanup. Create and discard operations in the uncertain state stay unresolved and don't count as running work. Exit Meaning 0 No queued or running work remains in the session store 1 The store is unavailable, damaged or uses an unsupported schema 2 The arguments are invalid 3 Work remains

heading: Upgrading a worker
text: A new co:op build may need to convert the worker's session data when it first opens it, and the previous build can't read that data afterwards. Each build can perform only one upgrade step. If the data is older than schema 26, the build stops and names the build that converts it first. Before replacing the worker, check its data with the new build: Wait for the commands the worker is carrying out, then stop the worker. Run the check with the new build or image, against the worker's state directory: coop sessions check --state /var/lib/coop/sessions In a container, run it from the new image with the worker's volumes mounted, as the worker's own user. Act on its exit status: Exit Meaning Next step 0 The new build can use the data unchanged, or the service has initialized its storage without saving any sessions yet Start the new build 3 The new build will convert the data, and older builds can't open it afterwards To keep a way back, copy the stopped state directory aside, then start the new build 4 The data is too old for this build to convert, or was written by a newer build Restart the old build. If the data is too old, first upgrade through a build that uses the session schema named in the message. 1 The check couldn't finish: the service is still running, the path has no session data, or some data can't be read Fix the reported problem and check again. A directory that no service has used can't pass, even if it's empty. Check for a mistyped --state or a new volume. A worker that has never run has no data to check. 2 The arguments are invalid Fix the command The command checks both the session database and the connector's command journal. It doesn't write to the state directory or create SQLite's -wal and -shm files. While checking, it holds a shared state lock to prevent a service from starting and converting the data. If a service is already running against that directory, the check refuses to read it, so stop the service first. You need this extra cleanup only if the worker ran a development build from co:op's main branch between 2026-09-15 and 2026-09-23. Those builds left a .service-launch.lock file in each execution-registry folder, and current builds refuse to launch in the affected repositories and report the file as an unsupported registry entry. Stop the worker, then run these commands as its OS user to delete the files and any folders left empty: find ~/.local/state/coop/executions/v1 -mindepth 2 -maxdepth 2 -type f -name .service-launch.lock -delete find ~/.local/state/coop/executions/v1 -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -empty -delete

heading: Session inspection evidence
text: Your controller can request a versioned, size-limited report about a session hosted by the worker. Send an api_request command with the payload {"method":"GET","path":"/v1/sessions/<id>/evidence"} (see the session evidence endpoint below). The connector forwards the daemon's answer unchanged. It doesn't choose fields, calculate extra values or reveal additional data. The report includes the network settings saved for the session, the activity observed during its runs and the approved task assigned to its workspace. Credentials, host paths and packet bodies are excluded. Destination names appear only if the session job set egress.export_destinations: true. The worker reports support for session-evidence version 1 only when its running daemon lists session_evidence_versions in GET /v1/capabilities. It checks this independently of the other capabilities, and configuration can't override the result. If the daemon doesn't list it, the worker doesn't report support, and your controller can show that evidence export is unavailable instead of an empty network report. The controller also receives blocked requests and alerts from filtered runs through the network session event. The daemon uses the same grouping, limits and destination-disclosure rules as coop net.

heading: Request rules
text: The examples below use curl's Unix-socket support: SOCKET="$HOME/.local/state/coop/sessions/control.sock" curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" http://localhost/healthz Every mutation is a POST with these headers: Content-Type: application/json Idempotency-Key: <globally unique caller-owned key> Idempotency-Key and Content-Type must each occur exactly once. Mutation URLs accept no query parameters. Ordinary mutation bodies are limited to 128 KiB. Turn-submission bodies are limited to 12 MiB, so they can carry input artifacts. A turn takes at most 5 input artifacts, 8 MiB in total. More artifacts, or more bytes, return invalid_request ("turn has too many artifacts" or "turn artifact content exceeds its bound"). co:op decodes every body as exactly one JSON value and rejects unknown fields. Prompts are limited to 256 KiB of valid UTF-8 without NUL.

heading: Idempotency keys
text: Choose one key for each action and keep using that key when you retry it. If the method, key and normalized request body match, co:op returns the saved result without running the action again. Reusing a key with a different method or body returns idempotency_conflict. After a lost response, retry the same request with the same key. If an earlier response supplied an operation ID, GET /v1/operations/{operation_id} reports its state, error code and resource ID. If the worker may have accepted a request but you didn't receive its response, look it up with GET /v1/operations?key=<idempotency-key>. Supply the exact idempotency key, within its size limit. The query accepts only one key. The response contains the public operation information and excludes the key, request hash, saved execution instructions, result body, stored request, private result, prompts, native provider IDs and host paths.

heading: Compacting old turn receipts
text: When a turn request succeeds, co:op saves a small public result to return if you retry, without the prompt or private execution settings. The daemon can still read older results that stored the full turn, and you can compact those during a planned maintenance window: coop sessions compact --state <state-root> --backup <new-backup.sqlite> The command locks the state directory so the daemon can't use it during maintenance. The backup path must not exist yet and must not be inside the state root. After verifying the backup, the command rewrites the old results in one transaction, checks database integrity and vacuums the database to reclaim space. It doesn't change the turn records themselves, and it never runs automatically at startup. The backup still contains the old prompt copies, so only its owner can access it. Keep it until you've verified both the compacted database and its normal backups. To restore: Stop the daemon. Move session.sqlite and both possible -wal and -shm sidecars aside together. Install the backup as an owner-only session.sqlite. Restart. Verify with coop sessions doctor before deleting the files you moved aside.

heading: Fencing an uncertain mutation
text: Your controller may withdraw permission for a session create or turn submission after saving the request, without knowing whether the worker received it. Don't resend the request just to find out what to stop, because that could start work you no longer want. Fence it instead. A fence blocks the request unless the worker has already accepted it. Call POST /v1/operations/fence with the original request's idempotency key and an envelope containing its exact method and request: { "method": "SubmitTurn", "request": { "session_id": "remote_...", "expected_revision": 3, "prompt": "the exact frozen prompt" } } Only CreateRemoteSession and SubmitTurn can be fenced. If the worker hasn't accepted the operation, including when it has only reserved it, co:op records a failure with operation_fenced. Sending that same request later can't run it. If the worker already accepted the operation, the fence returns it and its resource. Inspect that result and use the normal close or cancel request to stop the work. The enclosed request can be as large as a turn submission, with a separate size limit for the envelope. A lookup that finds nothing, or a client timeout, doesn't prove that the request never reached the worker.

heading: Asynchronous session create
text: To create a session without keeping the HTTP request open, send Prefer: respond-async on POST /v1/sessions. co:op saves the request and returns 202 Accepted with an operation that is still running or has already finished. Poll GET /v1/operations/{operation_id} until it succeeds with resource_type: session, then fetch the session it identifies. Creation continues in the daemon if the client disconnects. Retrying the identical request with the same key returns the same operation. Without the preference header, the request waits for creation to finish and returns the operation and session together.

heading: Revision checks
text: Session lifecycle, budget and cancellation requests include expected_revision. Read the session before acting. If you get revision_conflict, read it again and decide whether your action is still appropriate. Don't guess a new revision or action. Validation decisions don't include expected_revision. They check candidate_sha256 instead: they approve or reject one exact unpublished answer, regardless of other changes to the session.

heading: Lifecycle
text: create -> open/parked -> queued -> starting -> running -> awaiting_validation -> completed | -> queued (rejected candidate) -> failed|cancelled|interrupted -> parked -> exhausted when the turn budget is consumed -> closed -> discard plan -> discarded Each session belongs to one worker. The worker saves turns in a queue with a size limit and runs them one at a time, in the order received. The queue survives restarts. Without limits.warm_idle_timeout_ms, co:op starts a new coop fork <name> acp <target> process for each turn, which resumes the provider session saved for this co:op session. co:op publishes only the final assistant message, then stops the process and removes its box before marking the session as parked. A job with repository_read_only: true uses the same kind of process. The fork is mounted read-only, and files generated by a turn go into a writable output directory in the worker's private state. With limits.warm_idle_timeout_ms, you get a warm session: co:op can authenticate the ACP connection before the first turn and keep the same process and provider session for later turns. Turns still run one at a time. The daemon keeps at most four sessions warm, and each one occupies one of the four runtime slots while idle. co:op stops the process and removes its box, services and temporary credential files when any of these happens: The idle timeout expires. A turn is cancelled or fails. The session closes or is discarded. The daemon shuts down. The provider's saved conversation history remains, so a new process can resume the same session. Stopping a turn's runtime also removes the workspace's Compose service containers, but a successful warm turn keeps its runtime and services until warm-session cleanup. The service volumes remain after cleanup, so later turns can restart services with the same development data. Only an explicit session discard removes the workspace's volumes and network. The daemon repeats cleanup at startup after a crash or upgrade, and a background check retries idle-runtime cleanup every minute without interfering with an active turn. A turn that completed successfully stays successful if cleanup fails, and the background cleaner retries and logs the error. If the turn itself failed, its error includes the cleanup failure too. On restart: Queued turns that were never sent to the provider remain in the queue. A turn waiting for your validation keeps its unpublished candidate, and you can still accept or reject it by digest. Startup and the periodic cleaner remove its provider process, box, temporary credential files and services without deciding or changing the candidate. If co:op had recorded its intent to send a turn before the interruption, that turn is marked interrupted and isn't sent again automatically. Closing a session keeps its fork, conversation state, events and reviews. To delete the workspace, use the separate two-step discard process: make a plan, then apply it only if the session still matches that plan. Only a closed, idle session can be discarded. The API can publish an explicitly authorized, reviewed candidate as a draft pull request. It can't merge, sign, change the local parent ref, run an arbitrary host command or return a host workspace path.

heading: Structured output
text: Use the optional output_contract to require an answer that follows a JSON schema. It contains the exact schema bytes and their digest: { "json_schema": {"type":"object","required":["answer"]}, "sha256": "<lowercase SHA-256 hex of the exact json_schema bytes>", "require_semantic_validation": true } When output_contract is present: json_schema and sha256 are required. The schema is capped at 256 KiB. co:op checks that the schema matches the digest before compiling it to validate responses. co:op saves the contract, gives it to the model and checks the final answer against it. If the answer isn't valid JSON or doesn't match the schema, co:op asks the model to fix it in the same provider session. Without semantic validation, three invalid responses fail the turn with output_contract_failed, and no assistant message is published. Set require_semantic_validation: true when your controller must also check the answer against external data fixed for this request. After the answer passes schema validation, co:op returns its exact unpublished bytes and SHA-256 digest as turn.candidate, and sets the turn to awaiting_validation. The saved validation_candidate_sha256 remains visible after your decision, so you can check what happened if the HTTP response is lost. Send one decision with an idempotency key to: POST /v1/sessions/<session>/turns/<turn>/validation {"candidate_sha256":"<digest>","verdict":"accept"} To reject the candidate instead, send verdict: "reject" with 1 to 20 violations. Each violation is capped at 4 KiB, and so is the combined list. An acceptance must not include violations. co:op copies the stored candidate into assistant_message and returns a saved validation_receipt. A rejection asks the model to try again in the same provider session, as part of the same turn. Your controller can review up to three candidates that pass the schema check, and the model has up to three responses to produce valid output for each one. Responses that fail the schema check don't use up one of those review attempts.

heading: Health
text: Method Path Result GET /healthz {"healthy":true} GET /readyz {"ready":true} after daemon startup GET /v1/capabilities {"job_spec_versions":[2],"controller_tools_versions":[1],"repository_freshness_receipt_versions":[2],"session_evidence_versions":[1],"review_commit_message_versions":[1]}. Check these versions before choosing which protocol features to use. GET /v1/capacity Current shared active and warm runtime slots. The connector forwards this measurement in the hello it sends with every poll. GET /v1/storage Disk use measured by this daemon: storage (the summary for a fleet controller), budget, totals, roots, forks and problems The worker has four slots for model processes, shared by active turns and idle warm sessions. The session, turn and workspace counts all describe those same slots, so don't add them together. Time spent waiting in the queue doesn't count toward a turn's model timeout. If cleanup fails, the process keeps its slot until cleanup succeeds. At startup, the worker reports busy with zero free slots until it has checked which runtimes it owns. For a quarantined or retired session, cleanup frees a slot only after co:op confirms that no runtime remains with that session's exact labels. This doesn't make the workspace safe to run again. If co:op can't read capacity, it reports busy. The worker still polls for requests that read data or clean up existing work. /v1/storage measures the disk blocks allocated to files, not the file sizes that applications report. It reads file metadata without opening file contents, so it can count private session data without reading the credentials in it. Forks can share Git objects with their source checkout through hard links. Storage totals count the space that deleting the content would free, so shared repository data is counted once, in totals.baseline_shared_bytes. Read-only primary and companion repositories reuse verified snapshots that never change. Sessions with the same authorized repository and pinned revisions share unchanged source files, Git objects and LFS payloads, and storage totals count each payload once. Each session keeps its own Git configuration, index and outputs, and a primary fork also keeps its own branch and the default and base history its job approved. Private caches stay separate for each controller and workspace and for each repository binding. Only read-only jobs with a frozen source use this storage. Checkpoint, restore and writable jobs keep independent payloads, and existing sessions with independent payloads stay as they are. A missing, damaged or newer ownership receipt stops co:op from reusing the shared data, and an unsupported receipt also prevents destructive cleanup. Local fork commands and other writable mounts can't take over a read-only primary whose creation was interrupted. The normal authorized discard releases a primary's references to the shared data. Cleanup can remove an unused repository snapshot after an hour, or sooner when disk space is low or use is above the disposable-byte budget. A snapshot that a session references stays, so closing one session can't invalidate another session's files. Each cleanup pass has a 30-second limit. If cleanup can't prove an entry's ownership and cleanliness in that time, it keeps and reports the entry, then moves on to other entries in later passes, so large or slow entries can stay in place. Private ownership receipts let interrupted creation and removal resume, and coop sessions check checks their format before an upgrade. When free disk space falls to twice the default reserve, new source downloads and checkouts wait before they allocate space, while verified source cache hits keep working. The wait keeps the same saved worker command, resumes when space returns and doesn't use up a model attempt. A later job for the same repository, commit, tree and submodules links the verified checkout and LFS files already on disk, and keeps its own Git metadata and its record of how the source was resolved.
