An incomplete measurement reports totals.unknown and sets storage.unattributed_bytes to null. co:op measures the full tree at most once per budget.measure_seconds, and storage.measured_at lets callers check how old the measurement is. forks[] lists each directory under a fork root, its category and the evidence for that category. Only disposable and staged_discard can be removed through the authorized cleanup process. For active, grace, protected, control and unattributed, the response explains why removal is refused. A directory is protected in any of these cases: It belongs to a running worker or registered box activity. A merge was interrupted. The task system still needs it. Its session is quarantined. It holds uncommitted work. Without a co:op record identifying that fork instance, the directory is unattributed, and co:op reports it for inspection instead of guessing that it can be deleted. When disk space is too low, the daemon refuses new workspaces with storage_unavailable and explains the cause. Reads, cleanup and discard still work. co:op doesn't delete protected data to make room. Checkpoint capture and restore need space for extra copies, including during recovery. They have a separate storage check that waits for enough space above the reserve. While a restore is interrupted, the session remains blocked from running work. The worker stops creating workspaces when disk use reaches storage.high_watermark_bytes, and starts accepting them again only when use drops to storage.low_watermark_bytes or below. New work must leave storage.reserve_bytes free. These checks don't limit how much data an already-running task writes in its workspace. Before reporting support for job-setup:2, repository-freshness:2, session-evidence:1, controller-tools:1, project-runtime:1 or review-commit-message:1, the connector checks the running daemon's GET /v1/capabilities response for the matching version. If it can't verify a capability, it leaves it out of the next hello. Worker protocol v2 reports supported features, runtime capacity and optional disk measurements. It doesn't distribute lists of policies or repositories. Each controller job specifies its own exact code and execution settings, which can't change after submission. The shared protocol fixture shows one worker poll and the controller's reply.

heading: Sessions
text: Your controller creates create-session.json with these fields: task: your external task reference. co:op doesn't interpret its value. job: a version-2 JobSpec. expected_job_digest: the SHA-256 digest of the job's canonical representation. controller_tools (optional): connects the session to your controller's authenticated tool endpoint. co:op refuses a job that is missing a required field, has an unknown field or would change when co:op normalizes it. The error is invalid_request, and its detail names the problem. curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:create:01J...' \ -H 'Prefer: respond-async' \ --data-binary @create-session.json \ http://localhost/v1/sessions The job selects model targets, network rules, queue and turn limits, and the complete work and review setup. Its mode is always "normal". Set repository_read_only: true for a job that must not change its repository. A job that asks for readonly or bare mode is refused with invalid_request. Besides the other required fields, version 2 requires: { "environment": {"CI": "1"}, "check": {"argv": ["make", "test"], "environment": {"DATABASE_URL": "postgres://test-db/app"}}, "resources": {"cpu_millis": 2000, "memory_bytes": 4294967296, "pids": 512} } These fields must be present even when the environment maps and check argv are empty. co:op passes the job's environment variables only to processes in the box. Review uses those variables plus check.environment, and the check's value wins when a name appears in both. Names must be valid shell identifiers. COOP_*, provider credential variables, model variables and adapter-owned variables are reserved. Values must be UTF-8, with no line breaks or leading or trailing whitespace. Use these variables for job settings, not for model or GitHub credentials. The check is a list of command arguments, passed directly to the process and never interpreted as a shell command. If you need shell syntax, run a shell explicitly. If both check.argv and the check environment are empty, no check runs, so the review can't be published. Field Meaning Accepted range cpu_millis CPU, in thousandths of one core 10 to 128000 memory_bytes Memory, in bytes 6 MiB to 1 TiB pids Maximum processes per container 1 to 65536 Every job must set positive, finite CPU, memory and process limits. If a requested limit exceeds the worker's configured maximum, or the runtime can't enforce it, co:op refuses the job instead of silently lowering the value. co:op refuses retries that change the saved job. Task text and repository settings can't change what the worker is allowed to run. Your controller may use repository defaults, but it must choose and include every setting before submission. The worker has no local policy name, policy catalog or separate source selector. Writable source jobs may additionally include an optional project runtime: "runtime": { "version": 1, "dockerfile": ".agent/Dockerfile", "compose": "dev/services.yml", "environment": {"PGHOST": "db"} } These are canonical repository-relative paths resolved by the controller at the frozen source. An empty Dockerfile uses the shared image; an empty Compose path starts no services. Retained jobs without this field keep their exact authority and digest. Send runtime-bearing jobs only to workers advertising project-runtime:1, proven by project_runtime_versions: [1] on the local daemon. The runtime's environment holds frozen project defaults, with a 64 KiB limit measured as escaped JSON. Candidate review.env overrides those defaults. The job's root environment and check.environment remain controller authority and override candidate values. Work gets its own Compose project and default network, and services get finite job resource caps. At least one service must join the default network; custom-only network topologies are refused before startup. Service aliases and additional project networks are preserved. Required setup failures stop the command. Host ports and globally named/external volumes are refused or removed from the job setup. Named data volumes survive ordinary turns on the same worker; anonymous volumes and tmpfs are disposable. Final discard removes owned containers, networks and named volumes before deleting the workspace, using immutable labels even if project files changed. A replacement worker reconstructs test services; checkpoints do not transfer database volumes. A candidate's review.compose can replace the Work stack with a separate disposable review stack. co:op computes the job digest itself. It writes the job's JSON the way Go's encoding/json does: no extra whitespace, object keys in sorted order, and &, < and > inside strings escaped as \u0026, \u003c and \u003e. The digest is the SHA-256 of those bytes, in lowercase hex. If it differs from expected_job_digest, co:op refuses the session with invalid_request. To check your encoder, use the digest test vectors. Each one gives a job, the exact bytes co:op takes the digest of, and the digest. The file also lists values of source.binding.resolved_at that co:op refuses, such as a fraction with trailing zeros. Send version-2 jobs only to workers that report job-setup:2. co:op doesn't fill in missing execution settings for v1 jobs. Older sessions and their evidence stay readable, but their turns, reviews and interrupted creates can't run until they're resubmitted as v2 jobs.

heading: Frozen repository source
text: Before creating the job, your controller resolves the requested default branch, named branch, PR or commit to exact commits. job.source identifies the GitHub repository by its stable ID and slug, and records the default, selected and base commits, the approved tree and the information that binds the job to that source. It also lists every authorized submodule, including nested ones, with the exact repository, commit and tree. Don't include a host checkout path, remote URL or GitHub token in this document. The worker gets short-lived credentials through its authenticated connection to the controller, then downloads Git and LFS data directly from GitHub and verifies the complete working tree. Repository files such as .gitmodules and .lfsconfig can't redirect those authenticated requests. The job fails if history or LFS files are missing, submodule commit references don't match, or there isn't enough disk space. A job with source: null uses an isolated empty workspace.

heading: Session endpoints
text: The public session response identifies the fixed repository source, job_ref, job_digest, model target, execution mode, project exposure settings, saved network settings and repository freshness. It also includes companion aliases, base commits, the generated fork name, revision, state, activity, queue and budget counts, the event cursor and timestamps. It excludes host paths, provider state, prompts and credentials. Method Path Body/query POST /v1/sessions task, job, expected_job_digest, and optional controller_tools GET /v1/sessions?limit=100 limit is 1..1000 GET /v1/sessions/{session_id} none POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/prepare expected_revision. The job must turn on warm execution. POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/workspace expected_revision, task. The session must be open, writable and unused. A session stored in readonly or bare mode is quarantined at startup and never runs; a new turn returns invalid_session_state. Retire its record as described under quarantine, or close and discard it with a co:op build at or before commit 29133b0e.

heading: Task binding
text: POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/workspace writes one approved task into the session's workspace and binds the session to it. Send it before the first turn. The body holds expected_revision and a task object: offer_ref: your stable reference for the approved task. It is 1 to 256 bytes of letters, digits, _, ., : and -. title: one line, up to 120 bytes. prompt: up to 12,000 bytes. success_checks: 1 to 20 distinct items, each up to 1,000 bytes. authority_limits: up to 20 distinct items, each up to 500 bytes. instruction_ref (optional): one reference, with the same rules as offer_ref. source_refs: up to 20 distinct references, with the same rules as offer_ref. Every string must be valid UTF-8, not blank and free of NUL. The encoded task is capped at 64 KiB. co:op adds the task to the workspace's task queue as a to-do task, with one subtask per success check. The response includes the operation and session. The session's workspace_task contains queue_id, task_id, id, offer_ref and draft_sha256. queue_id and task_id are random values co:op generates and saves, id is the task's folder name, and draft_sha256 is the SHA-256 digest of the task as co:op encoded it. Binding the task increases the session revision by one and records a workspace.task_bound event. The session must be open, writable and parked, with no active, queued or previously used turns. Otherwise, the request fails with invalid_session_state. Changing a task that the workspace already holds under the same offer_ref also returns that error. A stale expected_revision returns revision_conflict. An invalid task returns invalid_request, as does submitting a different task to a session that is already bound. Repeating the exact binding leaves the session unchanged.

heading: Workspace checkpoints
text: Method Path Input/output POST /v1/sessions/{id}/checkpoint JSON: session_ref, expected_revision, placement_generation, repository_ref. Returns the operation and descriptor. GET /v1/operations/{id}/checkpoint-bundle Streamed tar, exact Content-Length, SHA-256 ETag POST /v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/restore Binary body plus X-Coop-Expected-Revision and base64-JSON X-Coop-Workspace-Checkpoint headers To capture a checkpoint, the session must be idle, writable and bound to a task. You can capture an open, exhausted or closed session, but not a discarded one. Capture keeps a closed session closed and can't restart model execution. To restore a checkpoint, create an unused replacement session with the same authorized base and task offer. Both requests require an idempotency key. Restore uses the content type application/vnd.coop.workspace-checkpoint.v2+tar, and its Content-Length must match the descriptor. A v2 checkpoint streams Git objects with their types and verified LFS files. It includes new commits, the final tracked tree, untracked files and task state. Restoring it recreates the exact HEAD and working tree, but not the original split between staged and unstaged changes. Changed submodule commits need a separate authorized process to keep and verify their data, so checkpoints refuse them, including intermediate submodule changes that were later reverted. Checkpoint processing limits memory use and metadata size, but it sets no fixed limit on the data itself. co:op checks disk space and cancellation throughout the transfer and Git operations, which can stop the operation when space is low but can't prevent other host processes from filling the filesystem. co:op checks every archive entry and the task's identity in a separate area before changing live files, and it saves the complete request body before marking the restore as running. If restore is interrupted, the session can't run work, even after a restart. Restore resumes from the saved body. Retry the same operation. Don't send a new key for a session that is already bound. Capturing a checkpoint also reserves the runtime so a model turn can't change files during capture. Restoring a checkpoint doesn't restore permission to publish. Review the candidate again before publishing it. Discard removes checkpoint artifacts only after verifying that the local session owns them, and it resolves any interrupted restores for that session. You can still read older v1 artifacts, but you can't restore them, because their patch-only format doesn't keep enough information to verify the complete Git and LFS data.

heading: Turns
text: Submit a turn: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:turn:01J...' \ -d '{"expected_revision":1,"prompt":"Investigate the failing readiness check."}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../turns Method Path Body/query POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns expected_revision, prompt. Optional: artifacts, min_target_index, rewind_target, output_contract GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns?after=0&limit=100 Continue after the numbered turn given by the cursor GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns/{turn_id} none GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns/{turn_id}/artifacts/{artifact_id} raw generated image POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns/{turn_id}/cancel expected_revision POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns/{turn_id}/validation candidate_sha256, verdict. accept forbids violations, and reject requires 1 to 20. Before accepting, rejecting or cancelling a turn awaiting validation, co:op stops and removes the provider runtime and temporary credential files that produced its candidate. If it can't confirm cleanup, the API returns 503 session_cleanup_error. The candidate remains awaiting_validation, and your decision hasn't taken effect. That failed operation is finished: retrying its idempotency key returns the same failure. After the background cleaner or an operator fixes cleanup, fetch the current candidate and submit your decision with a new idempotency key. The public turn response excludes the prompt, idempotency data, min_target_index and rewind_target. You can see the effect of those last two settings in the session's target and session.target_rotated event. For a completed turn, assistant_message is the response to show the user. co:op doesn't publish hidden reasoning, raw tool calls, raw ACP frames or box logs in that response. A completed turn includes usage when the adapter reports it. The fields are input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, output_tokens, reasoning_tokens and, when available, the provider's cost_usd. Check cost_recorded to distinguish a reported zero cost from a missing cost. ACP reports the cumulative cost of the provider session, and co:op calculates this turn's share before returning it, including after daemon restarts or adapter-process resets. Fresh and cached input tokens are reported separately because providers charge different rates for them, and combining them before calculating cost would overestimate the bill. If the adapter reports no usage, co:op leaves the object out. Missing measurements are never represented as zero usage or free work. A completed turn may include output_artifacts for images the agent generated or saved in the turn's .coop-output/<turn_id> directory. Each record has an opaque ID, a safe filename, the media type, a SHA-256 digest and the exact byte count, but not the image itself. Download it through the raw endpoint, which returns the saved file with matching Content-Type, Content-Length and ETag headers. The saved file can't change. co:op captures image blocks and embedded image resources from ACP tool updates in output order, naming them generated-1.<ext>, generated-2.<ext> and so on. Image bytes don't count toward the text transcript limit. co:op inspects text tool updates one frame at a time and then discards them, so a long turn doesn't fail just because its tool updates add up to a large transcript. Separate limits still apply to assistant text, each incoming frame, the turn's duration and saved output artifacts. Only PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF are accepted. A turn returns at most five images. Images from tool updates and files in the turn's directory share that limit, and a repeated image is kept once. A file in that directory without a .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .webp or .gif extension is ignored. co:op rejects symlinks, special files, mismatched content, a sixth image, a file over 8 MiB, or more than 8 MiB in total. co:op removes the temporary output directory before completing the turn, so generated charts don't become repository changes. In a read-only repository session, the container still sees the path .coop-output/..., but its files are stored in co:op's private session state on the host. Cancellation first asks ACP to cancel the turn. co:op then stops the turn's process group and removes its box. This doesn't undo actions already taken in external systems.

heading: Events
text: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ 'http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../events?after=41&limit=100' The events endpoint returns a JSON array ordered by sequence, which increases within each session. Save the last sequence you processed, and after a disconnect, request after=<sequence> to continue from that point. Events stored privately for the worker's owner include the identity, sequence, turn ID, type, version, timestamp and payload. Tool evidence has size limits but may include filesystem paths, arguments, results and diffs. Events describing tool starts and finishes, thoughts, progress, plans and permission decisions also carry checkout_root. The connector reads it to remove the checkout path before forwarding the event. The connector forwards a filtered version of activity events to the controller. It includes tool titles, inputs and results, plus the model's thoughts, progress and plan, with the session's host checkout path removed. Each field has a size limit: Field Limit Titles 1 KiB Text 8 KiB Tool fields 16 KiB. Larger fields are sent as a preview marked truncated. One event 64 KiB If a field appears to contain a secret, the connector withholds the entire field. The event's withheld object identifies the field and reason, such as likely GitHub token. When tool input is withheld, the event still identifies the MCP server and tool. The structured path_context includes only project-relative paths and scope warnings, never the host checkout root. Each event payload is limited to 256 KiB. A page also has a total byte limit, in addition to its limit on event count, and the endpoint returns fewer events instead of cutting one short.

heading: Lifecycle events
text: These event types record what co:op itself decided: session.created workspace.task_bound session.state_changed turn.queued turn.started turn.awaiting_validation output_contract.rejected assistant.message turn.completed turn.failed turn.cancelled turn.interrupted budget.exhausted session.target_rotated session.parked session.closed workspace.discarded network # one sealed filtered run's outcome: run_id, grouped denials, alerts co:op records a network event for blocked requests when a filtered run's network record is finalized. It can also report alerts, such as a mismatch in network permissions or incomplete evidence. A run with no refusals and no alerts produces no event, so this event isn't a heartbeat for every turn. In the payload: Destinations are grouped and capped, with an omitted_destinations count. Alerts are capped. evidence_id names the saved event that coop net blocked can open. The event follows the same disclosure rules as the network routes. A destination appears only when the session job set egress.export_destinations: true. workspace.task_bound records a task binding. Its payload holds offer_ref, draft_sha256, queue_id, task_id and id, the values in the session's workspace_task. A checkpoint restore appends it too, with base_commit and restored: true added. output_contract.rejected records a rejected candidate within a turn. When a provider response fails the schema check, co:op records attempt, the contract's sha256 and an error with a size limit. When your controller sends a reject verdict, the event instead includes attempt, candidate_sha256, semantic: true and your violations. The connector forwards lifecycle events without their payloads, except for network events.

heading: Activity events
text: Activity events describe what the model does during a turn. co:op records them before the event that ends the turn, so a client that stops polling at turn.completed has already received that turn's activity events: tool.started # tool_call_id, title, kind, input, path_context tool.completed # tool_call_id, title, kind, status, input, output, content, locations, terminal_exit, path_context model.plan # entries model.thought # text model.progress # outward commentary text, not private reasoning permission.decided # tool_call_id, title, outcome, option_id, option_kind activity.elided # dropped, reason provider.backoff # attempt, target, next_target, retry_after_seconds, reset_at, all_limited_until provider.alive # frames, bytes, last_kind When the provider reports it, terminal_exit contains the command's numeric exit_code, its termination signal or both. These fields are separate from the output, so truncating an output preview doesn't remove the exit result. When a tool provides structured file information, path_context includes basis: "lexical" and up to 16 paths entries. Each entry uses a JSON-pointer source to identify where the information came from. Its scope is project, outside or unknown. Only project-relative files receive a path. The host checkout root is never exported. partial: true means some path information was left out. co:op classifies paths by their spelling. It doesn't check where symlinks lead, decide whether access is allowed or guess missing paths from tool titles or shell commands. A later tool update can add paths to the completion event without changing the start event. co:op extracts paths before shortening large diffs into previews. It marks URI-shaped paths as unknown and doesn't treat them as checkout files. Before forwarding an event, the connector checks the path fields again, drops entries it can't verify and marks the context partial. It also applies the size limits and secret scan described under Events to titles and inputs. provider.backoff reports a confirmed provider rate limit. co:op sends at most one such event for each configured model target in a turn. attempt numbers the events from 1 within the turn. target identifies the model target that reached its rate limit. retry_after_seconds says how long that target must wait. co:op uses the provider's reset time when available, or its own limited backoff otherwise. If co:op switches to another target, the event includes next_target. If every target is limited, the last backoff includes all_limited_until instead. Use these events to tell a turn waiting for a rate limit from one that has stopped responding. Waiting can still be expected progress, so silence alone isn't a reason to cancel the turn. provider.alive confirms that the worker is still receiving data. It helps when the provider CLI retries a rate limit internally: co:op's model selection never sees that limit, so it can't send a backoff event, and the CLI may keep sending ACP frames with no tool calls or other activity events. frames and bytes count all ACP frames received for the current turn's prompt. Compare these cumulative counts, not the timestamp, to tell new activity from a repeated event. last_kind identifies the latest frame as its JSON-RPC method, a session-update type after a colon, or response, and contains no frame content. Repeated events with the same kind tell you what the provider is still sending. co:op sends this event at most once per minute, and only when it hasn't already reported other activity in that interval. If the provider sends no frames, there's no event, so your client still needs a timeout for turns that go completely silent. A turn fails with acp_quiet if the model sends nothing for 15 minutes after its tools have answered. Only the model's text, thoughts, plans and tool calls count as output, and liveness events don't. This timeout doesn't apply before the first tool finishes or while a tool is running. The error reports the silent duration and the provider's last frame kind. You may retry the turn, because this error reports a silent model and not a failed project task. If the ACP process exits before returning an answer, the turn fails with acp_process_error. The detail includes its exit status or signal and a summary of stderr: line and byte counts, a digest for grouping similar failures, and fixed categories such as rate limit, authentication, network or crash. co:op masks digits and hexadecimal runs before it calculates the digest. The stderr text itself never leaves co:op.

heading: Budget
text: Extend a session's turn budget: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:extend:01J...' \ -d '{"expected_revision":9,"additional_turns":20}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../budget You can extend the turn budget only up to co:op's global max_turns limit. Your controller must decide who may authorize an extension and how much to spend. co:op enforces the numeric limit and prevents the same request from being applied twice.

heading: Changes
text: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../changes GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/changes returns: the immutable base_commit, the current fork_head and fork_tree, and the current parent_head the fixed admitted_source_tree, for a repository-backed session with a source binding paths classified as committed, staged, unstaged, untracked or conflicted ahead and behind counts, and base-to-head divergence counts a page of the binary patch, with a size limit patch_digest, the exact patch_bytes, patch_offset, patch_next_offset and patch_has_more Compare admitted_source_tree with the current tree to distinguish changed content from empty commits or changes that were committed and later reverted. To fetch the next patch page, call GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/changes?patch_offset=<next>&patch_limit=<bytes>. patch_limit can't exceed the job's max_patch_bytes, and offsets can't exceed 1 GiB. Check patch_digest as you page through the result. If it changes, start again at offset zero so you don't combine pages from different patches. The truncated field is true whenever the response contains less than the complete patch. The JSON response encodes patch, path_bytes and old_path_bytes as base64. patch_bytes is an integer giving the complete patch's size. A valid UTF-8 filename also appears in path. Filenames containing arbitrary bytes are preserved in path_bytes. If Git fails, the endpoint returns an error, never an empty change list.

heading: Network
text: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../network curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../network/connections curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../network/explanations/<event_id> curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../network/receipt These four endpoints only read data. They don't probe a gateway or approve, grant or expand network access, and the session API can't grant network permissions. GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network returns: the session's fixed mode and fingerprint the requested and effective rule texts current: the newest run's saved observation summary, or {"status":"no run yet"} an alerts list with a size limit GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network/receipt combines the records for all of the session's runs into one versioned report. It tracks finality separately from completeness. The report becomes final only after the session is closed and every run's record is final. A final report can still be partial if some evidence is missing. The worker saves these records in the owner's registry, so both endpoints keep working after container cleanup. A session that never used filtered networking returns {"available":false,"reason":"..."} instead of an empty record. GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network/connections returns the collector's live connection records for the newest run, with a row limit. The response includes status to describe freshness, using the same values as the summary, plus as_of and detail_truncated. Before the first run, the endpoint returns {"status":"no run yet","connections":[]}. GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network/explanations/{event_id} returns one saved refusal from this session's runs. It includes the event, the reason, where the evidence came from and whether co:op drafted a proposed rule. Each run keeps a limited number of events. If the requested event has aged out, the endpoint returns {"available":false,"reason": "event_not_retained"}, which doesn't mean the event never existed. projection states what the response discloses. It is destinations-withheld unless the session job set egress.export_destinations: true. With that setting, it is destinations-included, and the response includes rule texts and observed names. The daemon controls this disclosure. The connector forwards each answer unchanged and can't choose different destinations, rules or disclosure settings. Method Path Body/query GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network none GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network/connections none GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network/explanations/{event_id} none GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/network/receipt none

heading: Session evidence
text: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../evidence This endpoint returns a versioned, size-limited report for a controller's session-inspection page. It covers: the network settings approved for the session activity observed during its newest run the combined network record for all its runs the approved task assigned to its workspace, read from the current task folder The endpoint reads saved evidence without probing a gateway or starting a runtime. It can't grant additional access and accepts no query parameters, so callers can't change what it discloses. The daemon checks the report against its format and disclosure rules before sending it. If the report fails that check, the endpoint returns 500 internal_error instead. Each section reports whether its data was available, so you can tell a failed read from a successful read that found no activity: Section Status words network.access captured, not_filtered, unavailable network.observation observed, no_run, not_filtered, unavailable network.receipt available, not_filtered, unavailable task bound, unbound, unavailable task.snapshot.state_note captured, absent, withheld An unavailable section includes a reason. A session that never ran filtered reports not_filtered. The network settings (mode, fingerprint) come from the saved session record and can't change. If the host can't read the network registry, those settings stay available while the affected sections report that they couldn't be read. Before its first run, a filtered session reports no_run and a provisional receipt with run_count 0, not an empty activity counter. Counters are unsigned decimal strings so JavaScript clients can preserve values above 2^53 without rounding them. A null counter means the metric was not measured, never that it was 0. Each response list has a size limit, and the report counts omitted entries in omitted_denials, omitted_connections, omitted_alerts and omitted_run_references. The report follows the network endpoints' projection setting. Destination names appear only with destinations-included. When a name is withheld, the refusal includes destination_withheld, so callers can distinguish a hidden name from a missing one. task includes the fixed task identity saved for the session and a snapshot of its folder at the time the report is captured: its state the same state_sha256 used for the task data in a workspace checkpoint the checklist labels that match the checkpoint's completion flags a list of files and their digests the agent-written state.md The state.md note has a size limit and is withheld in full if the scan flags a likely secret. The worker keeps the current snapshot, not a history of task transitions, so save successive snapshots if your controller needs that history. If a bound task's folder is missing, the report returns unavailable and keeps the task's identity instead of returning an empty task. Method Path Body/query GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/evidence none

heading: Review
text: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:review:01J...' \ -d '{"expected_revision":12,"commit_message":"Add per-worker memory metrics"}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../review Use the optional commit_message to set the reviewed commit's message, up to 4,096 bytes. If you omit it, co:op uses Reviewed changes. It also adds the Coop-Review: <operation id> trailer. The message is saved in the reviewed commit and stays the same when that commit is published. You can review a session only when all of these are true: It is parked. It is open or exhausted. It has no queued turns. Its fork is clean and committed. co:op records the exact source and parent commits and trees, then prepares a temporary candidate based on the current parent HEAD. It runs the saved job's check against that candidate and returns: the creation base, source, parent and candidate commit and tree identities the saved PR number, ref and head, when the session came from an existing PR the rebase and check results, including the startup error text in gate_error if startup failed gate_output: the check command, its exit_code if it returned one, the number of saved output bytes and whether all output was kept (complete confirms it was, incomplete explains what is missing, and lost means no output was kept) policy findings, with a size limit a size-limited inline preview of the patch from the parent tree to the candidate tree patch_truncated, candidate_retained, publishable and stable not-publishable reason codes The saved job's check.argv is the only remote review command. The worker's COOP_GATE, the parent's gate: and candidate changes can't replace it. The first two still apply to ordinary local fork merges. The check runs in an isolated container using the session's saved network mode and, for filtered runs, the exact saved network permissions. It ignores the repository's box: settings and the worker's runtime arguments, environment file and MCP configuration. It uses the saved work environment plus check-only overrides, with the same CPU, memory and process limits as model turns. It also applies the candidate's review: settings. Where the job and review.env set the same variable, the job's value wins. Project defaults in runtime.environment apply below review.env. The check uses the same granted project toolchain or worker-configured image as the turns. Without a project runtime, it continues to use the worker-configured image, or locked filtered client image. The check can create ignored build files in its temporary checkout. If it changes the reviewed source, the result can't be published. Publication is also blocked when no check is configured, or when the check fails or can't start. When your controller authorizes publication, the change may edit CI workflows. Running repository checks is part of the authorized task and doesn't need a separate human approval. The scan still checks workflow contents for credentials and refuses files hidden from the box, changed .coopignore files, automatic local hooks and new package installation scripts. A hook nested under .github/workflows/ still counts as a local execution finding. Local fork merges keep their own protections. Publication still needs a fresh controller grant for the exact saved candidate and destination, and repository CI permissions and environment protections also apply. The JSON response encodes the patch preview as base64. A shortened preview doesn't prevent publication, because co:op saves the exact candidate commit and verified LFS objects in private host storage, separate from the model's workspace. For the same saved inputs, co:op creates the same single candidate commit on the reviewed parent, before running the check. source_head records the model's original commit before that candidate was prepared. co:op scans the changes between the parent and candidate for secrets, including large files, binary Git objects and LFS files. If LFS attributes changed, it also scans the resulting LFS files. If any content can't be read, review fails, because co:op doesn't assume that unreadable content is safe. publishable tells you whether this exact candidate passed the requirements for publication. It doesn't grant permission to push or merge. It is false when there is: a conflict no configured check, or a check that failed a startup failure findings from policy checks a changed parent or source a remaining fork-worker record, even if its process has exited no changes to publish candidate_retained tells you whether co:op saved the exact candidate, which it can do even if the check is missing or fails. Saving it doesn't authorize publication. To publish, use the saved candidate_head unchanged, get a separate controller grant and update the destination ref only if it still matches the expected value. Never reconstruct the result from a patch or the model's later workspace. Discarding a session deletes its saved candidates, so keep sessions whose reviewed changes still need to be published. A review can continue after the requesting connection ends. Once its operation succeeds, fetch GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/reviews/{operation_id} for the saved operation and review response. This doesn't start or resume the check. The endpoint refuses requests for another session, an operation that isn't a review, or an unfinished review. policy_findings and not_publishable_reasons are always arrays, even when empty.

heading: Gate output
text: The review keeps the stdout and stderr of the gate (the check command) and co:op's startup messages as printed, whether the gate passes or fails. Read the output page by page with GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/reviews/{operation_id}/gate-output?cursor={cursor}, starting without a cursor: {"output":"1 test, 1 failure\n…","next_cursor":"1048576","bytes":1843200,"complete":true} Each page contains at most 1 MiB of output and ends at a character boundary. Invalid UTF-8 bytes appear as U+FFFD replacement characters. next_cursor is null on the last page. bytes reports the total amount of saved output. When complete: false, incomplete explains what is missing. co:op keeps at most the first 64 MiB. If no output was saved, the response is {"lost":"<why>"}. This can happen because no check ran, writing the output failed, or the session was discarded. Output can be read only through the session that owns the review, and discarding that session removes it.

heading: Publish a reviewed candidate
text: POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/reviews/{review_operation_id}/publish uses a new Idempotency-Key and this JSON body: { "authorization_ref": "approval:42", "candidate_head": "<exact reviewed commit>", "candidate_tree": "<exact reviewed tree>", "branch": "automation/fix", "base_branch": "main", "expected_head": "", "pull_request_number": 0, "title": "Fix retry handling", "body": "Reviewed changes and verification details." } Leave expected_head empty to require a new branch. To update a previously authorized PR, provide its number and the exact commit you expect it to point to. The operation returns 202 while running. Use the operation key to check its state, then fetch GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/publications/{operation_id} for the completed operation and publication response. Retry with the same key and identical request. The result is one of: published, with the exact commit, tree and PR result conflict, with the verified existing PR and its observed remote head refused, with a stable error code The worker requests fresh credentials from your authenticated controller at POST /v1/coop-workers/jobs/{job_ref}/publication-grants. The request identifies the session, job digest, review operation, original command key, repository and exact publication request. Your controller returns that same repository identity, a token, its expires_at time and the GitHub App's actor_id. Your controller decides whether publication is approved. co:op doesn't require a product-specific approval format. A 403 permanently refuses this operation. Temporary failures can be retried. The worker sends Git and LFS data directly from the saved candidate to GitHub, and creates a draft PR or updates the exact existing PR owned by the App. If a person has already marked that PR ready for review, co:op preserves that choice. If a push or PR response is lost, co:op checks the remote result before retrying. A candidate can't be discarded while publication is active. Later edits in the model workspace can't change what gets published.

heading: Close and discard
text: Close a session: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:close:01J...' \ -d '{"expected_revision":15}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../close You can close a session only when it has no active or queued turns. Closing keeps the fork. Plan a discard only after you close the session: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:discard-plan:01J...' \ -d '{"expected_revision":16}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../discard-plan The discard plan records the session revision, the specific fork instance and its reservation, and the workspace's inode, branch, head, status digest and running, dirty and unmerged states. The inode helps detect a replaced directory, but doesn't prove ownership on its own. By default, co:op refuses to discard uncommitted or unmerged work. If your controller has separate permission to destroy that work, set accept_dirty, accept_unmerged or both when creating the plan. Execute that exact plan: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:discard:01J...' \ -d '{"plan_operation_id":"op_..."}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../discard Discard first checks that the plan belongs to the session named in the request path, then compares the current workspace with every recorded detail in the plan. If the plan is stale, the workspace was replaced or work is running, nothing is deleted. Otherwise, co:op deletes the fork workspace and private ACP state, and saves a record that the session was discarded. At startup, the daemon blocks sessions whose workspace ownership it can't verify. This includes old session records without a store-owner binding, v1 reservations, and sessions whose fork record or workspace is missing. It also blocks a stored session this build no longer reads: one with no saved job, no execution or network mode, or one created in the removed readonly or bare mode. The log names the session. These sessions are quarantined: you can't create or apply a discard plan for them because co:op can't prove it owns the workspace. You can retire the session record instead: curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: controller:retire:01J...' \ -d '{"retire_quarantined":true,"expected_revision":16}' \ http://localhost/v1/sessions/remote_.../discard This marks the session record as retired without deleting its workspace: Queued turns are marked exhausted. A turn that was active when the daemon lost ownership remains in history without changes. The workspace, fork reservation, sidecar services and provider's ACP history are kept. A session that isn't quarantined is refused with invalid_session_state. Retiring a record doesn't show that its runtime has stopped. Separately, the daemon looks for boxes with the exact coop.run labels derived from the store's session and turn IDs, and removes matching boxes and temporary credential files in its private ACP state. If a check fails or finishes only partly, the daemon retries and reports busy until cleanup is fully verified. These checks continue after a restart. Once runtime cleanup is verified, the worker can report free capacity again. It doesn't take ownership of or delete the unowned workspace. Quarantined sessions still can't run and need explicit retirement or recovery. If capacity stays busy, inspect the worker's runtime-cleanup warning.

heading: Errors
text: Every error has one shape: { "error": { "code": "revision_conflict", "detail": "expected revision 4, current revision 5", "operation_id": "op_..." } } The error includes operation_id when co:op accepted an operation before it failed. The public API leaves out private internal details. The daemon also writes a size-limited JSON diagnostic to stderr, with the operation ID, method, resource identity, error code and a detail with sensitive information removed: repository and state-directory paths are replaced, and lines containing secrets are removed. Use the operation ID to connect the client error, saved operation and supervisor log without opening SQLite directly. Common status mapping: HTTP Meaning 400 Invalid request, or a field exceeds its allowed limit 404 Session, turn or operation not found 409 Idempotency, operation fence, revision, state, queue, budget, resume, uncertainty or discard conflict 413 Ordinary request body exceeds 128 KiB, or turn submission exceeds 12 MiB 500 Internal failure. co:op leaves host paths and raw internal errors out of the response. 503 The worker is not ready, or it temporarily can't verify or use the required repository, runtime, network or storage access storage_unavailable is a retryable 503. The worker has reached its configured disk-space limits and won't create another workspace until space is freed. If storage.refusal_reason is protected_storage_exceeds_budget, you must reduce the protected data itself before the worker can accept new workspaces. Read /v1/storage to see what is using space and why it is kept. Place the session on another worker or free storage through the appropriate cleanup process. Don't retry in a tight loop or delete protected workspaces just to meet the limit. network_unavailable is a 503. The worker can't enforce, or verify that it can enforce, the session's saved network permissions. Check its container runtime and network setup. The worker stops execution instead of falling back to open networking. Don't change a saved job to bypass the refusal. For operation_uncertain or turn.interrupted, inspect the saved operation and resulting session state to find out what happened. An unknown result isn't a reason to submit the same action with a new key: that could run it twice. RunReview is a limited exception because it only reviews a fixed candidate. Once co:op has saved the exact source, parent and job, repeating the request with the same key resumes that review under its original operation ID. It doesn't reread a moving branch to choose a new candidate. If the saved instructions can't be read or verified, the operation remains operation_uncertain.

heading: Operational recovery
text: Situation Action Client response lost Replay the exact mutation with the same idempotency key Permission is withdrawn while a prepared create or submit may be arriving Fence the exact operation. If it was already accepted, close or cancel the resulting work. Socket reconnect Resume event polling after the last sequence your controller saved as processed Daemon already owns state Stop or inspect that daemon. Don't remove the lock. Stale socket after crash Start the daemon with the same state directory. It acquires the state lock before removing the stale socket. Queued turn at restart co:op resumes queued turns in the order received Running session create at restart co:op resumes creation automatically from the saved request Reserved operation at restart co:op records that the operation was interrupted before acceptance. It hadn't attempted any external action. Running checkpoint restore at restart Resume from the saved request body while model work remains blocked. Never submit a new key. Other running operation at restart co:op marks it operation_uncertain. Inspect what happened before deciding what to do. Don't resubmit it under a new key. Operation remains running after startup The background watchdog resumes creates that are safe to retry. It marks stale operations uncertain when it can't determine their outcome. Turn interrupted after co:op recorded its intent to send it Report that the turn was interrupted. Don't submit the same user input automatically. Active turn must stop Cancel it with an idempotency key, then read the turn to confirm how it ended Session should stop using runtime resources Wait until it is parked, then close it if it is warm. co:op removes containers after each non-warm turn, or when a warm session times out or closes. If cleanup fails, it retries in the background. A parked state alone doesn't prove cleanup finished. Incident is over Close the session and keep its fork for review, or discard it explicitly later New co:op build for the worker Stop the worker and run coop sessions check with the new build before you swap it in. See Upgrading a worker. Review patch preview is truncated This response has no further patch pages. Don't treat a shortened preview as a complete diff. Publication uses the saved reviewed candidate, never a patch rebuilt from the preview. Stop the daemon before backing up the entire state directory. If you restore a database without its matching forks, an operator must resolve the mismatch. co:op won't assign ownership based only on directory names.

heading: Consumer responsibilities
text: When building a production controller, you are responsible for: deciding who can connect and which actions they may authorize reliably saving and delivering incoming and outgoing messages without processing duplicates assigning stable, globally unique idempotency keys saving event cursors and checking operations whose outcomes are uncertain preparing prompts and removing sensitive output before sending it through your chosen transport setting retention, audit, capacity and spending policies approving GitHub publication and supplying short-lived credentials for the authorized repository scanning for secrets before data leaves the host supervising the worker and providing a way to stop it Never put chat-service tokens, GitHub credentials, Emisar administrative credentials or other credentials that authorize publication into a co:op prompt or box.

heading: Migrating
text: What to change when you upgrade co:op, newest version first. Follow the steps for each version since yours. Upgrade notes for v7 and earlier are in the v12.1.0 copy of this file: git show v12.1.0:MIGRATING.md.

heading: Unreleased: old host state is refused or read as unknown
text: Coop no longer reads these records of builds up to v12.1.0. None is changed or deleted. A box left behind with a version 1 coop.host label. coop doctor lists it as a box coop cannot attribute. Remove it by hand: docker rm -f <name> (and docker volume rm for a run's volumes) once you know its coop is gone. A record with a linux-proc-v1: start token (a fork .pid file, a task claim, a network run record or a label written by a Linux Coop that could not read its PID namespace). It counts as unverifiable, so the record stays and its owner is never judged gone. Remove it by hand if you know the process is gone. A filesystem custody record in ~/.local/state/coop/filesystem/coop-fs-* that has an Image and no Controller. Written only by main builds of 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-02. The message "filesystem custody record from before the shared filesystem controller" names it. Its protection keeps holding. Run Coop v12.1.0 in the project: its daily sweep retires a record whose owner is gone. Then come back. A credential renewal journal without received_at (credentials/<account>/renewal.json, kept by Coop v11.3.0 or earlier). The message says it was kept without an arrival time. Open the account once with Coop v12.1.0 to finish it, or run coop login <agent>@<account>. Version 4 service approvals grant nothing and are not read. coop up shows the review again.

heading: Unreleased: old session store data is refused by name
text: Coop no longer converts session data below schema 26 and no longer reads a few old session shapes. Nothing is deleted: the data is refused or quarantined until you act. A turn that was running when the worker stopped is still marked interrupted, as before. Stop the worker or service, then run coop sessions check --state <path> with the new build. Exit 0 means the data is current. Exit 4 with "session schema N is older than this coop build supports" means the store needs the converting build first. For a store below schema 26, back up the stopped state folder, open it once with a Coop build at or before commit 29133b0e (it converts to schema 26 on start), stop it, then use the new build. For a stored session that the log names as quarantined (no saved job, a blank mode, or the removed readonly or bare mode), either retire its record with {"retire_quarantined": true, "expected_revision": N} on /v1/sessions/{id}/discard, or cancel, close and discard it with a build at or before commit 29133b0e before you upgrade. A read-only fork that the error says has no primary snapshot receipt: discard its session with a build at or before commit 29133b0e, then upgrade.

heading: Unreleased: old network records are refused by name
text: Coop no longer reads network approvals, withdrawals and run records written by Coop v11.3.0 and earlier. If your network folder (~/.local/state/coop/network) still holds any, a project they could belong to stops with a message that names each file. A withdrawal still keeps its project closed. For a project that still exists, run coop net forget --project <path>. It removes the old approval and withdrawal files, keeps the project closed, and coop approve there opens it again. If the project no longer exists, delete the files the message names from ~/.local/state/coop/network. Each name is approval-<64 hex digits>.json or withdrawn-<64 hex digits>.json; a matching project-<64 hex digits>-<32 hex digits>.anchor can go with them. A named execution-<32 hex digits>.json run record is not cleaned up by this Coop. Open the project once with Coop v12.1.0, which removes that run's leftovers, or delete the file if the run is long gone. Coop leaves these files on disk and changes none of them. A project they provably do not belong to starts as usual. Policy copies an old coop net setup check saved without a marker stay on disk, unused.

heading: Unreleased: logins and history from before v11 are not converted
text: Coop no longer moves a login out of profiles/<account> or host-credentials/<account>, and no longer imports history or editor thread bindings from the folders Coop before v11 used. Run coop login <agent>@<account> for every account that coop credentials shows as needing a new sign-in. The old folder stays where it is, untouched. A Coop-held API key (Gemini) is saved again the same way. To convert an account instead of signing in again, open it once with Coop v12.1.0 or earlier (for example coop credentials <agent> or starting a box with that account), then upgrade. A launch that says a history import "was started by an older Coop and never finished" needs the same: open that project once with Coop v12.1.0 or earlier, then upgrade. History and editor threads never imported stay in the old folders. They are not read, and a thread from before v11 reopens by its editor id only.

heading: Unreleased: old fork and task records are refused, not converted
text: co:op no longer converts the fork and task records that builds up to v12.1.0 could. It refuses them by name and leaves them as they are. Coop v12.1.0 is the last release that converts them. If coop fork ls or coop tasks names one of these records, open the project once with v12.1.0, then come back. Check before you upgrade; most installations have none. Fork generation records of version 1 or 2. The refusal says "version 1 generation record" or "version 2". Run coop fork stop <name>, then start the fork once with v12.1.0 (coop fork <name> <agent>). It anchors the fork as version 3. Version 1 workspace reservations. Every read of the project's reservations fails and the fork name stays blocked. Recover it offline, or end the remote session that made it with v12.1.0. Version 1 review candidates, and lands that lost their candidate record. Run the review or coop fork merge <name> once with v12.1.0. Version 1 task owner records (a coop tasks claim from v8.1.0 or earlier). Release the claim with v12.1.0: coop tasks release <id>. Version 1 pending final reviews, completion fingerprints without tree_format, and a completion window's allowed_done_departure. Finish the loop or review that left them with v12.1.0. owner-v1 worker records (<name>.pid, from v8.1.0 or earlier). coop fork stop <name> prints the steps that stop the worker and remove the file. Coop never edits a worker record. A discard interrupted by a build that let the fork take new work. The refusal says the fork "holds an assignment its interrupted discard did not journal". Finish it with v12.1.0: coop fork rm <name> --force. Execution records in ~/.local/state/coop/executions/v1/<key>/. Each is reported by path. If its process is gone, remove the file. Otherwise stop that process first. Fork records still in <project>-forks/.coop. Anything but lock files there is refused. Open the project once with v12.1.0 (any fork command), which moves them to ~/.local/state/coop/forks/<key>/. Nothing the new version refuses is changed, so v12.1.0 reads it as it always did.

heading: Unreleased: coop codex -p runs one prompt
text: coop codex -p <name> used to pick a Codex profile. It now runs <name> as a prompt, as -p does on every other agent. To pick a profile, use coop codex --profile <name>.

heading: Unreleased: boxes use filtered networking by default
text: Boxes now use filtered networking unless you choose another mode. An agent can reach its provider and the destinations you approved. A plain coop run or coop shell can reach only the destinations you approved. For unrestricted access, add --egress open to the command (in an editor, to the agent arguments), set COOP_EGRESS=open in your environment or coop.conf, or set box.egress: open in the project and approve it with coop approve. Installing .tool-versions tools when the box starts and starting .agent/compose.yml services automatically both need open networking. Run with --egress open, or build the tools into .agent/Dockerfile and start services with coop up. A project with its own .agent/Dockerfile and no box.egress needs one more coop build. After that, co:op rebuilds those files itself when its client image changes. Filtered project images have new names, so an existing filtered project also needs coop build once. coop update no longer builds new or changed files. Filtered networking needs Docker. On Apple's container, choose --egress open or --egress offline, or set COOP_EGRESS. The first filtered run on a host prepares the network images and checks the host, as coop net setup does.

heading: Unreleased: the no-network mode is called offline
text: The command line and COOP_EGRESS now say offline, as .agent/project.yaml already did. co:op refuses none with a message that names offline. Replace --egress none with --egress offline in scripts, aliases and editor agent settings (for example ["acp", "--egress", "offline"]). Replace COOP_EGRESS=none with COOP_EGRESS=offline in your environment and coop.conf. Controller JobSpec documents and the session API keep none for their offline mode.

heading: v12.0.0: network records are renamed
text: co:op now names each project's network records by the project's folder. Run coop net setup once. This release's new images already need it, and co:op no longer reads the old setup record. Run coop approve once in each project that uses filtered networking, and review its access again. Until you do, its runs stop with "coop renamed its network records". The review shows what changed since you last approved. To take a project's access back instead, run coop net forget. A project whose access you took back with coop net forget stays that way. Create a new session to replace each filtered worker session from before the upgrade. The old one can't find its saved network rules, and restarting the worker doesn't help. A filtered project with its own .agent/Dockerfile needs coop build --egress filtered once. Copies of launch network rules that earlier versions saved stay on disk, because co:op can't tell which sessions still use them. Copies made by coop net setup are the exception: co:op removes them with their check's run record.

heading: v12.0.0: fork records move into Coop's private folder
text: co:op now keeps each project's fork records in ~/.local/state/coop/forks/<key>/ instead of <project>-forks/.coop. Fork workspaces stay in <project>-forks/. Stop every co:op process that uses forks before you upgrade: fork loops, coop fork <name> acp sessions and the session service. The first command of the new version in a project moves its records, and an older process still running would keep writing to the old place, which the new version never reads. In each project that has forks, start a box or run coop fork ls once after upgrading. Do this before you start a box from a folder that holds several projects. Until a project's records move, a box that can write to that project's forks folder could change them. Forks need each fork's folder and your home folder on one disk. co:op refuses forks for a project on another disk (an external drive or a separate APFS volume) and names both folders. That project's old folder stays in place, so an older co:op can still use its forks. On a session worker, check before you upgrade that its state root (--state) is on the same disk as the worker's home folder, because its job forks live under the state root. To go back to an older co:op, move the folder back first: mv ~/.local/state/coop/forks/<key> <project>-forks/.coop. <key> is the SHA-256 of the project's real path: printf %s "$(cd <project> && pwd -P)" | shasum -a 256.

heading: v11.1.0: project image preparation
text: If you upgrade from v11.0.2 or earlier, run coop update --box-only once with the newly installed binary. The older updater keeps running in its old process after installation, so that first update can still build an ordinary image from the old definitions. When you start a provider interactively with filtered networking in a host terminal, co:op may also offer Build and continue. The default answer is No. Review the saved snapshot that the prompt shows, because a yes approves only those build files, not future edits. Headless commands, editor connections, loops and controller jobs don't get this prompt. Project builds still use ordinary networking, whatever network restrictions apply to the running box.

heading: v11.0.0: upgrading from v10.1.2
text: Coding and editor sessions now each use a complete native home for their repository: a folder with the provider's own history, settings and other files. An ordinary home also belongs to the selected account, while an editor home stays when you switch accounts. co:op copies native settings into a new home once, and after that they stay local to that home. The first time co:op uses a home, it imports only the older transcripts that it can prove belong to the repository, and leaves the originals as they are. It keeps history that's ambiguous or unsupported, and doesn't show it to another project. While older sessions are writing history, co:op postpones the import without stopping them, so finish them and retry. An old source can't silently bring back sessions you deleted natively. co:op moves account credentials into one main store that stays on the host, and retires the old credential sources only after it has saved the credentials in a form it can recover and has checked for other writers. It doesn't copy refresh grants into repository homes, and the host renews them. Online provider runs now require Docker, including open-network runs. Raw workloads without credentials can still use Apple's container runtime. To sign in, run coop login <provider>@<account> on the host. To remove an account, run coop credentials <provider> <account> rm, which asks you to confirm. Removal deletes that account's ordinary repository histories, but not editor conversations. Logging in or out with the native client inside a box isn't a supported way to manage the shared account. If it changes local credential files, co:op refuses to reuse that home, and its error names the native home and the home's recovery directory, labeled "recovery custody". To recover: Stop the sessions that use that home. Back up the entire recovery directory, including home/, owner.json, auth and import receipts. To recover credentials that were created locally, sign in explicitly on the host. Restore public auth files from a known-good backup, or explicitly move the entire backed-up recovery directory aside to start fresh. If you move only home/, the ownership receipts stay behind and co:op refuses to start. Keep the backup. A fresh home doesn't prove that the old home's unique history has been recovered. Before you upgrade an existing installation, finish older sessions and keep a verified backup of its stopped credential and history roots. After co:op moves the credentials, don't run older binaries against those roots. A rollback must use the current stored credentials or a fresh sign-in on the host, because restoring tokens from before a refresh can invalidate the account access you have left. Old binaries and native clients on the host don't take part in co:op's checks for other writers.

heading: v10.1.2: upgrading from v8.1.0
text: These steps cover the changes since v8.1.0. Do the ones that apply to you before you use the new binary to start workers, fork loops or sessions with MCP.

heading: Controller-owned workers and session schema 25
text: A worker now connects with one command: coop sessions connect --controller https://controller.example --token-file /private/enrollment-token Before you run it against an existing root, prepare that root: Stop the connection or service that owns it. Back it up. Use the old binary's sessions compact --backup <path> when it's available, or a verified copy of the stopped root. When the new service opens the state, it upgrades the SQLite schema to 25. An older binary can't reopen the upgraded root, so keep the backup and the old binary for rollback. Use --state <path> for a separate private worker root, and --ca-file <path> for a private controller CA. The connection owns its local service: it refuses a root that's already listening, and never reuses or replaces it. coop worker, sessions serve, sessions policies and connect --config are gone, and there's no worker JSON file or local execution-policy catalog to translate. Controllers must send worker protocol v2 and canonical version-2 JobSpec documents, and select workers that advertise live job-setup:2. Each job freezes its setup: source and companions, targets, mode, networking, explicit environment, check.argv and check.environment values, and positive CPU, memory and PID caps. Work and review use the same frozen setup, and check-only environment values override work values. Resolve repository defaults before you submit a job, because worker COOP_GATE and repository gate: no longer choose controller reviews. The session API lists the fields, limits and digest requirements. You can still read older jobs. A job without the current setup can't run new turns or reviews, and can't finish a session creation that was interrupted. For each of those jobs: Preserve the work and history you need. Where you can, finish, close or discard it through the supported old workflow. Resubmit unfinished work as a new v2 job. Never edit saved documents or create your own permission records to make an old record run. Sign in to the provider accounts on each worker with co:op's normal login flow. Controllers don't transfer model credentials.

heading: Anchored fork and network identity
text: co:op no longer identifies a fork or an approved project by directory metadata, because Linux overlay filesystems can reuse all of it, including the inode and birth time, right after a deletion. Fork generations and project network approvals now use a filesystem anchor: two hardlinks to one file. A fork has a .coop-fork-generation file, linked to a file in the fork state beside it. A reviewed project has a .coop-network-approval file, linked to a file in co:op's network state. Only the owner can access the fork state and the network state, and the visible files hold identifiers and no credentials. Whenever co:op uses an anchor, both names must still be the same owner-controlled 0600 inode with exactly two links. The two names must be on one filesystem that supports hardlinks. Fork state sits next to its workspace, so for forks this is normally automatic. For network approvals, keep the checkout and $XDG_STATE_HOME (or the default ~/.local/state) on the same filesystem. If co:op can't create the link, it reports a clear error and doesn't fall back to timestamps. co:op migrates a stopped v1/v2 fork record to a hardlink anchor only when all of these are true: Its Git branch and absolute local origin still match. It has no execution record and no unfinished merge. It has no reservation. co:op never guesses ownership from a missing or foreign reservation, or from a live execution. It quarantines a remote session with an old reservation, and Canonical tasks across isolated forks says what to do with it. If a legacy fork is still active, stop it and retry. Older network approvals grant nothing under the new binary. Run coop approve once to review and enroll the current project. Task records and remote-session discard plans keep their format. Ordinary Git status doesn't show the markers, but a manual git clean -x can still remove them. To repair a damaged project approval: Inspect it with ls -l -- ./.coop-network-approval. Once you've verified that the damaged name is stale, run rm -- ./.coop-network-approval. Run coop approve. If you move an intact checkout to a new path, run only coop approve. co:op verifies and retires the old pair before it enrolls the new path. Copying the marker's bytes never transfers access, and never retires the original project's anchor. To repair a damaged fork marker: Preserve any Git work, task notes or other data you need. Remove the fork and its anchor with the normal coop fork rm <name> --force flow, which asks you to confirm. This permanently deletes the fork's unmerged work and service volumes, so inspect the deletion preview before you confirm. Recreate the fork. Don't remove only .coop-fork-generation, because the generation record and the private link must retire together. When an anchor exists, runtime arguments may mount the exact project. They may not mount: a path inside the project that an existing agent could swap before the runtime resolves the bind a writable folder above the project that could replace it No mount may expose co:op's private anchor, execution-record or launch-lock state, even read-only. That includes paths the first approval or fork will create. co:op refuses --volumes-from, whose sources it can't inspect, and custom volume drivers. It inspects existing named volumes before launch. To mount a cache, put it outside the checkout and name its path explicitly, so co:op can inspect it. Saved service-file approvals from earlier formats, including the first repository-scoped format, no longer grant access. Run coop up at a terminal to review eligible read-only secret files again. You can't approve secret directories or writable binds. An external or custom-named Docker volume now also needs an explicit review at a terminal. Automatic, filtered and non-terminal starts refuse such a volume and stop, even after approval. Your approval applies only to the selected Docker daemon and the inspected plain-local volume object, so switching the daemon or replacing a volume needs another review. The approval belongs to the repository's .coop-service-approval marker and a private hardlink in co:op state. Keep both on one filesystem. Copying the marker into another checkout doesn't copy the approval. Inspect a damaged marker before you remove it and review again. co:op now refuses sidecar repository binds that use SELinux relabel or propagation options. Remove those options before you retry. A read-only session also requires its bind source to exist already, because Compose's short syntax would otherwise create a directory on the host.

heading: Canonical tasks across isolated forks
text: Fork loops now take their tasks from the project's canonical task queue instead of copying a complete .agent/tasks tree into each fork, and coop tasks split is retired. Before you upgrade: Stop every detached fork loop with the co:op version that started it. Inspect each fork's Git work and copied task folders. Preserve any fork-only notes, decisions, artifacts or unfinished changes before you start the new loop. The new controller won't choose which of two copied folders is correct. The first new loop on a fork refuses to start while that workspace still has tasks under its own .agent/tasks, including configured subproject queues. Review and reconcile those copies, then recreate the fork with coop fork <name> <target> --fresh --loop. Add --force only after you've reviewed any unmerged Git work and decided to discard it. co:op doesn't import or delete old .agent/tasks.sliceN directories in the canonical checkout. Turn work that's really separate into canonical tasks yourself, and archive the old slice only after you've verified that every note and change has a home. After you migrate, start any number of forks against the same queue: coop fork perf codex --loop -d coop fork docs claude --loop -d coop tasks watch --tasks <path> now selects a canonical queue, not a place to copy tasks to. The host gives each fork one assignment, which survives a stop or a crash, and shows the fork only that task in .coop/task-executions/. The canonical task completes only when the exact candidate reviewed for that fork generation lands through coop fork merge. Don't run an older worker that uses a copied queue beside the new scheduler. Current detached workers use owner-v2 state, which records a fork generation that can't change. An owner-v1 worker can't claim current task work or attach to a replacement workspace, and co:op reads its state only to handle an older worker that's stopped or waiting for cleanup. Never edit a pidfile to add a generation. Stop the old worker, let co:op bind a fresh generation, and restart it. Remote sessions created before their fork generation was saved need the same care. Before you upgrade, finish or discard them with the version that created them, and preserve any Git work you want to keep. On first start, the new co:op quarantines the record of each such session. Its session and turn history stays readable, but co:op doesn't run turns, inspect or review the workspace, clean its runtime or services, close it or discard it. This keeps a deleted and recreated fork with the same name from being mistaken for the old session. For a quarantined session: Inspect and preserve the quarantined workspace directly. Create a new remote session. Never fabricate a generation or reservation file to make the old record attach. When you're done with the record, retire it. POST /v1/sessions/<id>/discard with {"retire_quarantined":true,"expected_revision":<n>} marks the record as retired and leaves the workspace to you. The same applies to a session that co:op quarantines later because its workspace vanished.

heading: Strict coop.conf, one removal verb and supported runtimes
text: co:op validates coop.conf on every command. An unknown key, a duplicate key, a malformed line or a retired key stops co:op before any work, and the error names the file and line. Replace the retired loop settings with their .agent/loop.yaml fields: Retired coop.conf key .agent/loop.yaml field COOP_LOOP_MODEL work.agent COOP_REVIEW_MODEL signoff.agent COOP_MAX_REVIEW_ROUNDS signoff.rounds COOP_LOOP_CMD work.command COOP_PREFLIGHT preflight.enabled Remove COOP_AGENT_PACKAGES, because images that co:op manages use locked client versions. If you need different tooling, review a custom image and select it explicitly. Project networking uses box.egress: offline instead of none, so update .agent/project.yaml. Controller JobSpec documents still use none for their offline mode. Restricted project images need an explicit build. Review the project's build inputs, then run coop build --egress filtered before you reuse that image under filtered networking. Old automatic build records don't allow that reuse. Removal and privacy flags now have explicit names. Replace these commands and flags: Retired Use coop down -v or --volumes coop down --delete-volumes (still deletes stored service data) coop net export --include-destinations --include-addresses (still exposes hostnames/IPs) coop tasks clear coop tasks rm --all-done coop net approve coop approve coop net explain coop net blocked coop tasks flags is gone, with no replacement. No tagged release shipped it. A flags.json that an untagged build left in a task folder does nothing now, and co:op leaves it in place. On a machine with both Docker and Apple container installed, automatic runtime detection now picks Docker, where it used to pick container.
